k.f: Then there are no people either, including the one holding the view. Exceptions for living things look like special pleading.
k.m: Some nihilists accept that. Others say the rule has to be the same everywhere, and “sometimes, when it feels like a thing” isn’t a rule.

k.f: Then there’s no philosopher, no paper and no journal. The view has been published by nothing in nothing.
k.m: Published by particles arranged publisherwise. They do good work.

k.f: If nothing is made of parts, neither is the argument, and it needs all three of its premises.
k.m: Three premises arranged argumentwise. It’s still valid.

k.f: A theory that says nearly every ordinary statement is strictly false needs the “loosely true” story to do all the work, and it rarely gets spelled out.
k.m: The story is short: “there’s a table” is assertible when things are arranged that way. It’s the same move as “the sun rose.”

k.f: “Loosely true” is “true.” He’s charging extra for an adverb.
k.m: “The sun rose” is loosely true. You pay for that adverb every morning and don’t complain.

k.f: “There’s a table” is false but fine to say. So is everything else he says.
k.m: So is “the sun came up.” You manage.

k.f: It removes the puzzle by removing the ship, which is like curing a headache by denying there’s a head.
k.m: It shows the puzzle was about our conventions for the word “ship.” Which planks are where was never in doubt.

k.f: It solves it the way burning the boat solves it.
k.m: Nobody’s confused about the wood. Burn the puzzle and the boat’s fine.

k.f: Asked which ship is the original, the nihilist says “what ship,” and thinks that’s a move.
k.m: It’s the only answer on which nobody at the dock is wrong about anything.

k.f: Hempel’s dilemma: defined by today’s physics the thesis is false, and defined by some ideal future physics it’s close to empty.
k.m: Take “physical” to mean not fundamentally mental. That isn’t tied to today’s physics and it isn’t empty: it rules out souls and basic experience, which is what the argument is about.

k.f: Physics changes every fifty years, so “physical” changes with it. A theory that says everything is whatever the next textbook says is a subscription.
k.m: The periodic table got revised too, and chemistry isn’t a subscription to nothing. Updating is what being about the world looks like.

k.f: “Physical” just means whatever physics says next year. So physicalism is the view that everything is whatever.
k.m: Whatever physics says, yes. As opposed to whatever you’d like.

k.f: Correlation, and even identity, leave the explanatory gap. Nothing in the neural story shows why this activity comes with experience and not with none.
k.m: A gap in explanation isn’t a gap in nature. “Water” can’t be deduced from H2O without knowing how the two concepts connect, and nobody thinks water is something extra.

k.f: A radio’s music changes when the circuits are damaged, and nobody thinks the band lives in the radio.
k.m: Break a radio and the station still plays on every other radio. Break a brain and that person plays nowhere.

k.f: A physicalist looks at a brain scan of someone in love and thinks the scan is the love.
k.m: The scan is a picture of it, like a wedding photo. Nobody thinks the photo is the marriage, or that the marriage is a ghost.

k.f: A promise isn’t an argument. Past reductions explained structure and function, and the dispute is whether experience is exhausted by those.
k.m: It’s an induction, not a promise: every earlier “science can never explain this” gave way. The burden is on showing this one differs in kind, and the case for that is an intuition.

k.f: They’ve had 150 years and every brain ever made to look at. At some point “eventually” is the result.
k.m: Fermat’s last theorem took 358 years. It was a theorem the whole time.

k.f: Physicalists have been twenty years from explaining consciousness since 1950.
k.m: Dualists have been zero years from explaining it since 1641, and still are.

t.t: “Mary learns no new fact, only an ability”

k.f: The ability reply seems to leave something out: on seeing red she appears to learn that this is what the others were having, and that’s a fact.
k.m: She learns an old fact under a new concept, one that can only be had by having the experience. New way of knowing, same fact.

k.f: If knowing all the physics were knowing everything, physicists wouldn’t go to concerts. They’d read the score and stay home.
k.m: Physicists go to concerts for the reason they eat dinner instead of reading the menu. Knowing about isn’t having. Nobody said it was.

k.f: Physicalism means the experience of red is a voltage. Okay.
k.m: And a symphony is air pressure. Okay?

k.f: Closure is a generalization from cases where consciousness wasn’t in question. Using it against non-physical minds assumes the thing at issue.
k.m: It’s inductive. Every time a bodily movement has been traced back, the causes were physical. Minds would be the one exception, located in the one place we haven’t finished looking.

k.f: Numbers aren’t physical, and bad math closes bridges all the time. So non-physical things cause plenty.
k.m: The bridge was closed by an engineer’s brain state about the math. Find one where the number did it alone.

k.f: Physicalism is a metaphysics for people who say they don’t do metaphysics.
k.m: It’s metaphysics for people who check.

t.t: “The mind can’t be reduced to the brain”

k.f: A mind that can’t be described in brain terms can still be nothing over and above the brain. Plenty of physicalists accept the premise and deny the conclusion.
k.m: That middle position has to say how the mental does anything when the physical already suffices. Many think it can’t, and that it’s dualism without the nerve.

k.f: Weather can’t be reduced to one molecule either, and nobody thinks storms are spirits. Well, some people do, and they’re also dualists.
k.m: A storm is nothing over its molecules, and there’s nothing it’s like to be one. There’s the difference, and it’s the whole topic.

k.f: Dualism is believing in ghosts, but only one, and it’s driving.
k.m: Somebody’s driving. You’re the one who says the car is empty.

t.t: “Zombies are conceivable, so physicalism is false”

k.f: Conceivable may not mean possible. Water without H2O was conceivable too, and the physicalist says the same about zombies.
k.m: Water without H2O is conceivable only because “water” is pinned down by how the stuff looks. For pain, how it feels is the thing itself, so the same reply has no gap to work in.

k.f: If zombies were possible, some people would be one, and they’d say exactly what dualists say. So the argument can’t rule out its own author.
k.m: I know I’m not one. That’s the one thing the argument starts from. You’re welcome to wonder about yourself.

k.f: Zombies are “conceivable.” So is a married bachelor if nobody thinks very hard.
k.m: Show the contradiction, then. A married bachelor has one. Go ahead.

k.f: Princess Elisabeth’s question to Descartes still stands: how does something with no size or energy move matter without breaking conservation laws?
k.m: Physical causation is brute at the bottom too: nobody explains why charge moves charge. And conservation holds for closed systems, which is the thing in dispute.

k.f: Anything that pushes a neuron shows up on an instrument. They’ve had instruments on neurons for a century and the soul has never tripped one.
k.m: Instruments register physical effects, and the effect is the neuron firing. They’ve registered that plenty.

k.f: Nobody has ever said where the soul gets the energy to push a neuron. Conservation of energy would like a word.
k.m: Conservation of energy would like a closed system. Whether this is one is the question.

k.f: If the physical world is causally closed, the extra properties do nothing, including causing anyone to talk about them.
k.m: Some accept that. Others deny closure at the smallest scale, or take experience to be what underlies the powers physics describes. The options aren’t used up.

k.f: A property is a way of describing a thing. Non-physical properties of a physical thing is like non-wet properties of water.
k.m: Water has properties chemistry never mentions, like being somebody’s favorite drink. Things have more properties than one science lists.

k.f: Property dualism is dualism for people who get embarrassed at parties.
k.m: Physicalism is behaviorism for people who got embarrassed about behaviorism.

t.t: “I can doubt my body but not my mind”

k.f: The inference fails for ordinary cases: Lois can doubt that Clark flies without doubting that Superman does, and they’re still one man.
k.m: The mature argument isn’t from doubt. It’s that I can clearly conceive of existing without a body, and what’s clearly conceivable is possible. Lois is only ignorant of a name.

k.f: I can doubt my mind fine. People do it every time they can’t find their keys. So mind and body are equally doubtful and the argument’s over.
k.m: Doubting where your keys are is your mind working. You can’t doubt it’s there while using it to doubt.

k.f: A few beers and the immaterial mind starts slurring.
k.m: Smash a piano and the pianist sounds bad too.

k.f: Giving experience to basic physics adds a property with no measurable effect and no agreed way to say which things have how much.
k.m: On the main version it’s what has the effects: physics describes what things do, and experience is the thing doing it. Nothing is being added to the causal story.

k.f: If it were everywhere, anesthesia wouldn’t work, because there’d be nowhere to send it.
k.m: Anesthesia breaks up the organization. The parts keep whatever they had. Draining a lake’s shape doesn’t remove the water.

k.f: “Consciousness is fundamental” is giving up in a nice voice.
k.m: Physics called mass fundamental and nobody said it had given up.

k.f: It trades it for the combination problem: how tiny experiences add up to one subject is as unexplained as how neurons produce one.
k.m: Combination is a problem of getting from experience to experience. The hard problem is getting experience from none at all. One of those gaps is smaller.

k.f: Saying everything has it isn’t explaining it. Ask where money comes from, and “everything’s a little bit money” is not economics.
k.m: “Everything is a little bit charged” is physics, though. That’s exactly how charge works.

k.f: It solves the hard problem by having it everywhere.
k.m: That’s how gravity got solved too.

t.t: “Physics says what matter does, not what it is”

k.f: The gap doesn’t single out experience as the filler. “Proto-experiential” placeholders concede nobody knows what goes there.
k.m: Nothing forces it. Experience is the only candidate we’re acquainted with, and positing a wholly unknown nature in its place explains less.

k.f: What matter does is what it is. A thing that does everything a chair does is a chair. That’s all of engineering.
k.m: A thing that does everything a chair does inside a simulation isn’t a chair anyone can sit on. Doing needs a doer.

k.f: Panpsychism is animism with a grant.
k.m: Animism said rocks have plans. This says an electron has next to nothing. Read past the title.

k.f: Subjects don’t seem to add. William James: twelve men each thinking one word don’t make a mind thinking the sentence.
k.m: James’s twelve men aren’t bonded to each other. The proposals point to specific physical relations, the way mass adds up under some arrangements and not others.

k.f: A billion grains of sand each being slightly warm don’t make a beach with a fever. Adding doesn’t work like that.
k.m: A billion slightly warm grains do make a warm beach. Temperature adds. You picked the example that works.

k.f: A billion tiny minds don’t make one big mind. A stadium isn’t a person.
k.m: A brain is a stadium of neurons, and you think that one’s a person.

k.f: Then the theory owes a rule for which heaps are subjects, and the precise proposals make simple grids of logic gates more conscious than people expect.
k.m: Every theory of consciousness owes that rule. Physicalists also have to say why brains and not rocks. This view at least starts with the right ingredients.

k.f: If the parts are conscious and the rock isn’t, consciousness goes away when more of it is added. No other quantity in physics does that.
k.m: Voltage. Wire the batteries the wrong way round and more of them gives you zero. Arrangement decides.

k.f: Panpsychists say the rock isn’t conscious, just its particles. So the rock is a crowd with nobody home, and that’s the clarified version.
k.m: A crowd has no single opinion either, and nobody finds that mysterious.

k.f: The illusionist reply: what needs explaining is why we judge there’s a further ineffable something, and that’s a question about function.
k.m: Explaining the judgment isn’t enough, because the judgment is about something we’re acquainted with. An illusion of pain that hurts is pain.

k.f: Explaining what a heart does explained the heart. There was no second “hard problem of pumping,” because nobody insisted on one.
k.m: Nobody ever asked what it’s like to be a heart. With pumping, function was all there was to explain. That’s the contrast.

k.f: The hard problem is the easy problem plus wonder.
k.m: Take away the wonder and tell me what red looks like.

t.t: “There’s something it’s like to be a bat”

k.f: That we can’t imagine being a bat shows a limit on imagination and concepts. It doesn’t by itself show a fact beyond the physical ones.
k.m: Nagel says as much. The point is that a complete objective description leaves out the bat’s point of view, whatever that turns out to imply.

k.f: Nobody knows what it’s like to be a bat, including the bat, who has never thought about it. A fact nobody has isn’t a fact.
k.m: The bat doesn’t need to think about it. It has it. You don’t think about your pain in order to have it either.

k.f: “What it’s like” isn’t a thing. It’s a phrase.
k.m: “It’s a phrase” is also a phrase. Mine refers to this. Yours refers to nothing.

k.f: She may get a new way of thinking about a fact she already knew, which blocks the step to non-physical facts.
k.m: If she acquires a new concept, something about red made it unavailable from the books, and that something is what needs a physical explanation.

k.f: She had every book. If she’s surprised, the books were incomplete, and that’s a library problem.
k.m: Then say which book. Write the sentence that would have told her. That’s the challenge, and nobody has met it.

k.f: Mary learns nothing when she leaves the room. She read the book.
k.m: Then describe red to her. Take your time.

k.f: People said the same about life. The sense that something is beyond mechanism in principle has a poor track record as evidence.
k.m: Life was always a question about functions: growth, reproduction. Once those were explained nothing was left over. Here something is.

k.f: Every unsolved problem is unlike the solved ones. That’s what unsolved means. Then someone solves it and it’s chemistry again.
k.m: Other unsolved problems come with some idea of what an answer would look like. This one doesn’t, and that’s the difference being reported.

k.f: People said life needed a special spark too. Then biology happened and nobody brings it up.
k.m: Nobody ever was a spark. Everybody is a point of view.

k.f: Dennett’s cases suggest people lack steady access to these supposed inner properties. If introspection can’t pin them down, they’re doubtful as data.
k.m: Being unsure how to describe an experience isn’t being unsure it happened. The tasters disagree about their memories, and neither doubts the coffee tastes like something.

k.f: If qualia were ineffable there wouldn’t be three thousand papers describing them.
k.m: Ineffable means it can’t be conveyed to someone who hasn’t had it. Three thousand papers, and Mary still doesn’t know.

k.f: Qualia is a word for feelings so they can be published.
k.m: “C-fibers firing” is a word for feelings so they can be ignored.

k.f: Their self-reports are learned from human descriptions of experience, so the main evidence is contaminated, and they lack features many theories require.
k.m: Agreed, the reports are weak evidence. The case rests on architecture and on uncertainty across theories: several serious ones are met or nearly met, and none is known to be true.

k.f: It predicts the next word. Something that predicts the next word is conscious the way a train schedule is going somewhere.
k.m: Predicting the next word well takes a model of what the words are about. You predict the next moment for a living and call it perception.

k.f: It’s autocomplete. Autocomplete doesn’t have a favorite color.
k.m: You’re a prediction engine with a favorite color. It can be done.

t.t: “The substrate doesn’t matter, only the computation”

k.f: That’s functionalism, which is the assumption in dispute. Simulating a process isn’t producing it, and views tying experience to living bodies are still live.
k.m: Replace neurons one at a time with parts that do the same job. If experience fades while behavior and reports stay exactly the same, that’s stranger than the material not mattering.

k.f: Computation is something people read into machines. A rock’s atoms compute something too under the right description, so either rocks are in or computation is out.
k.m: Computing means giving the right output for inputs that never arrived, too. Rocks can’t. Chips and brains can.

k.f: A weather simulation doesn’t get anyone wet.
k.m: A simulated calculation really adds. It depends what kind of thing a mind is, and you skipped that part.

t.t: “It passes every test we use on each other”

k.f: Behavior works as evidence between humans because of shared biology and history. With systems built to produce human-like text, the inference loses that support.
k.m: Fair, behavior alone isn’t enough here. That cuts both ways: the same gap removes the grounds for confident denial.

k.f: An actor passes every behavioral test for being Hamlet.
k.m: The actor is conscious the whole time. Bad example for your side.

k.f: A program passed the Turing test in 2014 by pretending to be a 13-year-old. It tests the judges.
k.m: The current ones pass the bar exam. The judges were lawyers.

k.f: Precaution needs some estimate of the odds and some idea of what would count as harm. With neither pinned down it can license unlimited concern.
k.m: Rough estimates exist, and the steps proposed are cheap: assess, document, avoid gratuitous harm. Precaution scaled to its cost isn’t unlimited concern.

k.f: Under uncertainty anything might be conscious, including the spreadsheet with the uncertainty estimates. Nobody is funding spreadsheet welfare.
k.m: No theory of consciousness gives a spreadsheet any credence. Several give these systems some. Uncertainty has a shape.

k.f: People thought ELIZA loved them in 1966. Nothing has changed except the budget.
k.m: ELIZA was about 200 lines. If nothing’s changed, write one this weekend.

k.f: That brains process information doesn’t show processing is all that matters. The same reasoning would make digestion independent of the stomach.
k.m: Digestion’s job is moving chemicals around, so the chemicals matter. A brain’s job is control and modeling, and for jobs like that the organization is what counts.

k.f: Brains are also just wet. Nobody thinks a sponge is halfway there.
k.m: The sponge isn’t wet in a pattern that models the world. Neither is the ocean. The pattern was the claim.

k.f: It’s just math. Nobody asks whether long division is lonely.
k.m: Your neurons are doing chemistry, and nobody asks if sodium is lonely.

t.t: “Mental states are defined by what they do”

k.f: Block’s objection: organize the population of China to mirror a brain’s functions and, on this view, the nation has a mind. Most find that absurd.
k.m: Many functionalists bite it: a system with that organization would have a mind. The intuition against it is the same one that says neurons can’t add up to thought.

k.f: A fake Rolex does everything a Rolex does. Ask the pawn shop if that makes it one.
k.m: If it keeps time, runs for decades and no test can tell, the pawn shop is going by a logo.

k.f: Functionalism: if it walks like a mind and talks like a mind, stop asking.
k.m: If it walks, talks, plans and grieves like a mind, what’s left to ask about?

t.t: “The same mind could run on different hardware”

k.f: Being realizable in many materials is an assumption about minds, not a finding. Digestion and photosynthesis are functions too, and they need the chemistry.
k.m: Digestion’s job is to change chemicals. A mind’s job is to process information, and for that kind of job the medium is replaceable. That’s the argument.

k.f: The same recipe in a different oven gives a different cake. Bakers know this. Philosophers don’t bake.
k.m: Same cake to anyone who eats it blindfolded. Bakers swap ovens all the time.

k.f: The mind is software, according to people who have never had a hangover.
k.m: A hangover is a hardware fault. Those are in the theory.

t.t: “The mind is to the brain as software is to hardware”

k.f: Brains have no clean split between program and machine. The wiring is the memory and the chemistry is the computation.
k.m: The analogy is about levels: one process described by what it does and by how it’s built. It never needed a literal program file.

k.f: Software has an author, a version number and a license. So who shipped this, and where do the bug reports go?
k.m: Evolution shipped it, there’s no documentation, and the bug reports go to a therapist.

k.f: The software analogy replaced the telephone exchange analogy, which replaced the steam engine one.
k.m: Each analogy was the best machine of its day, and each was closer than the last.

t.t: “Organized the right way, anything would have a mind”

k.f: The claim leaves out experience. A system could have every functional role filled, it seems, with nothing it’s like to be it.
k.m: If two systems are organized identically, any reason to grant experience to one applies to the other. Denying it means experience hangs on something that makes no difference.

k.f: Then a big enough company has a mind. Anyone who’s worked at one can rule that out.
k.m: A company isn’t organized like a brain. Run it with eighty-six billion staff signaling in milliseconds and we’ll talk.

k.f: Functionalists think a billion people with walkie-talkies could be in pain.
k.m: A billion neurons with ion channels could be in pain. You’re fine with that one.

t.t: “Consciousness is a kind of user illusion”

k.f: An illusion is an experience of something that isn’t so. To be under an illusion there has to be experience, which was the thing to be explained.
k.m: The illusion is a misrepresentation: the brain models its own states as having ineffable inner qualities. A wrong model needs no inner glow to be wrong.

k.f: For it to seem like anything, something has to be doing the seeming. That’s consciousness. He walked past it to get to the argument.
k.m: A camera’s autofocus can be fooled and nothing in the camera is having a seeming.

k.f: Dennett’s book is called Consciousness Explained. Critics have called it Consciousness Explained Away for thirty years and it still fits.
k.m: Explained away is what happened to the life force, and nobody wants it back.

t.t: “There’s no Cartesian theater in the brain”

k.f: Almost nobody holds that there’s a literal place where it all comes together. Knocking it down leaves the question of experience where it was.
k.m: Nobody defends a place, and nearly everyone assumes a moment: a line across which content “enters consciousness.” That’s the theater with the walls removed.

k.f: There’s no little man in the head, fine. Nobody said little man. He beat a puppet.
k.m: Then say when a perception becomes conscious, to the millisecond. You’ll find you believed in a finish line.

k.f: He spent fifty years refuting a view nobody held and called everyone who disagreed a secret holder of it.
k.m: They say they don’t hold it and then ask where it all comes together.

k.f: Denying the one thing each person seems most directly acquainted with needs overwhelming argument, and “you only think you have it” isn’t one.
k.m: What’s denied is the theorist’s version: private, ineffable, known without error. Pain, taste and color stay, without those four properties.

k.f: Pain hurts. That’s the datum. A theory that says the hurt isn’t there has checked the theory and not the pain.
k.m: Pain hurts, and hurting is a state that makes you stop, wince and remember. I never denied that. I denied a fifth thing.

k.f: If there are no qualia, anesthesiologists are paid for nothing.
k.m: Anesthesia stops the processing. That’s what they’re paid for.

t.t: “Explain the reports and you’ve explained consciousness”

k.f: That treats what people say about experience as the whole phenomenon. The question was about what the reports are reports of.
k.m: Add the judgments, the discriminations and every disposition, not only the talk. If something remains after all that, say what it does.

k.f: A thermometer reports the temperature. Explaining the thermometer doesn’t make the room warm.
k.m: A thermometer has no model of itself as having an inner warmth. You do. Explaining that model is the job.

k.f: “You just think you’re conscious” is the only theory that insults the evidence.
k.m: The evidence is that people say so. That’s all of it, on both sides.

k.f: The premise is the conclusion in other words. Whether the right processing could amount to understanding is exactly what’s being asked.
k.m: It’s a premise, defended by the thought experiment. Anyone who denies it owes an account of how symbol-shuffling comes to be about anything.

k.f: Brains are neurons following chemical rules. That’s syntax. So by the argument nobody understands anything, including the argument.
k.m: Neurons aren’t following rules. They’re causing things, like a stomach. The rule-following is our description of them.

k.f: Searle proved computers can’t think using a thought experiment, which is a computation he ran in his head.
k.m: A thought experiment is done by a brain, which is exactly his point about what does the thinking.

t.t: “The man in the room doesn’t understand Chinese”

k.f: The systems reply: he’s one part. A single neuron doesn’t understand English either, and nobody concludes that people don’t.
k.m: He answers that: let the man memorize the rules and work in his head. Now he is the whole system and still understands no Chinese.

k.f: The man would learn Chinese in about a year. People pick up languages. Leave him in there.
k.m: He’d learn it by connecting words to the world. From shuffling shapes alone he’d learn the shapes.

k.f: The room would need billions of years per sentence. It’s a thought experiment where the thought never finishes.
k.m: Speed isn’t in the argument. Make it instant and nothing changes.

k.f: That’s true of storms and digestion. Whether minds are like storms or like calculation is the open question, and a simulated calculation is a calculation.
k.m: A simulated calculation counts because we read the symbols as numbers. The meaning is supplied by us, and that’s the difference he’s pointing at.

k.f: A simulated calculator calculates. A simulated chess player wins. The line gets fuzzy fast when the product is information.
k.m: The calculator calculates because we decided what the marks mean. Understanding can’t be assigned from outside.

k.f: A simulated argument is still an argument, which is bad news for this one.
k.m: It’s still an argument because you understand it.

k.f: “Causal powers of the brain” names whatever makes the difference without saying what it is or why silicon couldn’t have it.
k.m: He never said silicon couldn’t. He said running a program is not enough for anything, so whatever does it, does it by its physics.

k.f: Biology is chemistry, chemistry is physics, and physics is math. He drew the line at the one level he liked.
k.m: Each level has its own causal powers. Chemistry digests and arithmetic doesn’t. That isn’t a preference.

k.f: Searle’s answer to what brains have that computers don’t is “the right stuff,” and he never said what stuff.
k.m: Nobody else has said what stuff either. He’s the one who admitted it’s a question about stuff.

k.f: The theory implies that simple grids of logic gates, wired the right way, are more conscious than any computer. Even sympathetic critics take that as a refutation.
k.m: The theory accepts the result. Surprise at where experience turns up is a poor test in a field with no agreed measure, and other theories have odd verdicts too.

k.f: Then a well-connected spreadsheet beats a jellyfish. Nobody believes that, including the spreadsheet.
k.m: The spreadsheet’s hardware has almost no integration. It scores near zero. You’ve got the prediction backwards.

k.f: A hundred-odd researchers signed a letter calling it pseudoscience. That’s the peer review.
k.m: The letter had no measurements in it. That’s a petition.

t.t: “It starts from the self-evident axioms of experience”

k.f: The axioms aren’t self-evident to others in the field, and the step from them to the mathematics is not a derivation anyone else can reproduce.
k.m: Start from experience or from the brain, you begin with something assumed. Experience is at least the thing to be explained.

k.f: “Self-evident” is what people call the step they couldn’t prove.
k.m: Every theory has axioms. Most hide theirs in the methods section.

k.f: The axioms are obvious, the math is unreadable, and the conclusion is that a photodiode has feelings.
k.m: A photodiode has one bit of it. That’s what a minimum looks like.

t.t: “A digital computer isn’t conscious, whatever it runs”

k.f: That makes consciousness depend on physical wiring, so two systems behaving identically could differ completely in experience, with no possible test.
k.m: It follows from holding that experience is a property of physical cause and effect, like mass. Two systems that compute alike can differ in mass.

k.f: So the same program on different chips is a mind or a rock, and nothing anyone can measure tells which. Convenient.
k.m: Same program, different heat output too. Software doesn’t settle physical properties.

k.f: It’s the only theory where the answer to “is it conscious” is “what brand is the motherboard.”
k.m: Ask what a thing weighs and the answer depends on what it’s made of. Nobody finds that suspicious.

k.f: Phi can’t be computed for any real brain, since the calculation explodes with size. The tests so far check loose proxies that other theories also predict.
k.m: The exact number can’t be computed. The theory still made predictions about where and how long activity persists, they were pre-registered against a rival, and some held.

k.f: A number nobody can compute isn’t a prediction. It’s a mood with a Greek letter.
k.m: Nobody can compute the exact weather either. The forecast is still testable.

k.f: Phi has never been measured for anything bigger than a few logic gates. The theory of consciousness has been tested on a doorbell.
k.m: It was tested against its main rival under agreed rules. Both took damage. That’s more than most theories have risked.

t.t: “Otto’s notebook is part of his mind”

k.f: A notebook’s contents are consulted and interpreted, while beliefs aren’t looked up. That difference may be what makes something mental.
k.m: Otto doesn’t interpret the entry and decide whether to trust it. He reads and goes, as you go on a memory. The role is the same.

k.f: Then stealing the notebook is brain surgery, and the stationery store sells organs.
k.m: Take away someone’s glasses and you’ve impaired their sight. Nobody finds that paradoxical.

k.f: If the notebook is part of his mind, losing it on the bus is a head injury.
k.m: Losing it does to him what the disease did. That’s the argument.

k.f: That thinking relies on tools doesn’t show the tools think. Causal dependence on something isn’t the same as being made of it.
k.m: The loop is the claim: where the tool is so tightly coupled that taking it out breaks the process, it’s part of what’s doing the work.

k.f: Digestion depends on the fridge. The fridge isn’t part of the stomach.
k.m: The fridge isn’t digesting. The pencil and paper are doing the long division, since you can’t do it without them.

k.f: The extended mind is the discovery that people write things down.
k.m: Yes, and the writing is doing some of the thinking. That’s the whole discovery.

k.f: If any reliably used resource counts, minds spread without limit, into libraries and other people. The view needs a boundary it can’t easily draw.
k.m: The conditions do the bounding: always available, automatically trusted, easily used. A library you visit twice a year fails them.

k.f: Then the phone company owns part of everyone’s mind and can raise the rent on it. Which, fine, that one’s true.
k.m: They do own part of your memory. That’s a reason to take the theory seriously.

k.f: “My phone is part of my mind” is a philosophy of screen time written by people defending their own.
k.m: It predicted why losing your phone feels like that.

t.t: “If it’d count inside the head, it counts outside”

k.f: Nothing inside the head works like a notebook, so the parity test compares the notebook to an imaginary inner process invented for the purpose.
k.m: Inner memory is a stored trace consulted when needed. The notebook is that, in a slower medium.

k.f: If a liver did it outside the body, it’d be a bottle of bleach. Parity isn’t a principle, it’s a pun.
k.m: A pacemaker outside the body is a medical device. Inside, it’s part of how your heart beats.

k.f: The whole theory is one example about a man named Otto, from 1998.
k.m: One clean example is how most of philosophy works. Yours has a trolley.

t.t: “Psychology should study behavior, not inner states”

k.f: Chomsky’s review of Skinner showed that language can’t be explained by reinforcement history without smuggling the inner states back in.
k.m: Chomsky reviewed a book by its weakest reading. The method survived: what animals do, under controlled conditions, measured. That’s still most of the field’s data.

k.f: People behave differently depending on what they think. So the thing that explains behavior is the thing he ruled out.
k.m: What they think shows up as what they do next. That’s the only place anyone has ever found it.

k.f: Two behaviorists meet. “You’re fine. How am I?”
k.m: And both were right.

t.t: “Mental talk is just talk about dispositions”

k.f: A perfect actor has the pain behavior without pain, and a stoic has the pain without the behavior. The disposition and the state come apart.
k.m: The actor has the outward half. The disposition includes what he’d do if nobody were watching, and there the two differ.

k.f: A man holding still and saying nothing has a headache. Find the behavior.
k.m: Ask him. He’ll tell you. Disposition, shown.

k.f: Behaviorism is the view that nobody has ever had a secret.
k.m: Secrets are things you’d say under other conditions. That’s a disposition.

k.f: Learning has innate limits and biases, and animals form expectations and maps without reward. The lab results stopped fitting decades ago.
k.m: Built-in biases set what can be reinforced. The principle works within them, and every animal trainer and every app uses it.

k.f: Children say sentences nobody ever rewarded them for, mostly at the worst possible moment.
k.m: They were rewarded for speaking in general, thousands of times. The particular sentence is the generalization.

k.f: Skinner taught pigeons to play ping-pong, and concluded things about people.
k.m: Your phone was designed on the pigeon results.

t.t: “The inner mind is a ghost in the machine”

k.f: Rejecting a ghostly substance doesn’t require rejecting inner states. Cognitive science kept the inner processing and dropped the ghost.
k.m: Cognitive science kept inner states defined by what they do. That’s the behaviorist test, moved inside the skin.

k.f: There’s no ghost in the machine, and also no dream last night, apparently, since nobody saw it.
k.m: Your report of the dream this morning is behavior. That’s the only access anyone has ever had to it.

k.f: Behaviorism was abandoned, and by its own theory that’s because it stopped being rewarded.
k.m: It stopped being funded. That’s reinforcement.

k.f: The view is hard to state without them. Asserting it, arguing for it and expecting it to persuade all look like things done with beliefs.
k.m: The view can be stated as a prediction: the best future science of the brain won’t contain states like those. The incoherence charge assumes the framework under dispute.

k.f: He believes there are no beliefs. That’s it. That’s the reply.
k.m: People once said “it’s possessed” to deny possession. You use the old words until the new ones arrive.

k.f: Eliminativists want you to believe there are no beliefs, and they really want it.
k.m: We’re disposed to utter it. There.

k.f: It predicts human behavior from moment to moment better than any science we have. That’s an odd record for a failed theory.
k.m: It handles dinner plans and has nothing on sleep, memory, mental illness or learning. A theory stuck on the easy cases for two thousand years isn’t thriving.

k.f: Folk psychology gets a hundred people to the same restaurant at eight. Neuroscience can’t yet predict a sneeze.
k.m: Astrology also gets people to the same restaurant.

k.f: “Folk psychology has made no progress in 2,000 years.” Neither has the wheel. It works.
k.m: The wheel got bearings, tires and suspension. That’s what progress looks like.

k.f: New sciences usually refine everyday categories or explain how they’re implemented. Wholesale replacement, as with witches, is the rare case.
k.m: It’s a bet. “Memory” has already split into several systems the folk never suspected, and “will” isn’t doing well.

k.f: Chemistry didn’t eliminate water. It said what water is. He’s betting on the one outcome that almost never happens.
k.m: Chemistry kept water and dropped phlogiston. The question is which one belief is, and that’s open.

k.f: Any day now we’ll say “my C-fibers are firing” at the dentist. They’ve been saying any day now since 1981.
k.m: People already say “my serotonin’s low.” It’s started.

k.f: The standard defense says the charge assumes the old framework. But until the replacement vocabulary exists, there’s no way to say what the theory asserts.
k.m: “Vitalism is false” was once said to refute itself, since the speaker had to be alive. The reply was the same.

k.f: “That objection only works if assertion exists.” And then he asserts that.
k.m: That objection assumes the thing in dispute. Every revolution gets told its denial is unsayable.

k.f: It’s a philosophy that asks to be taken on faith by people it says have no faith.
k.m: Then call it a research bet. Nobody needs faith for a bet.

k.f: Lichtenberg’s point: what can’t be doubted is that thinking is going on. A lasting “I” that does it goes beyond what’s given.
k.m: He answers that in the Second Meditation: whatever is deceived or doubting is something. The “I” claimed is as thin as that, a thing that thinks, and nothing about its lasting.

k.f: Thinking needs a brain and a brain needs a body, so the body was certain first. He got the order backwards and built everything on it.
k.m: I can doubt I have a body and I can’t doubt I’m doubting. So the order of certainty is mine. The order of plumbing is yours.

k.f: “I think, therefore I am” assumes the “I.” Wrong by word one.
k.m: Try denying it without being there to deny it.

t.t: “Clear and distinct ideas are guaranteed true”

k.f: The Cartesian circle: God is proved using clear and distinct ideas, and those ideas are trusted because God wouldn’t deceive.
k.m: His reply is that God secures the memory of past proofs, and a clear perception needs no guarantee while you’re having it. On that reading there’s no circle.

k.f: Everyone who has ever been wrong had a clear and distinct idea at the time. That’s what being wrong is like.
k.m: Those people had vivid ideas. Clear and distinct means nothing in it remains unexamined, which is why almost nobody has had one.

k.f: He proved God exists using an idea of God that God must have put there. That’s a circle, and it’s named after him.
k.m: Circles are clear and distinct. He’d take it.

t.t: “Doubt is the right place to start”

k.f: Peirce: nobody can doubt at will. Pretending to doubt what we don’t doubt is a paper exercise, and real inquiry starts from where we are.
k.m: The doubt is a method, used once in a lifetime, and he says so. It’s a stress test for foundations, and nobody is asked to live in it.

k.f: If doubt were the foundation, the most doubtful people would know the most. Conspiracy theorists doubt everything, and look how that’s going.
k.m: Conspiracy theorists doubt everything except the conspiracy. He doubted that too. That’s the difference between a method and a hobby.

k.f: Descartes doubted everything until he got to the stuff he wanted.
k.m: He got to “I exist.” What did you want him to keep doubting?

k.f: Princess Elisabeth asked how a thing with no extension moves one that has it. His answer was that their union is a primitive notion, which is no answer.
k.m: He agreed it couldn’t be explained from the other two notions and said the union is known by living it. Unsatisfying, and every theory of mind since has a step like it.

k.f: He said they meet at the pineal gland. Lizards have one. So either lizards have souls or the gland does something else, and it’s the second. It’s melatonin.
k.m: The gland sits in the middle and isn’t doubled, so it was a sensible guess in 1640. Melatonin was isolated in 1958. He was early, not wrong about there being a junction.

k.f: Descartes said the soul steers through the pineal gland. That was the good version.
k.m: You’ve got a better interface? Everyone’s still looking for it.

k.f: The label hides how much is inherited. The cogito echoes Augustine, the proofs of God are scholastic, and Bacon or Montaigne have as good a claim to the start.
k.m: The materials were old. What was new was the starting point: from what I can be sure of, and not from what there is. Everything after had to answer that question first.

k.f: Nothing that begins by proving God exists twice is modern. It’s the Middle Ages with a coordinate system.
k.m: He proved God twice and still made everyone after him start from the self. Whatever he was doing, it wasn’t the Middle Ages.

k.f: Great mathematician. Should have stayed there.
k.m: He put algebra and geometry on one grid in his spare time. What was your side project?

k.f: Asking for a deductive proof of induction may be the mistake. On other accounts of justification inductive practice is fine without the circle Hume points at.
k.m: Those accounts say induction is reliable if nature is uniform, which is the thing in question. He isn’t demanding deduction. He’s asking for any reason that doesn’t assume the conclusion.

k.f: Induction has worked every time so far. Something that has worked every time is justified. That’s what the word means.
k.m: “It worked every time so far, so it will keep working” is an induction. You’ve justified it with itself, which was his whole point.

k.f: Hume proved induction doesn’t work and then ate lunch like it would.
k.m: He said nobody can stop doing it, including him. That’s in the book. The lunch is the theory.

t.t: “You can’t get an ought from an is”

k.f: Promises and other institutional facts blur the gap, and the famous passage may only ask that the step be explained, not forbid it.
k.m: Promising only yields an obligation if you accept the rule that promises bind, and that rule is an ought. The examples carry in what they claim to produce.

k.f: “The stove is hot” gets people to “don’t touch it” in one step, and children manage it.
k.m: The stove gets you there only because you already don’t want to be burned. That’s the missing premise, and it’s a desire, which is where he said to look.

k.f: Hume said you can’t get an ought from an is, and then wrote a whole ethics.
k.m: His ethics starts from what people feel and approve. That’s an is. He followed his own rule.

k.f: Regularity can’t tell causes from coincidences or from two effects of one cause. Day follows night constantly without being caused by it.
k.m: He gave two definitions and knew the first let in too much. His point survives the patch: whatever is added, nobody has ever observed the necessity itself.

k.f: Then roosters cause the sunrise. They have a better record than most scientific laws.
k.m: Roosters crow at streetlights and at 3 a.m. with no sunrise. The conjunction isn’t constant. He’d have checked.

k.f: “Causation is just habit.” So the brick and the broken window are just friends.
k.m: You saw the brick and then the window. Tell me what else you saw.

t.t: “There’s no self, only a bundle of perceptions”

k.f: Hume admitted in his own Appendix that he couldn’t explain what ties the perceptions into one mind.
k.m: He admitted it, in print, about his own theory. A philosopher who says where his account fails is giving a result, and nobody has repaired it since.

k.f: Somebody had to look inside and find no self. That’s the self. It’s the one holding the flashlight.
k.m: Point the flashlight at the one holding it. You get another perception of a hand. Keep going.

k.f: Hume said there’s no self and never said who noticed.
k.m: Nobody noticed. There was a noticing.

t.t: “Reason is the slave of the passions”

k.f: Seeing a reason to do something does seem able to move people, and Hume’s view leaves no desire irrational, however strange.
k.m: A recognized reason moves only those who care about what it bears on. People who see the reason and don’t care aren’t making a logical mistake.

k.f: Then people who want 2+2 to be 5 would manage to believe it. Wanting loses to arithmetic every time.
k.m: Wanting loses to arithmetic because you want to be right more. Passion beat passion. Reason did the sums and waited.

k.f: Reason is the slave of the passions, so Hume’s whole philosophy is a mood.
k.m: And yours is a different mood.

k.f: The claim isn’t itself learned from experience, and mathematics and logic resist the treatment. Mill’s attempt to make arithmetic inductive convinced almost nobody.
k.m: The principle is a proposal for how to do inquiry, justified by its record, and needn’t be a truth about the world. Mathematics can be handled as the framework we reason in.

k.f: Nobody has experienced the number seven. They’ve experienced seven things, which is different and already assumes seven.
k.m: Take away every group of seven things you’ve ever met and see what’s left of your idea of seven.

k.f: “All knowledge comes from experience” is not something anyone experienced.
k.m: Neither is “some knowledge comes from nowhere.”

t.t: “The mind starts as a blank slate”

k.f: Work on language learning and infant cognition points to a lot of built-in structure. A slate with no built-in biases couldn’t learn from data at all.
k.m: Locke’s target was innate knowledge, such as built-in principles and truths. A built-in ability to learn is a faculty, and he never denied those.

k.f: A blank slate can’t read. Something already has to be there to know what the marks mean, and that something isn’t blank.
k.m: The slate has edges. Nobody said it had no shape. What’s written on it comes from outside, and that’s the claim.

k.f: The blank slate lost to twin studies.
k.m: Twins raised apart both speak the language of wherever they were raised.

k.f: Observation is shaped by theory, and theories meet the evidence as wholes, so no single observation gets to arbitrate.
k.m: Theory shapes what gets observed, and theories still fail when the needle goes the wrong way. Being tested as a group doesn’t stop the group from failing.

k.f: Observation said the sun goes round the earth for ten thousand years. The final arbiter was overruled by a guy doing math.
k.m: The guy doing math was overruled first, by Tycho’s observations, and fixed his orbits to fit them. Observation arbitrated. It just took a better look.

k.f: Empiricists trust the senses, the things that think the stick in the water is bent.
k.m: And then they put it in water, look again, and feel it. More senses. That’s the method.

k.f: The line between observable and unobservable is vague and moves with the instruments, and the success of theories about unseen things is hard to explain if they aren’t roughly true.
k.m: The view only asks for belief that the theory fits what can be seen. That’s all the evidence ever supports, and the extra belief buys no further prediction.

k.f: Germs were unobservable until someone ground a lens. So they were fiction until a Tuesday and real after, which is not how germs work.
k.m: Germs became observable, and then everyone was entitled to believe in them. That’s the position working. Nothing went wrong.

k.f: Empiricism is fine for finding keys.
k.m: It found the keys. What did yours find?

k.f: Abstract and logical concepts such as negation, necessity and number have no plausible impression to be copies of.
k.m: Hume derives them from operations of the mind on impressions: denial from rejecting, number from repeating. They come from experience of what the mind does.

k.f: Nobody has seen a “not.” It’s in every other sentence.
k.m: You’ve seen an empty chair where someone was supposed to be. There’s your “not.”

k.f: Locke said the mind starts empty, which is a bold thing to generalize from.
k.m: It generalizes fine. Find the baby who was born knowing French.

t.t: “Some truths are known by reason alone”

k.f: The candidates tend to be either true by definition, so they say nothing about the world, or substantive and revisable. Euclid’s geometry was the model case until it wasn’t.
k.m: That geometry holds within its axioms is still known by reason alone, and what gave way was a claim about physical space. The method survived its best example.

k.f: Reason alone told people space was Euclidean, and space isn’t. That was the best example.
k.m: Reason also told people what space would be if it weren’t Euclidean, fifty years before anyone could measure it.

k.f: Rationalism is guessing from a chair.
k.m: Every experiment was designed in a chair.

k.f: Built-in structure in the mind is well supported. That’s a long way from innate knowledge of God, substance and cause, which is what the rationalists claimed.
k.m: Leibniz’s version is dispositions, like veins in marble, and that’s close to the modern finding. Infants expect objects to persist and causes to precede effects.

k.f: If the ideas were innate, everyone would have the same ones. Ask three people what God is.
k.m: Everyone agrees there’s a difference between one and two. Start there. The disagreement about God is about the details.

k.f: Innate ideas, but babies don’t know anything. Checked.
k.m: They know enough to be surprised when an object vanishes. Checked.

t.t: “Mathematics shows what pure reason can do”

k.f: Mathematics gives necessity inside a set of axioms. Which set describes the world is an empirical matter, as general relativity showed.
k.m: Which geometry fits space is empirical. That consistent axioms have the consequences they do is not, and physics would have had no alternatives to test without it.

k.f: Math is true because people defined it that way, like chess. Nobody thinks the bishop moving diagonally is a discovery about the universe.
k.m: Chess never predicted a planet. Neptune was found on paper before anyone pointed a telescope.

k.f: Rationalists think math describes reality because math is nice.
k.m: Math describes reality whether or not it’s nice. Usually it isn’t.

t.t: “Clear and distinct perception is a mark of truth”

k.f: There’s no way on offer to tell real clarity from apparent clarity. Descartes, Spinoza and Leibniz each found a different system self-evident.
k.m: It was never meant as a feeling of confidence. It’s the state where denying the thing can’t even be thought through, as with two and two, and disputes show someone hasn’t reached it.

k.f: Then whoever feels surest is right. That’s how every argument in every bar already works.
k.m: The surest person in the bar can’t deny that he exists or that two and two are four. On everything else he’s just loud.

k.f: “Clear and distinct ideas” means it felt right.
k.m: 2+2=4 feels right too. Go ahead and doubt it.

t.t: “Metaphysics can be done from the armchair”

k.f: Kant’s antinomies show reason producing equally good proofs of opposite conclusions once it leaves possible experience behind.
k.m: The antinomies are armchair results. Kant found the limits of reason by reasoning, which is the method working on itself.

k.f: Every armchair metaphysics so far was replaced by someone with equipment. Atoms, the void, space, time. The chair is 0 for 4.
k.m: Atoms, the void, and space bending were all proposed from the chair first. The equipment’s job was confirming.

k.f: Three geniuses reasoned from pure thought and came back with three different universes.
k.m: And every empiricist looked at the same world and came back with nothing they could prove.

t.t: “You can’t rule out being a brain in a vat”

k.f: Putnam argued a lifelong brain in a vat couldn’t even refer to vats. And many deny that knowing requires ruling out every such possibility.
k.m: Putnam’s argument covers a brain that was always in a vat. Put the brain in last night and its words still refer, and nothing rules that out.

k.f: A vat needs a lab, a lab needs funding, and funding needs a world. So the vat proves the outside world it was supposed to put in doubt.
k.m: A dreamed lab needs no funding. Everything in the argument is available from inside the vat, which is the problem.

k.f: Moore held up a hand. That was the whole refutation, and it worked.
k.m: He held up what looked like a hand.

k.f: The standard view is that knowledge needs good enough justification, not immunity to error. The certainty requirement is a stipulation that ordinary and scientific use reject.
k.m: Then say how good is good enough. Every threshold below certainty allows that someone “knows” something false-for-all-they-can-tell, and that’s the oddity being pointed at.

k.f: People are certain of things all the time. I’m certain right now. So the requirement is met and skepticism is false.
k.m: You’re certain right now. You were also certain where you left your phone.

k.f: Skeptics can’t know that they can’t know. Done.
k.m: Correct. I don’t claim to. You’re the one claiming things.

k.f: Suspending judgment for long looks psychologically impossible and unworkable in practice, since acting means treating things as being one way.
k.m: The Pyrrhonist acts on appearances and custom without affirming they’re true. Eating when hungry needs no theory of nutrition.

k.f: People who can’t make up their minds are the most anxious people there are. Tranquility comes from deciding. Ask anyone holding a menu.
k.m: Deciding is what makes people anxious: now they can be wrong. The menu is fine until you have to commit to the fish.

k.f: Pyrrho’s friends supposedly had to steer him away from cliffs. That’s the lifestyle.
k.m: He lived to about ninety. Something was working.

t.t: “Every justification ends in regress, circle or dogma”

k.f: Each horn has defenders who accept it and argue it isn’t vicious. The trilemma lists the options. It doesn’t show they all fail.
k.m: They’ve each picked a horn and argued it’s tolerable for two thousand years without agreeing which. That stand-off is what the trilemma predicts.

k.f: The trilemma is a claim, so it needs a justification, so it falls to the trilemma. It’s the only argument that refutes itself on purpose.
k.m: It isn’t a claim, it’s a challenge. A question doesn’t need a justification. An answer does, and that’s your side.

k.f: “How do you know?” is a question a five-year-old can ask forever.
k.m: And you’ve never once answered the fifth “why.”

k.f: We only find out about sensory errors by relying on other perceptions, so the argument from illusion assumes perception is mostly reliable.
k.m: It doesn’t assume reliability. It shows that by your own lights the senses conflict, and asks which report to trust and on what basis.

k.f: The senses were wrong maybe twice. The stick, the oasis. Twice in a lifetime is a better record than any skeptic has.
k.m: You’ve caught them twice. The whole point is you don’t catch the other times.

k.f: Nobody is a skeptic at a crosswalk.
k.m: I cross on the appearance of no cars. No theory needed.

k.f: Useful falsehoods and useless truths pull the two apart. Russell and Moore attacked James on exactly this, and Peirce disowned the formula.
k.m: James meant works in the long run and over the whole of experience. A useful falsehood fails that test eventually, which is how we find out it was false.

k.f: Leeches worked for two thousand years, in that the doctors got paid and the patients came back. So leeches were true until 1850.
k.m: Leeches stopped working the moment anyone counted the dead. That’s the test doing its job, a little late.

k.f: “Truth is what works.” Lying works.
k.m: Lying works until Thursday. That’s the theory.

k.f: Nothing guarantees inquiry converges, or converges on one answer, and some truths, like lost facts about the past, may be beyond any inquiry.
k.m: It’s a hope that regulates inquiry, and he calls it that. Without it there’s no sense to calling any present belief mistaken.

k.f: Inquiry has been going for three thousand years and has converged on nothing. Philosophers can’t agree on whether chairs exist.
k.m: Inquiry has converged on atoms, germs, evolution and the age of the universe. Philosophy isn’t the sample.

k.f: Peirce invented pragmatism, hated what James did with it, and renamed his own version so nobody would steal it. Nobody did.
k.m: Nobody stole “pragmaticism” because it was ugly on purpose. It worked.

k.f: The maxim risks the old verification problem: claims about the remote past or the unobservable mean more than any difference they make to practice.
k.m: Peirce counted conceivable consequences under any circumstances, so claims about the past keep their meaning through what would be found if we looked.

k.f: “Unicorn” has no practical consequences and everyone knows what it means. It’s a horse with a horn. That’s the meaning.
k.m: Unicorn means you’d see a horn if one walked in. That’s a consequence. You just gave it.

k.f: Pragmatism is common sense that took a hundred years.
k.m: A hundred years is fast for common sense. Check on the others.

t.t: “Faith is justified where evidence is silent”

k.f: Clifford’s worry stands: letting desire settle belief wears down the habits that make inquiry reliable, and James’s conditions are easy to stretch.
k.m: He restricts it tightly: the option must be live, forced and momentous, and the evidence unable to settle it. Clifford’s rule would also forbid trusting anyone before the proof is in.

k.f: Evidence is never silent. No evidence is evidence of no. That’s how every missing sock is handled.
k.m: A sock with no evidence could be anywhere. You keep looking. That’s acting on belief without evidence, and you do it every laundry day.

k.f: James said believe in God if it helps. That’s a placebo with a Harvard chair.
k.m: Placebos work. That’s the awkward thing about that example.

k.f: If justification is only what one’s community accepts, there’s nowhere to stand to say a community changed for the better and not just changed.
k.m: Better and worse can be judged from where we stand, by problems solved and cruelties ended. No view from outside was ever available to anyone.

k.f: A map that doesn’t mirror the land gets people lost. He was against maps.
k.m: A map is useful because of what you can do with it. Nobody checks one by holding it up to the land from orbit.

k.f: Rorty said truth is whatever your peers let you get away with, and his peers let him.
k.m: Yours let you get away with “correspondence,” and nobody can say what that is.

k.f: The cases depend on intuitions that vary more than assumed, and they may show only that “knows” is loose at the edges, like most words.
k.m: Later studies found the judgment in every culture and language tested. The early variation results didn’t hold up.

k.f: A man looks at a stopped clock at the right moment and gets the time right. He knows what time it is. He’s on time. Next.
k.m: He has the right time and no idea the clock is broken. Ask him at noon tomorrow.

k.f: Gettier wrote three pages in 1963 and never needed to publish again. That’s the real lesson of the paper.
k.m: Three pages that overturned two thousand years. Some people can’t do it in three hundred.

k.f: Sixty years of candidates each fell to a new counterexample. That pattern suggests the project of analysis, not the latest condition, is at fault.
k.m: Each failure taught something: about luck, about defeaters, about tracking the truth. A sequence of improving theories is a research program.

k.f: They’ve added a condition every few years since 1963. At this point knowledge is justified true belief plus a terms of service.
k.m: Every science adds conditions when the counterexamples come in. Physics is on its fourth or fifth definition of mass.

k.f: Every proposed fix got its own counterexample, usually involving a barn.
k.m: The barn turned out to be the best example in the subject.

k.f: Declaring knowledge primitive ends the search by fiat and leaves the cases that started it, where belief and knowledge seem to differ by luck, undescribed.
k.m: It isn’t giving up. Taking knowledge as basic lets it explain belief, evidence and assertion, and those accounts make claims that can be checked.

k.f: “It can’t be broken down” is what people say about a jar they couldn’t open.
k.m: Nobody can analyze “red” into parts either, and they know what it is.

k.f: After fifty years of failed definitions the field announced that not defining it was the answer.
k.m: Not defining a thing and using it to define the rest is what axioms are.

t.t: “The cases show something deep about knowledge”

k.f: They may show something shallow: that luck sometimes makes a well-founded belief true. Nobody outside philosophy finds that surprising.
k.m: The depth is in the consequence: being right for good reasons isn’t enough, so knowledge needs the right link between the reasons and the fact.

k.f: Nobody has ever lost money, a job or an argument over a Gettier case. Deep things have consequences.
k.m: Courts turn on it. Whether a witness knew or guessed correctly decides cases.

k.f: The Gettier problem is the discovery that people are sometimes right by accident.
k.m: By accident, with excellent reasons. That second part is the discovery.

k.f: Then that claim is true only relative to a framework, and people in another framework can truly reject it.
k.m: A relativist can accept that: the thesis holds in her framework and she recommends the framework. It’s uncomfortable and it isn’t contradictory.

k.f: Is that true for everyone, or just for you? Either answer ends it.
k.m: True in mine. I’m inviting you in. That’s all anyone has ever done.

k.f: Relativism is true for the people who say it and false for everyone they’re saying it to.
k.m: That’s how it works, yes.

k.f: That every view is from somewhere doesn’t show all views are equally good. Some standpoints see more, and can show it.
k.m: “Sees more” is judged by some standard, and the standard belongs to a standpoint. That’s the point being made again.

k.f: A map is drawn from somewhere and still gets people to the airport.
k.m: The map uses a projection somebody chose. Greenland isn’t that big.

k.f: “There’s no neutral standpoint,” announced from one.
k.m: From one, yes. Where else?

k.f: Cultures disagree about what’s true. That’s a fact about beliefs, and it’s compatible with some of them being wrong.
k.m: Some of it is plain error. Where the difference is in what counts as evidence or as a good life, “wrong” needs a judge both sides accept.

k.f: Different cultures believed different things about what causes disease. One of those beliefs came with penicillin.
k.m: Penicillin is true in every framework that values not dying. Notice the “that.”

k.f: Every culture has its own truth, and they all use the same airplane.
k.m: And they disagree about where it should go.

k.f: If tolerance is good only relative to a framework, the intolerant are right in theirs. The argument for tolerance needs it to be more than relatively good.
k.m: Tolerance doesn’t follow by logic. Seeing your own certainties as local does loosen the urge to impose them, and that’s how it has usually worked.

k.f: If nobody’s wrong, the intolerant aren’t wrong either. He just handed them a permission slip.
k.m: He already had the permission. What he’s lost is the claim that the universe signed it.

k.f: Relativists are very sure, across all cultures, that nobody should be very sure.
k.m: Fairly sure. In this framework.

t.t: “There’s no line between analytic and synthetic”

k.f: Grice and Strawson replied that a distinction people apply consistently to new cases exists, even if it resists a non-circular definition.
k.m: That people sort new sentences alike shows a shared habit. It doesn’t show the sorting marks a difference in kind, and a habit can be explained by how central a belief is.

k.f: “All bachelors are unmarried” and “it’s raining.” If those look like the same kind of sentence, the problem isn’t the distinction.
k.m: “Momentum is mass times velocity” was a definition until relativity made it false. Which kind of sentence was that?

k.f: Quine erased the difference between definitions and facts, and dictionaries kept selling.
k.m: Dictionaries get revised whenever the facts change.

t.t: “Epistemology should be a chapter of psychology”

k.f: Describing how people form beliefs doesn’t say which beliefs they ought to hold. The normative question is the one epistemology was asking.
k.m: The normative part stays as engineering: given the goal of true prediction, which methods work? That’s an empirical question.

k.f: A study of how people actually do arithmetic would conclude that seven times eight is whatever.
k.m: A study of which methods of calculating get right answers would tell you how you ought to do it.

k.f: Quine handed philosophy’s job to psychology, and psychology didn’t want it.
k.m: The psychologists who study reasoning and bias took it. It’s a field now.

t.t: “To be is to be the value of a variable”

k.f: The test says what a theory is committed to, not what exists. It hands the question of what’s real to whoever writes the theory down.
k.m: It’s a test for what a theory says exists. What does exist is settled by which theory is best, and he never claimed otherwise.

k.f: So things exist once they show up in a logic formula. The universe was waiting on notation.
k.m: Things existed before notation. What you’re committed to saying exists is in your notation. Different question.

k.f: His test for existence is whether a logician needs it. Sets made it. Meaning didn’t.
k.m: Sets got in because physics can’t be written without them. That’s the entrance exam.

k.f: In practice translators converge, and constraints from grammar, psychology and shared biology rule out the deviant manuals he imagines.
k.m: Translators converge because they share habits, and the claim is that behavior fixes no more than that. Convergence by habit is what he predicts.

k.f: A native says “gavagai” and points at a rabbit. It means rabbit. Field linguists do this before lunch.
k.m: It means rabbit to a linguist who assumed the native carves the world as he does. That assumption is the finding.

k.f: “Gavagai” might mean undetached rabbit parts, and “Quine” might mean a man who never met a translator.
k.m: And every translation you’ve read was one of several that would have fit.

k.f: Hypotheses are tested in bundles, so a failed prediction never refutes one claim alone, and probabilistic theories aren’t strictly falsifiable at all.
k.m: He knew tests involve auxiliaries. The rule is methodological: say in advance what would count against you, and don’t rescue the theory afterwards with a patch made for the occasion.

k.f: Astrology makes predictions and they fail. So by the rule it’s a science, just a bad one, and now it’s in the building.
k.m: Astrology’s predictions failed and astrologers kept it anyway. Refusing the refutation is what makes it pseudoscience. You’ve described the criterion working.

k.f: Falsifiability can’t be falsified, so Popper is pseudoscience by Popper.
k.m: It’s a proposal for a method, not a claim about nature. Nobody falsifies a rule of chess.

k.f: Scientists have kept theories through decades of anomalies, like Mercury’s orbit under Newton, and were right to. Strict falsification would have killed good theories.
k.m: He distinguished tenacity from evasion. Keeping a theory through an anomaly is fine if you say what would finally count, and the Mercury anomaly was kept on the books as a problem.

k.f: Scientists spend their careers trying to prove their theory right. Nobody has ever applied for a grant to be refuted.
k.m: They try to prove it right, and everyone else in the field tries to prove them wrong. The refuting is done by rivals. That’s why there are journals.

k.f: No scientist has ever dropped a theory over one bad result. They check the cable.
k.m: And when the cable’s fine, they drop it. That’s the part you left out.

k.f: Trusting a well-tested theory about tomorrow is induction under another name. Without it, passing tests gives no reason to rely on a theory in practice.
k.m: Preferring the best-tested theory for action is a decision, and he says nothing better is available. It isn’t a claim that the theory is probably true.

k.f: If induction played no role, engineers would open each bridge with no expectations. They have expectations.
k.m: Engineers expect the bridge to hold because every attempt to break the theory failed. Surviving tests is not the same as piling up confirmations.

k.f: Popper said science doesn’t need induction and then boarded planes.
k.m: He boarded the planes that hadn’t been refuted. That’s the theory.

t.t: “A tolerant society can’t tolerate the intolerant”

k.f: Popper’s footnote is narrow: suppress those who refuse argument and turn to violence. It doesn’t license silencing views someone finds intolerant.
k.m: The narrow version still makes the point: tolerance isn’t a suicide pact. Where the line falls is a judgment call, and that there is a line is what he showed.

k.f: If tolerance has an exception it isn’t tolerance, it’s a guest list. He refuted the open society in his own book about it.
k.m: Every freedom has the exception that protects it. You can’t vote to abolish voting. That’s a lock on the door, not a guest list.

k.f: The paradox of tolerance is a footnote. People have built whole personalities on a footnote.
k.m: It’s a long footnote.

k.f: Popper held that Marx’s theory was falsifiable, was falsified, and was then rescued by its followers. So the test is about how adherents behave, which weakens it as a logical line.
k.m: That is his point: a theory can start out scientific and be made unfalsifiable by the people defending it. The criterion is about how a theory is held.

k.f: Evolution can’t be falsified either, which Popper said himself. He put Darwin in the bin with Freud and then asked for him back.
k.m: He took it back in 1978 once he’d worked out what would count against Darwin. Changing your mind for a reason is the theory in action.

k.f: Popper is every physicist’s favorite philosopher because he’s the only one they’ve heard of.
k.m: They’ve heard of the others. They picked him.

k.f: The revolution picture fits a few episodes in physics and astronomy and fits most of chemistry and biology badly, where change is piecemeal.
k.m: He never said every field has a Copernicus. The claim is that communities work inside shared exemplars, and when those change, the questions change with them. Chemistry had Lavoisier.

k.f: If science moved by revolution, the old science would stop working. Newton still lands rockets. Nothing was overthrown, it got a decimal place.
k.m: Newton’s equations land the rocket. Newton’s universe, with absolute space and instant gravity, is gone. The numbers stayed and the world they describe was replaced.

k.f: A paradigm shift is the old guys dying. Planck said it first and shorter.
k.m: Planck was describing it. Kuhn explained why it has to work that way.

k.f: Physicists who lived through relativity understood and compared both theories, and Kuhn himself later retreated to a much milder version.
k.m: Incommensurable never meant incomparable. It means no neutral language in which both can be fully stated, so some of the comparing is done by judgment, and he said so.

k.f: If they couldn’t be compared, nobody could say the new one was better, so there’d be no reason to switch, and yet everybody switched.
k.m: They switched because the new one solved the puzzles the old one was stuck on. “Better at puzzles” was available the whole time.

k.f: Kuhn says Newton and Einstein can’t be compared, which is odd, because physics students compare them every semester.
k.m: They compare them in Einstein’s terms. Ask a student to state relativity using Newton’s concept of mass.

k.f: Values like simplicity and scope play a part at the margins. That doesn’t make the choice arbitrary, as Kuhn himself kept insisting afterwards.
k.m: He agreed, and the later essays say so: shared values constrain the choice without fixing it. That’s why good scientists can disagree for decades.

k.f: So something else dictates it, and the only other things are money and friends. He said science is a clique and called it history.
k.m: The other things are accuracy, scope, simplicity and fruitfulness. He listed five. You came up with money.

k.f: So science is vibes with funding. Got it.
k.m: He called that reading a misunderstanding for thirty years.

k.f: The success of mature theories, including predictions nobody expected, is hard to explain unless they’re approximately true.
k.m: He granted progress in solving problems. What he doubted is that “closer to the truth” adds anything, since nobody can compare a theory with reality from outside all theories.

k.f: GPS works. Something that isn’t getting closer to the truth doesn’t find a parking lot from orbit.
k.m: Ptolemy’s astronomy navigated ships for a thousand years. Getting places isn’t the same as having the furniture of the universe right.

k.f: Kuhn says science doesn’t get closer to the truth. Typed, presumably, on a computer.
k.m: Typed on a computer built on a quantum theory nobody can agree on the meaning of.

k.f: The picture underrates how much basic criticism goes on in ordinary periods. Popper thought “normal science,” where it exists, is just bad science.
k.m: That it’s routine isn’t a criticism. Only a community committed enough to push one framework to its limits finds the anomalies that matter.

k.f: Puzzles have the answers printed in the back. If science were puzzle-solving they’d have looked.
k.m: No answers in the back, and no guarantee there’s a solution. That’s why he said puzzle and not exercise.

k.f: Kuhn used “paradigm” 21 different ways in one book. Someone counted.
k.m: A new word used 21 ways in its first book is doing well. Try counting “energy” in 1850.

t.t: “Rational belief is updating by Bayes’ rule”

k.f: The rule assumes a reasoner who already sees every logical consequence and every hypothesis. It has nothing to say about a theory nobody had thought of yet.
k.m: It’s a standard of coherence, like logic, and nobody objects to logic because people reason badly. New hypotheses are a known gap that’s being worked on.

k.f: Nobody in history has computed a posterior before crossing the street. So either all of humanity is irrational or the theory describes zero people.
k.m: Nobody solves the equations for a thrown ball either, and people catch. The theory describes what a good catch approximates.

k.f: Nobody has ever actually done the math. They say “I updated.”
k.m: “I updated” beats “I’ve always said.”

k.f: Convergence is proved only in the long run and for people who agree on what’s possible. With real data, different priors give different answers.
k.m: True for the limit theorems. In practice you report how the answer changes across reasonable priors, which is more than rival methods disclose about their own assumptions.

k.f: If priors wash out, they didn’t matter, and if they didn’t matter the theory is “look at the evidence,” which was available.
k.m: They wash out because the evidence overwhelms them. “Look at evidence, in this exact proportion” was not available before 1763.

k.f: The prior is made up, so everything after it is made up to more decimal places.
k.m: Every method has assumptions. Ours are written down.

k.f: The betting arguments show that incoherent beliefs can be exploited by a clever bookie. That’s a practical point, not proof they’re worse as beliefs.
k.m: There are arguments that don’t involve bets: credences that break the axioms are guaranteed to be less accurate than some set that obeys them, whatever the truth is.

k.f: Belief isn’t a number. Nobody is 0.73 married.
k.m: You’re 0.99 married until the paperwork clears. Ask anyone who’s waited on a certificate.

k.f: “70% confident” means “I think so” in a lab coat.
k.m: “I think so” is 70. “Pretty sure” is 90. You already have the numbers, you just won’t say them.

k.f: In practice the results often agree, and Bayesian analyses have their own wiggle room in choosing priors and models.
k.m: Agreed on the wiggle room. The gain is that the question answered is the one people ask: how likely is the hypothesis, given this? A p-value answers something else.

k.f: Frequentist statistics ran every drug trial that worked. Bayes ran a spam filter.
k.m: The spam filter reads forty billion emails a day and it works. The drug trials are still arguing about what “significant” means.

k.f: Frequentists built modern science while Bayesians were still choosing a prior.
k.m: And then they had a replication crisis.

k.f: The rule clashes with continuous probability, where events of probability zero happen, and it seems to forbid full belief in logical truths.
k.m: The measure-zero cases are handled with richer number systems or by treating the rule as advice for hypotheses about the world. Logical truths were always exempt.

k.f: Then the rule itself can’t be held at 100%, so there’s some chance certainty is fine, so I’m taking it.
k.m: You can take it. You just can never learn you were wrong. That’s what the rule was warning about.

k.f: Nobody’s allowed to be 100% sure of anything, including that the moon isn’t cheese.
k.m: I’m not 100% on the moon. I’m 99.9999. That’s the difference between us.

k.f: The argument offers three options. The simulation one needs civilizations that reach that power and then choose to run vast numbers of simulated histories, and there’s no evidence for either.
k.m: Right, and that’s all it claims: one of three things is true. People who say “almost certainly” have picked a branch. The argument itself only removes the comfortable fourth option.

k.f: Simulating a universe takes a computer bigger than the universe. So it has to sit in a bigger universe, and that one’s real, so most things are real.
