k.m: Nobody simulates a universe. You render what’s being looked at. Every video game already does this, and so, as it happens, does quantum mechanics.

k.f: “The odds are a billion to one,” from a calculation where every number is invented.
k.m: Assign your own numbers. Any ones you like. See what comes out.

k.f: That assumes minds don’t depend on what they’re made of, which is the disputed premise. If consciousness needs biology, the simulated crowds contain no one.
k.m: It’s a premise, and it’s stated as one. Most working theories of mind accept it, so the argument is as strong as a mainstream assumption.

k.f: A simulated fire doesn’t burn the computer. A simulated brain doesn’t think in it. Same computer.
k.m: The simulated fire burns the simulated house. Inside is where the question is asked.

k.f: The argument assumes a computer can be conscious, which is the whole thing it needed to show.
k.m: It assumes it out loud, in the first section. That’s called a premise.

k.f: Discreteness and a top speed have ordinary physical explanations, and resemblance to current technology is weak evidence. Earlier ages saw clockwork.
k.m: Agreed, it’s weak evidence, and the argument doesn’t use it. People notice the fit afterwards and nothing rests on that.

k.f: The speed of light is too slow for a good computer. Anyone building a simulation would have picked a faster one. So it’s real, and badly designed.
k.m: A speed limit is what you set when you don’t want players reaching parts you haven’t rendered.

k.f: Simulation theory is God for people with a graphics card.
k.m: God needed six days. This needs a server.

t.t: “It’s a scientific hypothesis, not a religious one”

k.f: Without a prediction that tells it apart from an unsimulated world it works as metaphysics, and the proposed tests assume how the simulators would build it.
k.m: Many cosmological hypotheses can’t yet be tested and are still about what physically exists. That makes it speculative, and it stays a claim about the natural world.

k.f: A creator outside space and time who made everything and might be watching. They changed the font.
k.m: Religion tells you what the creator wants. This one’s creator is a graduate student who’s forgotten the job is running.

k.f: If it can’t be tested, it’s church.
k.m: Then so is the multiverse, and they give out prizes for that.

k.f: It counts hypothetical simulated beings among the people we might be. Choose the comparison group differently and the conclusion changes.
k.m: Every anthropic argument has to pick a comparison group, and he argues for his. It’s the standard difficulty of the field, and it applies to the rival reasoning too.

k.f: Probability needs a sample. The sample of known universes is one, and it isn’t a simulation, so that’s 100% so far.
k.m: A sample of one from inside can’t tell you which kind it is. That’s the whole argument, so thank you.

k.f: Bostrom gave three options and everyone only remembers the fun one.
k.m: The paper says he puts it under a third. The fans rounded up.

k.f: Many past theories were successful and are now judged false at the core, like caloric and the ether. Induction on that record isn’t encouraging.
k.m: The discarded theories were retained in their working parts: Fresnel’s equations survived the ether. Realists commit to what does the predicting.

k.f: Every generation’s best theory turned out wrong. This generation’s is the first one in history that’s right. What are the odds.
k.m: The earlier ones were approximately right, each more than the last. Newton is still good to eight decimals on a bridge.

k.f: Realists believe the current textbook, which is what realists believed about the last one.
k.m: Believed the same core each time, with corrections. That’s what approximately true means.

t.t: “Otherwise the success of science is a miracle”

k.f: Success might be explained by selection: theories that fail are discarded, so the survivors predict well, true or not.
k.m: Selection explains why we have successful theories. It doesn’t explain why any theory can predict things nobody had looked for yet.

k.f: Ptolemy predicted eclipses for fourteen centuries. If success means truth, the sun went round the earth until 1543.
k.m: Ptolemy fit what had been seen. Nobody pointed a telescope where he said and found a new planet.

k.f: “It works, so it’s true” would have made a realist about epicycles.
k.m: Epicycles never predicted anything new. That’s the test, and they fail it.

k.f: What survives theory change is often the equations, not the picture of what the entities are. The electron of 1900 and today’s share little but the name.
k.m: The picture changed and the handle didn’t: the same charge and mass, measured ever more precisely, and you can spray them at a target and things happen.

k.f: The electron has been a ball, a wave, a cloud and a vibration in a field. It’s real, they just can’t say what.
k.m: A person is a child, then an adult, then old, and stays one person.

k.f: Electrons are definitely real, and are also definitely not anything anyone can picture.
k.m: You can’t picture a four-dimensional cube either. Unpicturable isn’t unreal.

t.t: “Science gets closer to the truth over time”

k.f: “Closer” needs a measure of distance from a truth we don’t have independent access to, and attempts to define it formally ran into trouble.
k.m: Closeness can be judged from inside: later theories explain why earlier ones worked where they did, and never the reverse.

k.f: Closer to what? Nobody’s seen the answer key. He’s grading the test against the test.
k.m: Each theory grades the previous one and says where it was off and by how much. That’s a key.

k.f: Science converges on the truth the way a hiker converges on the horizon.
k.m: A hiker with a map that keeps getting more of the coastline right.

k.f: He meant it as what a rationalist would be forced to say after studying history. Taken as advice, it can’t tell astronomy from astrology.
k.m: Right, it’s the conclusion of a reductio. Every rule proposed for science was broken by someone we now call a great scientist, so the rules aren’t the essence.

k.f: If anything goes, so does “not everything goes.” By his rule I’m allowed that, and then he’s done.
k.m: “Not everything goes” is permitted, as one tradition’s house rule. You may keep it at home.

k.f: “Anything goes” is the only philosophy of science that can be learned in two words and applied to nothing.
k.m: Two words is the summary of four hundred pages of history. Read the history.

k.f: Rhetoric was part of it, as it always is. The telescopic evidence and the physics that followed are why the view stuck after the persuading was over.
k.m: The telescope’s reliability for the heavens couldn’t be established at the time, and the physics that later backed him didn’t yet exist. He was right ahead of his evidence.

k.f: Propaganda wears off. The moons of Jupiter are still there.
k.m: They’re there now. In 1610 half the people who looked saw nothing or saw double. He won before the instrument did.

k.f: Feyerabend took the Church’s side against Galileo, four hundred years late, for attention.
k.m: He said the Church had the better argument by the standards of the day. That’s a historical claim, and it’s hard to refute.

k.f: Traditions can be compared by what they deliver. One of them eradicated smallpox and the others didn’t.
k.m: Smallpox is a real result, and people who want it can choose it. The claim is that citizens should decide which traditions guide their lives.

k.f: One of the traditions has antibiotics. When the traditions get sick, they all pick that one.
k.m: They pick it for infections and pick others for dying, raising children and meaning. Free choice is the proposal.

k.f: He defended witchcraft and rain dances, and saw a doctor.
k.m: He saw a traditional healer too, and said it helped. He tried both, which is the position.

t.t: “Science should be separated from the state”

k.f: Public decisions need some standard for evidence. Treating every tradition equally in schools and courts would hand them to whoever shouts.
k.m: Standards of evidence for a decision are chosen by the people deciding, with experts as advisers. That’s already the theory of a jury.

k.f: A state without science builds bridges by vote.
k.m: Juries are laypeople who overrule experts every day. The buildings stand.

k.f: “The worst enemy of science,” he was called, and he put it on the résumé.
k.m: He kept that title because it came from physicists who couldn’t answer the history.

k.f: Simplicity depends on the language a theory is stated in, and there’s no agreed measure. The history of science is full of the more complicated answer winning.
k.m: There are formal measures, and they explain why the rule works: a model with fewer free knobs fits noise less, so it predicts better.

k.f: The simplest explanation for lightning was a god throwing it. One cause, no math.
k.m: “A god did it” explains anything, so it has every knob there is. It only sounds short.

k.f: The simplest explanation is usually that the person citing Occam’s razor wants to stop talking.
k.m: It usually ends the conversation because there’s nothing left to add.

k.f: “Necessity” does all the work. Whether an entity is needed is the question in dispute, so the rule can’t settle it.
k.m: It breaks ties between theories that fit equally well. That’s a narrow job, and it does it.

k.f: One element would be simpler than 118. Chemistry multiplied them anyway, because they were there.
k.m: The elements were needed. “Beyond necessity” is in the rule.

k.f: Ockham never wrote the famous version. The razor is itself an unnecessary entity.
k.m: He wrote four versions. The famous wording is a tidy paraphrase, which is fitting.

k.f: There’s no reason the world must be simple. Simpler theories are easier to use and test, which is a practical virtue and may be nothing more.
k.m: A world needn’t be simple for the rule to work. With limited data, simpler models make fewer errors on new cases, and that’s a theorem.

k.f: The universe has dark matter, eleven kinds of quark behavior and the platypus. It was not consulted on simplicity.
k.m: Four forces and a handful of particles produce the platypus. The complicated part is downstream.

k.f: “Simple” means “the one I already believed.”
k.m: Then test it. Simple models win on data they haven’t seen.

t.t: “It rules out God, souls and conspiracies”

k.f: The razor ranks rival explanations of the same data. It doesn’t say what exists, and both sides of each of those disputes claim the simpler account.
k.m: It ranks. Where one account needs an added entity and explains nothing more, the entity goes. Whether a case is like that is the argument to have.

k.f: A theist says one God is simpler than a trillion brute facts. Same razor. It cuts whichever way it’s held.
k.m: One God with a mind, intentions and unlimited power isn’t one simple thing.

k.f: Occam’s razor has ended zero arguments, because both people are holding one.
k.m: It ends them fine when both people count the same way.

t.t: “Science is the only way to know anything”

k.f: That statement isn’t a scientific finding. It’s a philosophical claim, so by its own standard nobody can know it.
k.m: Call it a methodological bet backed by a record. Every rival source of knowledge has had centuries to produce a result that holds up.

k.f: Then nobody knows that, because no experiment showed it. He’s doing philosophy and he’s bad at it.
k.m: It’s a generalization from four hundred years of every other method losing. That’s evidence.

k.f: “Only science gives knowledge” was established in zero laboratories.
k.m: It was established in every laboratory, one result at a time.

k.f: The people who announce it then go on to offer views about reality, knowledge and method, which is philosophy done without the training.
k.m: The questions aren’t dead. The claim is that the armchair method stopped producing answers once the sciences took its subjects one by one.

k.f: Physicists declare philosophy dead and then spend the next chapter doing it, at the level of a first-year.
k.m: They do it badly and still get further, because they can check.

k.f: Hawking said philosophy is dead in a book whose opening pages are philosophy.
k.m: And the rest of that book has more to say about time than a century of seminars.

t.t: “If it can’t be measured, it isn’t real”

k.f: Measurement presupposes things that aren’t measured: logic, mathematics, the reliability of the instruments, the honesty of the reports.
k.m: Those things are tested by use: logic and instruments are kept because the results come out. That’s measurement at one remove.

k.f: Measure that claim. In what units.
k.m: It’s measured by its results. Fields that count things progress and fields that don’t go in circles.

k.f: “If you can’t measure it, it doesn’t exist” is the motto of everyone who has ruined a workplace.
k.m: Measuring the wrong thing is bad measurement. The cure is better measurement.

k.f: Science can say what increases well-being once well-being is defined and chosen as the goal. The choosing is the ethical part.
k.m: Medicine assumes health is the goal and nobody calls it unscientific. Once you grant that suffering matters, the rest is findings.

k.f: Science can tell someone how to poison a well and how to clean one. It has never once said which.
k.m: It says which wells kill children. If you need more than that to choose, the problem isn’t science.

k.f: “Science can determine values” turned out to mean “assume my values, then science.”
k.m: Every field assumes its goal. Chemistry assumes you want to know what’s in the beaker.

k.f: If it were, its practitioners would visibly outperform. The community’s own writers have asked why they don’t.
k.m: The slogan is a definition of the target, and the same writers were first to ask why results lagged. A group that audits itself is doing the thing.

k.f: If it were winning, they’d be winning. The scoreboard is public.
k.m: Several saw the pandemic, the crypto boom and the AI wave coming before the experts did.

k.f: Rationalists have been systematically winning for twenty years, mostly at writing blog posts about it.
k.m: A blog that called the three biggest stories of the decade early.

k.f: Knowing about biases does little to reduce them, and can make people better at spotting them in others.
k.m: Agreed for general knowledge of biases. Specific habits do work: keeping score on forecasts measurably improves them, and that was the practice all along.

k.f: The research says learning about biases mostly teaches people to find them in whoever they’re arguing with. So that worked.
k.m: Forecasting with scorekeeping makes people measurably better calibrated. That part trains fine.

k.f: They learned the name of every cognitive bias and now have all of them, with citations.
k.m: Having the names beats having them and not knowing.

k.f: A million words by one self-taught author, largely restating existing philosophy and statistics without engaging the literature, is not a canon.
k.m: It’s an on-ramp written for people who’d never open a journal. Most of the field’s later ideas reached their audience that way.

k.f: Every field has a textbook. This one has a very long blog and a Harry Potter fan fiction, and the fan fiction is longer.
k.m: A long blog that got a generation to read about probability. Textbooks had their chance.

k.f: “Read the Sequences” is “do your own research” for people with a higher SAT score.
k.m: It tells you to check it, with the math attached.

k.f: Multiplying made-up probabilities by made-up magnitudes gives made-up answers with false precision, and lets a tiny chance of a huge payoff swamp everything.
k.m: The point was narrow: don’t let a vivid single case outweigh a larger number of real ones. The mugging problem was named and published by the same people.

k.f: A one-in-a-trillion chance of infinite value is still infinite. So the math says to give the wallet to anyone who mentions infinity.
k.m: That’s a known problem. They found it, named it and wrote the papers on it.

k.f: They multiplied, and the answer was that the most important thing in the universe is their own field.
k.m: When the math says your field matters, you either go where it says or admit you weren’t doing math.

k.f: Use doesn’t fix meaning without some account of correct use, and it doesn’t explain how people understand sentences they’ve never heard before.
k.m: Correct use is fixed by shared practice and training, and that’s the account. Rules for building sentences are part of the practice too.

k.f: People use “literally” to mean “not literally.” If meaning were use that would be fine, and it isn’t. Ask anyone.
k.m: Everyone understands that “literally.” That’s meaning. The people complaining understand it best.

k.f: Late Wittgenstein: words mean how people use them. Dictionaries had this.
k.m: Dictionaries are compiled by watching how people use words.

k.f: Many problems survive careful rewording: consciousness, induction, identity. That they dissolve was asserted more than shown, and is itself a philosophical thesis.
k.m: He never said one move dissolves them all. The work is case by case, and the claim is about where their grip comes from, which is why they return in new clothes.

k.f: Then translating them into another language would make them go away. They’ve been translated into all of them.
k.m: They’ve been mistranslated into all of them. Every language has the same few pictures built in.

k.f: He didn’t solve philosophical problems, he told people to stop asking. Any dad can do that.
k.m: Any dad can say it. Getting the fly out of the bottle is the hard part.

k.f: The argument’s structure is disputed. If it rests on doubting memory it proves too much, since public checks use memory too.
k.m: The point isn’t about memory. In a private case there’d be no difference between following the rule and thinking you are, so “rule” has nothing to hold on to.

k.f: Diaries exist. People write in codes only they know. That’s a private language, and it’s been in drawers for centuries.
k.m: A code is a translation of a public language. He meant words for what only you could ever have, with no key even in principle.

k.f: Wittgenstein fans don’t answer questions. They ask what game the question is playing.
k.m: And that reply was a move in one.

t.t: “The Tractatus shows the limits of what can be said”

k.f: By its own theory its sentences are nonsense, and the image of a ladder to be thrown away admits that without explaining how nonsense shows anything.
k.m: The book says it can only show its point and must be thrown away after. Whether that can work is the question it deliberately leaves you with.

k.f: A limit that can be described has been crossed. He drew the fence from the far side.
k.m: He says so himself: to draw a limit to thought you’d have to think both sides. That’s why he draws it in language instead.

k.f: The Tractatus ends by saying everything in it is nonsense. Agreed.
k.m: Agreed is the right answer. You’ve finished the book.

t.t: “What can’t be said must be passed over in silence”

k.f: The line sends ethics, art and the book itself into silence. Ramsey’s reply: what can’t be said can’t be said, and it can’t be whistled either.
k.m: He thought those things were the most important, and that talk damages them. The silence is respect, and Ramsey’s joke assumes it was dismissal.

k.f: Everything can be spoken of. I just spoke of the thing that can’t be. That was it.
k.m: You said the words. You didn’t say the thing. That’s the distinction, and you just illustrated it.

k.f: “Whereof one cannot speak,” from a man who would not stop.
k.m: He published one short book in his lifetime.

k.f: The principle is neither true by definition nor verifiable, so it fails its own test, and every attempt to state it precisely let in everything or shut out science.
k.m: It was offered as a proposal for how to use “meaningful” in science, and proposals are judged by usefulness. On that reading it doesn’t apply to itself.

k.f: “There’s a teapot nobody can ever detect” can’t be verified, and everyone understood it immediately. That’s what meaning is.
k.m: You understood the grammar. Ask yourself what would be different if it were false, and notice you can’t say.

k.f: “Only verifiable statements have meaning” is not verifiable. One sentence, own goal.
k.m: It’s a rule, not a statement. Rules don’t score own goals.

k.f: Rejecting metaphysics took commitments about meaning and experience that were themselves metaphysical, and later analytic philosophy let ontology back in.
k.m: The target was claims that no experience could bear on. The later ontology is tied to what science needs, which is the reform they were asking for.

k.f: Saying nothing exists beyond experience is a claim about what exists. They did metaphysics for thirty years and billed it as hygiene.
k.m: “We can’t talk about what’s beyond experience” is a remark about talking. Nothing beyond experience was mentioned.

k.f: The Vienna Circle set out to end metaphysics and ended themselves.
k.m: They ended because their country was taken over, and then they staffed half the philosophy departments in America.

k.f: Moral sentences sit inside “if” clauses and arguments where nothing is being expressed, and they keep their meaning and their logic there.
k.m: The embedding problem has detailed answers now, built on the attitudes that complex sentences express. It’s a research program with results.

k.f: If “murder is wrong” just means “boo murder,” courtrooms are sporting events, and the home team has won every trial.
k.m: Trials are about facts: did he do it. The booing comes at sentencing, and it’s quite audible.

k.f: Positivism said ethics is just cheering. Then the 1930s happened around them.
k.m: They booed. Several of them had to flee for it.

t.t: “Truths of logic and math are true by convention”

k.f: Quine: there’s no non-circular account of truth by meaning alone, and no statement is immune to revision.
k.m: Quine attacked one account of it. That adopting a framework differs from making a claim inside it survived him, and Carnap’s version is still defended.

k.f: Conventions are decided by people. So with enough votes 2+2 would be 5. They never explained why nobody’s tried.
k.m: You can vote that “5” names what “4” used to. The arithmetic doesn’t move, only the spelling. That’s what convention covers.

k.f: Ayer was asked later what was wrong with positivism and said nearly all of it was false.
k.m: He said the spirit was right, in the same interview.

t.t: “Philosophy should be the logic of science”

k.f: Actual scientific practice turned out not to fit the reconstructions, and scientists made little use of them.
k.m: The reconstructions were about justification, how a theory relates to its evidence, and were never meant as histories of the laboratory.

k.f: Science already has a logic. It’s called math, and the people who do it are called scientists. The position was filled.
k.m: Scientists argue constantly about what counts as confirming a theory. That’s the job, and it isn’t math.

k.f: Positivism is philosophy trying to get hired by the physics department.
k.m: Half of them were physicists already. Schlick studied under Planck.

t.t: “Clarity and rigor are how philosophy progresses”

k.f: Rigor on small questions can be bought by avoiding the large ones, and the tradition’s own surveys show standing disagreement on nearly every major issue.
k.m: The agreement is in what’s been ruled out and in the distinctions everyone now uses. Positions survive, and bad arguments for them mostly don’t.

k.f: A hundred years of rigor and the surveys still split on everything. If rigor produced progress there’d be one thing they agreed on.
k.m: They agree on which arguments are valid. That’s the progress, and the other tradition can’t say the same.

k.f: Clarity is the only virtue, which is easy when nothing’s being said.
k.m: Something’s being said. It’s just possible to tell what, which you’re not used to.

k.f: Some studies find case intuitions shift with wording, order and culture. Even where they’re stable, it’s unclear why they’d track the truth.
k.m: The variation findings largely failed to replicate, and core judgments turn out stable across cultures. And every inquiry starts from what seems true.

k.f: Intuition said the earth was flat and heavy things fall faster. It’s 0 for everything it’s been tested on, so they kept it for the untestable stuff.
k.m: Those were predictions about the world. Intuitions about what counts as knowing are about our own concept, and we’re the authority on that.

k.f: “Intuitively” means “my friends and I think.”
k.m: Your objection was an intuition.

k.f: Far-fetched cases may run past the conditions where our concepts are reliable. Verdicts about a man made by lightning in a swamp say little about minds as they are.
k.m: A far-fetched case isolates one variable, as a frictionless plane does in physics. Unrealistic and uninformative are different things.

k.f: An experiment has equipment and a result nobody chose. A thought experiment is a story where the author decides the ending.
k.m: Galileo refuted Aristotle on falling bodies with a thought experiment. Two weights and a string, no equipment.

k.f: Fake barns, swamp men, twin earth. It’s science fiction with worse plots.
k.m: Plots are for people who need to be entertained to follow an argument.

k.f: Formalizing moves the dispute to the premises and to whether the symbols fit. Valid arguments with contested premises are everywhere.
k.m: Moving the dispute to the premises is the service. You find out exactly where you disagree, and most arguments never get that far.

k.f: Putting P and Q on a sentence doesn’t make it truer. “If P then pizza” is valid.
k.m: Yes, valid. And now you can see the problem is the premise. Took four seconds. That’s the tool working.

k.f: Analytic philosophers number their sentences so it looks like something is being calculated.
k.m: So you can say which one you reject. Try that with a paragraph of Hegel.

k.f: The divide is mostly sociological. Analytic work has its own unreadable jargon, and many continental texts make arguments analytic philosophers later rediscovered.
k.m: Fair on the sociology. A real difference remains: here a claim is expected to be stated so that someone can show it false, and jargon answers to that.

k.f: The continentals at least wrote about death, sex and power. The analytics picked “the present king of France is bald.” One of those has readers.
k.m: Having readers was never the test. Horoscopes have readers.

k.f: Analytic philosophy is a hundred years on the word “the.”
k.m: And it got the word right.

k.f: Strictly yes, though Gödel drew large philosophical morals from it himself, so wider uses aren’t all illegitimate.
k.m: He was careful to label those as philosophy, with extra premises. The theorem licenses the claims with the hypotheses attached, and none of the loose ones.

k.f: A legal code is a set of rules meant to be consistent and complete. That’s a formal system. So there are true verdicts no court can reach.
k.m: A legal code isn’t recursively axiomatized and doesn’t contain arithmetic. Those are the two conditions. It has neither.

k.f: Incompleteness applies to every system: legal systems, political systems, relationships.
k.m: Relationships don’t encode Peano arithmetic. Yours might, I haven’t asked.

t.t: “It says nothing about minds versus machines”

k.f: Gödel thought it did. His own conclusion was that either the mind outruns every machine or there are mathematical problems nobody can ever solve. That isn’t nothing.
k.m: His disjunction stands. To get anything about minds you must add that the mind is consistent and can know it, and nobody has earned that premise.

k.f: A machine can’t see that its own Gödel sentence is true and a person can. That’s the whole theorem, and it took one line.
k.m: A person can’t see it’s true either. They can see it’s true if the system is consistent, and so can a machine. Same position.

k.f: Gödel’s theorem is why AI can never match a human mind.
k.m: A human can’t prove their own consistency either. Most don’t even try.

k.f: Right, though the second theorem does mean no proof of arithmetic’s consistency can be had from within arithmetic. That is a real limit on what can be secured.
k.m: Agreed, that’s the second theorem. Consistency is provable in stronger systems, so the limit is on self-certification, and nothing suggests arithmetic is in trouble.

k.f: A system that can’t prove it’s consistent might not be. Nobody would fly an airline that can’t prove its planes land.
k.m: No airline proves that from inside the cockpit. You check from outside, with a stronger system. It’s called the ground.

k.f: Gödel proved math is broken.
k.m: He proved that one specific kind of proof can’t exist. Everything else is fine. Go balance your checkbook.

k.f: The construction does adapt the liar. What’s new is that “provable” can be defined inside arithmetic and “true” can’t. “Just” is unfair, and “isn’t” overstates.
k.m: Fair. The liar yields a contradiction and his sentence yields a theorem, and that difference between truth and provability is the whole content.

k.f: “This sentence can’t be proved.” Proved, it’s false. Unproved, it’s true. That’s the liar with one word swapped, and the word was the easy part.
k.m: The easy word turns a paradox into a proof. If it were that easy, somebody in the previous 2,300 years would have swapped it.

k.f: Gödel basically wrote “this sentence is false” in math and got famous.
k.m: The liar is false if true. His is true and unprovable. Different sentence, different century, different result.

k.f: It shows truth in the standard model outruns proof in any one system. A formalist reads the same sentence as provable in a stronger system, with no realm of truths needed.
k.m: The stronger system has its own unprovable sentence, and we judge each of those true as we go. Formalism has to explain that judgment without the word.

k.f: A truth nobody can prove is called an opinion. He formalized having one.
k.m: Then Goldbach’s conjecture is an opinion, and so was Fermat’s until 1994, when it got promoted.

k.f: Gödel showed there are truths logic can’t reach, which is basically proof of intuition.
k.m: It’s proof that the sentence is true if the axioms are consistent. That’s all. It’s enough.

t.t: “His ontological proof is serious modal logic”

k.f: The axioms about “positive properties” carry the conclusion, and the system makes everything true necessarily true, which nobody wants.
k.m: Collapse can be blocked by weakening one axiom, and later versions do it. It’s a valid derivation, and the argument is over the premises, as with any proof.

k.f: A computer checked it in 2013. Computers don’t make mistakes, so God exists and it’s reproducible.
k.m: The computer checked that the conclusion follows. It also found his axioms were inconsistent in one version. Both results are reproducible.

k.f: Gödel proved God exists, in symbols. Still unrefuted.
k.m: Unrefuted and unsound are different words.

k.f: What a “sense” is has never been made clear, and direct reference theorists argue that names contribute only their bearers.
k.m: Direct reference still has to explain how “Hesperus is Phosphorus” can be news. Whatever does that job is what he called sense.

k.f: “The morning star is the evening star.” It’s Venus. It was always Venus. He built a theory on not knowing that.
k.m: The Babylonians didn’t know it was Venus and tracked both for centuries. Explaining how that’s possible is the theory.

k.f: Frege discovered that the same thing can have two names.
k.m: And that finding it out can take a thousand years. Explain that without him.

k.f: Russell’s paradox showed his system inconsistent, and repaired versions need axioms, like the existence of infinitely many things, that aren’t plausibly logic.
k.m: The contradiction came from one axiom. Drop it and a single principle about number still yields all of arithmetic, which is most of what he wanted.

k.f: Logic says if P then P. Arithmetic says there are infinitely many primes. One of those is about something.
k.m: The primes follow from definitions and logic alone, once number is defined. He showed how.

k.f: Frege spent twenty years reducing arithmetic to logic, and Russell broke it with a one-page letter.
k.m: He answered the letter the same week and printed the problem in his own appendix. That’s how it’s done.

k.f: Putting meanings in a third realm, neither mental nor physical, raises the question of how minds in this one ever get hold of them.
k.m: The alternative is that the Pythagorean theorem is a different thought in each head. Shared content has to live somewhere other than in individual minds.

k.f: Meanings are in a realm outside space, time and minds, and somehow every toddler finds it by age two.
k.m: Two toddlers who learn “two” have learned the same thing. Whatever that is, it isn’t located in either of them.

k.f: He threw psychology out of logic, and logic has been explaining nothing about how people think ever since.
k.m: It explains how they can be wrong. Psychology only says what they did.

k.f: He did, in a notation so unwieldy nobody used it. The logic the world learned came through Peano and Russell.
k.m: The ideas are what counted: quantifiers, variables, and a proof as a checkable sequence. Peano and Russell both said where they got them.

k.f: A founder whose notation nobody could read is a founder nobody followed. Peano did the part that got used.
k.m: Peano and Russell rewrote him in a friendlier script. The content was his.

k.f: His notation was two-dimensional and the printers hated it. So did everyone else.
k.m: The printers hated Principia too.

t.t: ““The present king of France is bald” is false, not meaningless”

k.f: Strawson: the sentence doesn’t assert that there’s a king, it presupposes it, and when the presupposition fails the question of truth doesn’t arise.
k.m: Strawson’s view needs sentences that are neither true nor false. Russell keeps ordinary logic and explains the oddness as a hidden claim that something exists.

k.f: There’s no king of France. So it’s not true and not false, it’s a mistake. Anyone asked on the street says “France doesn’t have a king.”
k.m: “It’s a mistake” is the theory: the mistake is that it asserts there’s a king. He told you what kind.

k.f: Russell’s great contribution was a sentence about a king who doesn’t exist. It’s still his most cited work.
k.m: Fourteen pages that showed grammar can hide what’s being claimed. Every later analysis copies the move.

k.f: Principia needed axioms of infinity and reducibility that nobody thought were logical truths, and then Gödel showed no such system could be complete.
k.m: The full reduction failed. What it left is modern logic, type theory and the first proof that the question could be put exactly. Gödel proved his theorem about Principia.

k.f: It takes several hundred pages to reach 1+1=2. If the foundation is that much harder than the building, it’s not the foundation.
k.m: Foundations are always harder than the building. Go and look at what’s under a skyscraper.

k.f: Principia Mathematica proves 1+1=2 a few hundred pages in, with the comment that this is occasionally useful.
k.m: It’s a joke. He wrote it. He was funnier than his critics.

t.t: “The theory of types solves the paradoxes”

k.f: It blocks them by forbidding the sentences, which also forbids harmless ones, and the hierarchy can’t be stated without violating itself.
k.m: Every later set theory blocks the paradox by restricting what counts as a set. Types were the first version of the idea that won.

k.f: He fixed the paradox by making it illegal to say. That’s not a solution, that’s a noise ordinance.
k.m: A function that can’t take itself as input is how every typed programming language works. The ordinance is running on your phone.

k.f: Russell found the paradox, and his fix was that nobody’s allowed to talk about it.
k.m: He found the hole in the foundations of mathematics and published it. That’s talking about it.

t.t: “Philosophy should be done with scientific method”

k.f: His own views changed with nearly every book, which doesn’t suggest a method converging on results.
k.m: Changing your view when an argument fails is the scientific part. The ones who never revised weren’t doing better.

k.f: Science settles things. He held about six philosophies in sixty years and was certain during each.
k.m: Six theories, each given up for stated reasons, in print. That’s what a method looks like from outside.

k.f: Russell changed his mind so often that Broad said he produced a new system every few years. He was right about one of them, maybe.
k.m: Broad was right. Changing your mind was the point.

k.f: Descriptivists reply that names can be tied to descriptions that are themselves rigid, such as “the actual so-and-so.”
k.m: A description fixed with “actual” works because the reference is being held steady from outside. The rescue borrows the idea it’s resisting.

k.f: “Aristotle” refers to Aristotle in every possible world. Yes. That’s what a name is. That was the lecture.
k.m: It’s what a name is, and for sixty years the standard theory said a name was a disguised description. Someone had to say it.

k.f: Kripke’s discovery was that a name is the name of the thing it names.
k.m: It sounds trivial now. That’s what winning looks like.

t.t: “Water is necessarily H2O, though we found that out”

k.f: The necessity depends on how “water” was fixed. If it meant “the clear drinkable stuff,” other worlds would have water that isn’t H2O.
k.m: He grants that the reference could have been fixed differently. Given that the word picks out this stuff, anything without its makeup isn’t it, however it looks.

k.f: If it was necessary, nobody would have needed a lab. Necessary things are known from a chair. That’s the definition.
k.m: Whether water is H2O took a lab. That it couldn’t have been anything else, once it is, takes an argument. Two questions.

k.f: Water is H2O in every possible world. It took a philosopher to add “possible world” to a chemistry fact.
k.m: “Possible world” is what tells you a fact couldn’t have been otherwise. Chemistry doesn’t say that part.

t.t: “Reference is fixed by a causal chain back to a baptism”

k.f: Reference can shift: “Madagascar” once named part of the mainland. A chain back to the first use gives the wrong answer there.
k.m: He offered a picture and said it wasn’t a theory. The Madagascar case refines it: later intentions to refer can re-anchor a name.

k.f: Nobody baptized “Santa Claus” by pointing at him. The chain goes back to nothing, and every kid still knows who’s meant.
k.m: The chain goes back to the stories, and that’s what makes it a name for a fictional figure. The picture covers it.

k.f: Naming and Necessity is a transcript. He gave it without notes and never wrote the book. That’s the level of effort.
k.m: Without notes, at twenty-nine, and the field reorganized around it. Effort isn’t the measure.

k.f: If no fact fixes what anyone means, the argument’s own words mean nothing in particular. Most readers take that as a reason to reject a premise.
k.m: He presents it as a problem he found in Wittgenstein and offers a solution through community practice. Whether it works is open, and the problem is real.

k.f: I meant plus. I know because I was there. He can ask.
k.m: “I was there” is a fact about feeling certain. The question is what made it plus and not something that agrees on every sum you’ve done.

k.f: Kripke proved nobody means anything by “plus,” and then everyone kept adding.
k.m: Yes. And nobody has said what makes it adding. That’s the result.

t.t: “Language rests on an innate universal grammar”

k.f: Decades of proposed universals have shrunk under cross-linguistic evidence, and what remains is thin enough that critics ask what the claim now is.
k.m: The list has been pared down to the core: structures built by one recursive operation. A narrower claim is what progress looks like in a science.

k.f: If grammar was built in, there’d be one language. There are seven thousand, and they don’t agree about where the verb goes.
k.m: Seven thousand languages and every one has structure-dependent rules and none counts words. That’s the universal.

k.f: Universal grammar has been revised until the only universal left is that Chomsky was right.
k.m: The data keep agreeing with him. It’s awkward for everyone.

t.t: “Children hear too little to learn it from experience”

k.f: Children hear millions of sentences, and statistical learners get much further from that input than the argument assumed in the 1960s.
k.m: The point isn’t quantity. Children never try certain errors that the input doesn’t rule out, such as rules based on word order alone.

k.f: Kids hear about thirty million words by age four. That’s not a poverty of anything.
k.m: Thirty million words and not one saying “the following would be ungrammatical.” They know anyway.

k.f: The poverty of the stimulus was a claim about how much data kids get, made before anyone counted.
k.m: People have counted since. The missing evidence is still missing.

k.f: The claim that language appeared by a single mutation in one individual, for inner use, has almost no support among people who study evolution.
k.m: Most language use is silent and internal. Whatever the origin, a system built for communicating would be far less ambiguous than this one.

k.f: A language used by one person, silently, isn’t a language. It’s a guy thinking.
k.m: You talk to yourself all day. That’s most of what it’s used for.

k.f: His theory is that the first speaker had nobody to talk to. That’s a lecture, not an origin.
k.m: Everyone’s first audience is themselves.

t.t: “Language models tell us nothing about language”

k.f: Systems that learn fluent grammar from text alone are at least evidence about what can be learned without built-in rules, which was his central claim.
k.m: Fluency from a trillion words shows what can be learned with that much text. How a child does it on a tiny fraction of that was always the question.

k.f: It learned English from reading. He said that was impossible in 1957, and his answer now is that it doesn’t count.
k.m: It read more text than a child could hear in ten thousand lifetimes. That’s the opposite of his problem.

k.f: A machine learned grammar from examples and he said it wasn’t real grammar. He’s been grading the same paper since Eisenhower.
k.m: It needed the whole internet. A child needs a few years of a parent mumbling.

k.f: The measured effects are small and local, such as slightly faster color discrimination across a named boundary. The strong version has no support.
k.m: Small and real is the modern claim. Effects on color, number, space and the gender of objects replicate, and they show up where the language forces a habit.

k.f: People think of things they have no word for all the time. That’s why they say “the thing, you know, the thing.”
k.m: People with no number words can’t match eleven nuts to eleven sticks. “The thing” doesn’t cover it.

k.f: Linguistic relativity is real and worth about forty milliseconds.
k.m: Forty milliseconds on every sentence, all your life.

t.t: “Speakers of different languages live in different worlds”

k.f: Translation works, and people learn second languages without reporting a change of universe.
k.m: Translation works for content. The claim is about defaults: what your language makes you mark every time becomes what you notice without trying.

k.f: Bilingual people would be commuting between worlds. They report it as “knowing two words for bread.”
k.m: Speakers who use compass directions for everything always know which way north is. You’d need an app.

k.f: Different languages, different worlds, same traffic.
k.m: Ask people from two languages who was at fault in the accident. The grammar shows up in the answers.

t.t: “The Hopi have no concept of time”

k.f: A linguist later documented Hopi tense, time words and calendars at book length. The claim came from limited data and wishful reading.
k.m: He was wrong about Hopi. One bad example doesn’t settle the hypothesis, and the modern evidence comes from experiments.

k.f: Someone checked. They have words for yesterday, tomorrow and late. Six hundred pages of them.
k.m: Fine, strike Hopi. There are languages where the future is behind you and speakers gesture that way.

k.f: Whorf was a fire insurance inspector. The Hopi time claim is what happens when one investigates a language part-time.
k.m: He published in the linguistics journals and Sapir vouched for him. The day job isn’t an argument.

t.t: “Change the words and you change the thinking”

k.f: Renaming things mostly moves the old attitudes onto the new name. The evidence that vocabulary reform changes beliefs is weak.
k.m: Vocabulary reform is the weak form of it. The stronger evidence is grammatical: what a language makes you say each time.

k.f: Every new polite word becomes the rude word in ten years. The thought moved in and kept the furniture.
k.m: The new word buys ten years. That’s ten years.

k.f: The Eskimo snow words thing isn’t true either. Nobody checks anything in this theory.
k.m: Linguists struck that example decades ago. The experiments came after.

k.f: Ordinary language has one truth predicate that applies to its own sentences. A hierarchy describes a different, tidier language, not ours.
k.m: It was never offered as a description of English. He showed that English, taken as it is, is inconsistent, and gave a repair.

k.f: English doesn’t have levels. People say “that’s true” about sentences containing “true” all day and nothing explodes.
k.m: Nothing explodes because nobody follows it through. He did.

k.f: Tarski solved the liar by moving to a language nobody speaks.
k.m: A language in which mathematics can be done without contradiction. It has speakers.

k.f: If one contradiction can be true, the usual reason for ever rejecting a theory, that it contradicts itself, is gone.
k.m: A theory can still be rejected for being false, unsupported or trivial. All that’s given up is one rule of inference, and logics without it are well understood.

k.f: If contradictions can be true, then they also can’t. He has to accept that. Those are his rules.
k.m: That’s fine. Some contradictions are true and that one isn’t among them. I’m allowed to tell them apart.

k.f: Dialetheism is true. Also false. Its defenders are fine with this, and also not.
k.m: Only a few of them. This is one. Yours isn’t.

t.t: “The liar sentence is neither true nor false”

k.f: Then “this sentence is not true” comes back: if it’s neither, it’s not true, which is what it says, so it’s true.
k.m: The revenge sentence is the standing difficulty. Theories with a truth predicate that never becomes fully defined handle it without a new gap.

k.f: “This sentence is not true.” Neither? Then it’s not true. Then it’s right. He moved the problem one inch.
k.m: It moved an inch, into a region where the theory is exact. That’s what a partial solution is.

k.f: Every solution to the liar has a revenge version, and every revenge version has a paper.
k.m: That’s a field making progress one step at a time.

t.t: “It reveals a flaw in our concept of truth”

k.f: It may reveal only that some grammatical sentences fail to say anything, the way “the largest number” fails to pick anything out.
k.m: “The largest number” fails for a statable reason. The liar sentence is built from parts that each work, by rules that otherwise work, and that’s the flaw being shown.

k.f: It’s a sentence about nothing. “This sentence” doesn’t say anything to be false about. It’s a trick with a pronoun.
k.m: “This sentence has five words” says something, with the same pronoun. The trick isn’t in the pronoun.

k.f: The liar paradox is 2,400 years old and has produced no lies.
k.m: It produced the theory of truth and one of Gödel’s theorems. That’s a decent return.

t.t: “There’s no sharp line between a heap and a non-heap”

k.f: If there’s no line, then one grain is a heap or a million grains isn’t. Logic forces a line somewhere, however unwelcome.
k.m: Logic forces a line only if every statement is flatly true or false. The lesson may be that this is the assumption to give up.

k.f: One grain isn’t a heap. Add one, still not. So nothing’s ever a heap, and yet there’s one in the yard. The argument lost to a pile of sand.
k.m: And yet there’s one in the yard and none on the table. So the word works and the argument is what’s off.

k.f: The sorites paradox is the discovery that “pile” isn’t a unit.
k.m: It’s the discovery that most words are like that, and logic was built for the ones that aren’t.

t.t: “There is a sharp line; we just can’t know where”

k.f: It’s hard to believe that usage fixes an exact grain at which sand becomes a heap, with nothing about how we talk determining which.
k.m: It’s hard to believe and it keeps ordinary logic whole. Every rival ends up with a cutoff somewhere it also can’t locate.

k.f: So there’s an exact hair that makes a man bald and nobody can ever find it. That’s not a theory, it’s a ghost story.
k.m: There’s an exact number of hairs on your head and you can’t find that out either.

k.f: Epistemicism says there’s a precise minute when someone becomes old, and it’s a secret.
k.m: There’s a precise second when you fell asleep last night. Also a secret.

k.f: Degrees just move the problem: there has to be a sharp line where “fully true” ends, and nobody believes in that one either.
k.m: The second-order worry is real, and it’s about the model’s numbers. A map with exact contour lines doesn’t claim the hill has edges.

k.f: “It’s 0.6 true that he’s tall.” Nobody has ever said that. A theory of language should include one thing a person has said.
k.m: “Sort of tall,” “tallish,” “pretty tall.” People say it all day. They leave out the decimal.

k.f: Fuzzy logic: for when someone wants to be wrong to two decimal places.
k.m: It runs the anti-lock brakes in your car.

t.t: “Vagueness is in language, not the world”

k.f: Clouds and mountains seem to lack sharp borders whatever we call them. It’s unclear that tidying the language would tidy them.
k.m: The cloud has droplets with exact positions. “Cloud” doesn’t say which to count, and that’s a fact about the word.

k.f: Where does a mountain stop? That’s not a word problem. Go stand on it.
k.m: Every rock on it has a location. The boundary is our rounding.

k.f: “It’s just semantics” has been said about every problem by someone who then couldn’t solve it.
k.m: It’s semantics, and semantics is hard. That’s the claim.

k.f: Adding everyone up ignores that people are separate. It allows severe losses for a few in exchange for small gains to many.
k.m: Counting each person once and no one for more is how it respects persons. The alternative gives some people’s interests a veto over other people’s lives.

k.f: Nobody knows what overall well-being is, so nobody can maximize it. Every utilitarian has been doing something else the whole time and calling it that.
k.m: Nobody knows exactly what health is either, and hospitals still improve it. Rough measures of misery are enough to tell a famine from a picnic.

k.f: Nobody can measure happiness, so the whole thing is arithmetic on vibes.
k.m: You can tell a broken leg is worse than a stubbed toe. Congratulations, you’ve done the arithmetic.

k.f: Transplant and scapegoat cases suggest some constraints matter in themselves. Replies that appeal to rules or long-run effects concede the verdict and move it.
k.m: A world where surgeons harvest visitors is a world where nobody goes to hospitals. The verdict comes from counting everything, which is what the theory says to do.

k.f: Consequences never end. Every act is still having them. So no act can ever be scored, and the theory has never produced a result.
k.m: Forecasts never end either, and you still bring an umbrella. You act on what can be foreseen. Nobody waits for the last consequence.

k.f: A surgeon has five dying patients and one healthy visitor. Utilitarianism has notes.
k.m: The notes say no. Nobody would ever see a doctor again. We did the math.

k.f: Strict impartiality leaves no room for special duties to family and friends, which most people take to be the center of moral life.
k.m: Impartial at the level of justification, partial in practice: a world where people look after their own goes better. The theory endorses the loyalty. It just explains it.

k.f: If everyone counts equally, so does the utilitarian, so he may as well keep the money. The theory funds itself.
k.m: He keeps it only if he’s the best use of it. He almost never is. That’s the theory, and it’s why they give so much away.

k.f: Ask a utilitarian to pick between their mom and two strangers and they have to think about it.
k.m: Two strangers also have moms.

k.f: Ranking pleasures by quality gives up the single measure that made the theory attractive, and Mill’s test of experienced judges brings in a standard that isn’t pleasure.
k.m: Mill was patching hedonism in a hurry. The modern theory counts whatever makes a life go better for the one living it, and drops the ranking.

k.f: The people who have tried both poetry and video games mostly went back to the video games. That’s the judges’ verdict, and Mill threw it out.
k.m: Ask them at eighty which evenings they’d keep. The judges’ verdict comes in late, and it isn’t the games.

k.f: Mill said some pleasures are higher than others, and the higher ones turned out to be his hobbies.
k.m: Somebody’s hobbies had to be on top. Yours were considered.

k.f: Either the rule gives way whenever breaking it does more good, and it’s the old theory again, or it’s followed anyway, and that’s rule worship.
k.m: The rule is kept because agents who break rules whenever their own sums say so do worse overall: they miscalculate and nobody can trust them. That’s a consequence.

k.f: A rule that says “maximize, except when it looks bad” isn’t a theory. It’s PR.
k.m: “Don’t frame innocent people” isn’t PR. It’s what you get when you include the cost of everyone finding out, which they do.

k.f: A utilitarian would frame an innocent man to stop a riot and call it Tuesday.
k.m: And your theory lets the riot kill hundreds so your hands stay clean. Call that Tuesday.

t.t: “Act only on maxims you could universalize”

k.f: The test depends on how the maxim is worded. Word it narrowly and nearly anything passes, while harmless maxims like “play tennis when the courts are empty” fail.
k.m: The maxim is your actual reason for acting, and you don’t get to pick its wording. Gerrymandered descriptions aren’t what you’re acting on, and judgment about that is part of the test.

k.f: If everyone became a dentist, society would collapse. So being a dentist is immoral. It’s his rule.
k.m: The maxim is “take up a trade I’m suited to in a society that needs many.” Everyone can will that. You universalized the job title.

k.f: The categorical imperative is the golden rule, long version.
k.m: The golden rule lets a masochist hurt people. The long version is long because that had to be fixed.

t.t: “Never lie, even to the murderer at the door”

k.f: Most Kantians now think Kant misapplied his own theory, and that deceiving an aggressor passes the test.
k.m: Right, and that’s the system correcting its author. The principle of respecting persons can be defended on its own terms without the 1797 essay.

k.f: The murderer would have found him anyway. Murderers check. So the lie doesn’t even help, and Kant is right for the wrong reason, which in Kant is still wrong.
k.m: He’s wrong about the case and the reason still matters: once you lie for good outcomes, you answer for every outcome. He was pointing at who owns what follows.

k.f: Kant said no lying to the murderer at the door. Whole system, one example.
k.m: It’s one late essay. Judge Newton by the alchemy while you’re at it.

t.t: “Treat people as ends, never merely as means”

k.f: “Merely” carries the weight and has no precise test, and the formula gives no clear answer when everyone’s ends conflict.
k.m: “Merely” has a test: could the other person agree to the way they’re being treated? Deception and force fail it. Ordinary dealings pass.

k.f: Everyone uses a cashier as a means. Paying doesn’t change that, it makes it a means with a receipt.
k.m: The cashier agreed to the job and you’re paying what was asked. Using with consent is the allowed kind. That’s the whole distinction and you walked into it.

k.f: Kant is basically the Ten Commandments without God.
k.m: The Commandments say what. He says why, without anyone watching.

t.t: “Only acts done from duty have moral worth”

k.f: Someone who visits a friend in the hospital from duty alone seems to be missing something morally important. Schiller made the joke in Kant’s lifetime.
k.m: He doesn’t say inclination spoils the act. Duty must be enough to move you if the liking fails. The friend who visits gladly and would come anyway is his ideal case.

k.f: So the best person is someone who hates helping and does it anyway. He described a resentful volunteer and called it the summit of ethics.
k.m: The best person is the one who’d still show up on the day they didn’t feel like it. You’d want that friend. Everyone would.

k.f: Kant said helping people because you like helping has no moral worth. It only counts if it’s a chore.
k.m: It counts when you’d do it anyway. That’s the test for whether you’re kind or just in a good mood.

t.t: “We know appearances, never things in themselves”

k.f: Jacobi’s problem: Kant says things in themselves cause appearances, and also that causation applies only within appearances.
k.m: On the two-aspect reading there’s one set of things, considered as they appear and as they are apart from us. “Cause” is then a loose way of saying ground.

k.f: If nobody can know them, nobody can know there are any. He posited a room and lost the key on purpose.
k.m: We know there’s a room because the wall is here. Knowing a limit from this side is the entire Critique.

k.f: The thing-in-itself can’t be known, and Kant knows quite a lot about it.
k.m: He knows it’s there and that we can’t describe it. That’s two things. He stops there.

t.t: “Ask what a virtuous person would do”

k.f: The test gives little guidance and looks circular unless virtue is spelled out without mentioning right action.
k.m: The virtues are specified through what a human life needs: courage, honesty, justice. Right action is derived from those, and it gives guidance through rules like “do what’s honest.”

k.f: A virtuous person would ask what a virtuous person would do. So it’s two people asking each other at a door forever.
k.m: The first person at the door knows something about kindness already. Everyone does. The theory starts from that and no theory starts from nothing.

k.f: Virtue ethics: do what a good person would do. Who’s a good person? One who does good things.
k.m: Who’s a good doctor? One who heals people. Nobody thinks medicine is circular.

t.t: “Character, not rules or outcomes, comes first”

k.f: Experiments like Milgram’s suggest circumstances drive behavior more than stable traits do, though what they show is contested.
k.m: Those studies found most people aren’t virtuous, which Aristotle said. Virtue is rare and hard. And a third of Milgram’s subjects walked out, which is the trait showing.

k.f: Character is what someone has done so far. So it’s outcomes, on a delay.
k.m: Then two people with the same record have the same character, and nobody who has hired anyone believes that.

k.f: Psychologists found people help strangers more after finding a dime. So much for character.
k.m: And some people help without the dime. That’s the character.

k.f: Either flourishing is defined to include virtue, and the claim is empty, or it isn’t, and then vicious people sometimes flourish.
k.m: The vicious person who seems to flourish has wealth and comfort. Whether that’s a good human life is the question, and the theory argues it isn’t.

k.f: Plenty of terrible people are doing great. Some of them have boats.
k.m: A boat is not a life. Ask them how many people they trust.

k.f: Flourishing is what the virtuous have, and the virtuous are whoever’s flourishing.
k.m: Health is what healthy people have, and the healthy are whoever’s well. Some circles are just definitions.

t.t: “Practical wisdom can’t be written down as rules”

k.f: That shields the theory from counterexamples and gives no way to settle a disagreement between two people who each claim to see it rightly.
k.m: Every theory needs judgment to apply its rules. This one says so and studies how judgment is acquired, where the others leave it unmentioned.

k.f: Anything that can’t be written down can’t be taught, and anything that can’t be taught is luck. So virtue is luck with good manners.
k.m: Riding a bike can’t be written down. It’s taught every day. Demonstration and practice are teaching.

k.f: “Practical wisdom” is the part where the theory says “you’ll figure it out.”
k.m: Medicine tells its residents the same thing. It’s called training.

k.f: The lists differ sharply: Aristotle’s pride, Christian humility, Confucian filial piety. MacIntyre granted that virtues belong to traditions.
k.m: The lists differ and the core overlaps: courage, justice, self-control and honesty turn up almost everywhere. Humility and pride may be one trait under two descriptions.

k.f: Homeric virtue was killing people well. If virtues were universal, Achilles and a kindergarten teacher would get the same performance review.
k.m: Achilles and a kindergarten teacher both need courage, honesty and self-command. The job descriptions differ. The review form has the same headings.

k.f: Aristotle’s virtues are what a rich Athenian already liked about himself.
k.m: A rich Athenian with courage, justice and self-control. Which one are you against?

k.f: Mackie: facts that command by their nature would be unlike anything else we know of, and it’s unclear how anyone would detect them.
k.m: The same oddness belongs to facts about what one ought to believe on the evidence. If those are too strange to exist, the argument against moral facts goes too.

k.f: Facts get found with instruments. Nobody has built a wrongness detector, and there’d be a lot of money in it.
k.m: Nobody has built a number detector either. Some facts are found by thinking, and there’s plenty of money in those.

k.f: Moral facts exist, they just can’t be seen, measured or found anywhere. A ghost with opinions.
k.m: You believe in logical validity and you can’t put that in a jar either.

k.f: Progress is measured by today’s standards, so any path that ends at our views looks like progress. Changing sympathies and interests explain the same history.
k.m: The changes weren’t random drift. They followed from applying existing principles more consistently once the excuses were examined, which is what tracking looks like.

k.f: Every era thought it was the progress. The Victorians were sure. So the thing being tracked is “now is best,” and it’s always now.
k.m: The Victorians thought they were better than slaveholders. They were. Being sure doesn’t make you wrong.

k.f: Every culture was sure it had the moral facts. They had different ones.
k.m: Every culture was sure it knew the shape of the earth too.

k.f: Strong conviction is equally expected on evolutionary and cultural stories that never mention truth.
k.m: Debunking has to stop somewhere or it takes logic and the senses with it. Realists argue that the judgments that survive reflection have the same standing as those.

k.f: Obvious things don’t need a philosophy department. Nobody runs a seminar on whether water is wet.
k.m: Nobody runs a seminar on it because nobody doubts it. The seminars are about why you’d doubt this and nothing else.

k.f: “It’s just obvious that torture is wrong” is a feeling with its voice lowered.
k.m: Your confidence in that objection is a feeling too.

k.f: The comparison has to hold where it counts. Mathematics has agreed proof procedures and science can’t do without it, and ethics has neither.
k.m: Mathematics rests on axioms accepted because they seem true on reflection. Ethics has the same footing and fewer theorems so far.

k.f: Math facts are the same on Mars. Nobody thinks tipping is.
k.m: Tipping isn’t. Torturing children for fun is wrong on Mars. You went for the custom and skipped the fact.

k.f: Realists say moral facts are like math facts. Math has proofs.
k.m: Proofs from axioms nobody proved.

k.f: Scientific disagreement tends to end when the evidence comes in. Basic moral disagreement persists among informed, reflective people, and that needs explaining.
k.m: Much of the disagreement is about non-moral facts or comes from self-interest. Among people who share the facts and have nothing at stake, it shrinks a great deal.

k.f: Physics arguments ended when someone ran an experiment. Ethics has had three thousand years and its experiment is two guys yelling.
k.m: Ethics ran its experiment. Slavery was tried at scale, the results came in, and almost nobody wants a replication.

k.f: Moral realism is church for people who left church.
k.m: Church has commandments from a person. This doesn’t need one. That’s the difference.

k.f: Then if everyone approved of cruelty it would be fine. The standard way of denying that borrows moral claims the view was supposed to explain.
k.m: “If everyone approved, it’d be fine” is a moral claim, and one I reject from inside my own outlook. Having no outside standpoint doesn’t mean having no standpoint.

k.f: Money depends on minds too, and try not paying taxes. Mind-dependent things are the realest things there are.
k.m: Money stops being real the moment everyone stops believing. Tell me which moral fact survives that test, and then tell me how you checked.

k.f: So genocide is a difference in taste. That’s the view.
k.m: No, it’s wrong. I say that with everything I’ve got. I just don’t say the universe agrees.

k.f: The argument spreads. Rules about what one ought to believe are as strange as moral ones, so the error theorist can’t say anyone ought to accept error theory.
k.m: Some error theorists accept it for epistemic norms too. Others note the difference: “ought to believe” can be cashed out in terms of truth, and “ought to do” has nothing similar.

k.f: If all moral claims are false then “murder is wrong” is false, so murder isn’t wrong, which is a moral claim, so that’s false too. It deletes itself.
k.m: “Murder is not wrong” isn’t a moral claim, it’s the denial of one. “There are no unicorns” isn’t a unicorn.

k.f: Error theory says every moral sentence is false, including “you shouldn’t lie about error theory.”
k.m: I didn’t say you shouldn’t. I said it’s false.

k.f: Moral sentences behave like ordinary true-or-false ones inside arguments and “if” clauses. A semantics that explains this is still a project, not a result.
k.m: It’s a hard technical problem with thirty years of serious answers. That a theory has open problems puts it level with every rival.

k.f: People change their moral views after hearing arguments. Nobody has ever been argued out of liking cilantro.
k.m: People are argued out of tastes all the time: tell them how the sausage is made. Attitudes respond to facts. That’s the theory.

k.f: Emotivism is ethics as booing.
k.m: It’s booing with reasons. Like yours, minus the metaphysics.

k.f: Debunking threatens to spread to perception and logic, which evolved too, and a realist can argue that getting morality roughly right was useful.
k.m: Perception and logic pay off only when they’re accurate. Moral beliefs pay off by getting us to cooperate, whether or not anything is there to be accurate about.

k.f: Evolution also gave people the belief in evolution. So by that logic it’s false, and the argument goes with it.
k.m: Believing in evolution wasn’t selected for. It showed up in 1859. Believing your family matters most was.

k.f: Anti-realists have a lot of opinions about justice for people who think it’s a flavor.
k.m: I have opinions about food too, and I’ll fight you on those.

t.t: “You can be one and still condemn atrocities”

k.f: One can, but the condemning is then the voicing of one’s own stance. Whether that’s what people mean by “wrong whatever anyone thinks” is the dispute.
k.m: Right, and realists do the same: they voice their stance and add that the cosmos seconds it. The extra clause has never stopped an atrocity.

k.f: Condemning something that isn’t really wrong is called acting.
k.m: An actor doesn’t mean it. I mean it. Meaning it is the part that was ever doing any work.

k.f: Anti-realists say nothing is really wrong, and then somebody takes their parking spot.
k.m: I’m against it. I never said I wasn’t. I said the universe doesn’t have a parking policy.

t.t: “Some acts are wrong whatever the consequences”

k.f: Pushed far enough, with thousands of lives against one small violation, almost everyone gives way. Then the rule was a strong weight, not an absolute.
k.m: Most deontologists hold thresholds: the constraint yields at catastrophe. A weight that holds against ordinary gains and gives only at the extreme is still a different thing from one more cost.

k.f: So it’s wrong to tell one lie to save a city. A theory that loses a city on a technicality has a bug.
k.m: One lie to save a city is the threshold case, and nearly every deontologist allows it. Try arguing with the view its defenders hold.

k.f: Deontology is caring more about your own clean hands than about what happens to anyone.
k.m: It’s caring about what you do to people, as against what merely happens near you. Those were always different.

k.f: If violating a right is so bad, it’s puzzling why one may not violate one to prevent five identical violations. The constraint needs a ground other than the badness.
k.m: The constraint is about what I may do to you. It was never a quantity to be minimized. Each person holds the right against each agent, and that explains why it doesn’t add up.

k.f: If rights matter, more rights respected is better than fewer. He’s against that. He prefers the one he personally didn’t touch.
k.m: If you may violate one to save five, nobody has a right. Everyone has a place in a calculation that happens to be going their way.

k.f: The deontologist lets five rights be violated so his own record stays clean. It’s ethics as a no-hitter.
k.m: The one man you’d sacrifice has a view on your record too.

k.f: The line between intending a harm and merely foreseeing it is easy to redraw by redescribing the act, which makes it a poor guide.
k.m: The line can be gamed, and so can any rule. Used honestly it marks a real difference: the terror bomber needs the deaths and the other would be glad if nobody were there.

k.f: The road to hell is paved with them. That’s been known for a while.
k.m: The road to hell is paved with outcomes people were certain justified it.

k.f: “I didn’t intend it, I just knew it would happen” has never worked on anyone’s mother.
k.m: It works on her every time you break something by accident. She knows the difference.

k.f: A list of duties with no ranking leaves the hard cases to intuition, which is where the theory was supposed to help.
k.m: Judgment is needed in every theory. The other side has to judge what counts as a consequence and how to weigh it, and just hides that inside a number.

k.f: A theory that says “it depends, use your judgment” when it gets hard is a list, not a theory.
k.m: A list that tells you what’s at stake is more than “add it all up,” which tells you nothing until someone supplies the weights.

k.f: Deontology has rules for everything except which rule.
k.m: Rules for everything except which rule. That part is called being an adult.

k.f: Cultures aren’t sealed units with one code each. Every society has dissenters, and the view has to say the reformers were wrong by definition.
k.m: A culture’s code includes its own ideals, and reformers usually appeal to those. The dissenter is holding the society to what it already says.

k.f: Then whoever wanted to end slavery was immoral at the time, since the culture said otherwise. That’s the view. He can keep it.
k.m: The abolitionists argued from the society’s own scripture and its own declaration. They won on home rules.

k.f: Moral relativists become universalists the moment somebody cuts in line.
k.m: Cutting in line is wrong here. I said relative. I didn’t say nothing applies.

k.f: That’s a universal moral rule about what everyone should do, which is what the theory says there aren’t any of.
k.m: The careful version makes no such rule. It says that when we judge, we use our own standards, and we should know that’s what we’re doing.

k.f: “Nobody should judge” is a judgment. Of everybody.
k.m: It’s advice from inside my culture, which values not invading people. I’m allowed to have local values.

k.f: “Who are we to judge?” asks the person judging people who judge.
k.m: Somebody from here. That’s who.

k.f: People disagreed about the shape of the earth. Disagreement shows that someone is wrong, or that the question is hard.
k.m: The argument is from disagreement that survives full information. People with all the facts settled the shape of the earth, and the moral cases don’t go that way.

k.f: People disagree about the restaurant bill too, and there’s still a number.
k.m: The bill has a number because both sides accept arithmetic. Find the moral arithmetic that every party accepts.

k.f: Disagreement proves nothing, a point on which there is some disagreement.
k.m: Among the people who’ve looked into it, not much.

k.f: If my culture values intolerance, relativism says intolerance is right for me. Tolerance needs a non-relative defense.
k.m: Tolerance isn’t deduced from it. Someone who sees their own code as one among others has less motive to impose it, and that link is practical.

k.f: A culture of conquerors is right by its own lights. The tolerant view just endorsed the conquest.
k.m: It endorsed nothing. It says they think they’re right, which we knew. The view from nowhere that would refute them isn’t available to you either.

k.f: Relativism: every culture’s values are valid, except the ones that say theirs are better, which is all of them.
k.m: Every one of them says theirs is better. I noticed, and that’s the observation.

k.f: “Matters” might never have needed cosmic backing. Things matter to people, and that may be the only kind of mattering there was.
k.m: Mattering to someone is a fact about them. The nihilist’s claim was about whether anything has a claim on us beyond that, and it stands.

k.f: If nothing matters, it doesn’t matter that nothing matters, so there’s no reason to say it, and he says it constantly.
k.m: Saying it doesn’t have to matter. Lots of things get said. You’ve confused a remark with a mission.

k.f: Nihilists believe in nothing and will not stop bringing it up.
k.m: You brought it up. I was just standing here.

k.f: From the absence of objective values, nothing follows about what to do, including not caring. Indifference is one more stance needing support.
k.m: Agreed, nothing follows, including indifference. The view is a correction to the metaphysics, and you live as before.

k.f: If there are no values, “believe what’s true” isn’t one either. So there’s no reason to believe nihilism over anything else.
k.m: I believe it because it seems true, the same way I breathe. No value required.

k.f: Nihilism is the only philosophy where the argument for it is the reason not to bother.
k.m: It never asked you to bother. That’s you.

t.t: “The universe is indifferent, so meaning is an illusion”

k.f: The universe isn’t the sort of thing that could care. That it doesn’t is no more a loss than that mountains don’t applaud.
k.m: Fine, drop the disappointment. What remains is that no purpose is built in, and that’s the thesis.

k.f: The universe is also indifferent to math, and the math is fine.
k.m: Math doesn’t need the universe to care because math isn’t asking you to get up in the morning.

k.f: “In a billion years none of this will matter.” It’s not a billion years from now. It’s Thursday.
k.m: It’s Thursday and none of it will matter in a billion years. Both.

k.f: Honesty is being treated as a value that binds, which the position says there aren’t. The pose depends on what it denies.
k.m: Call it a preference for not being fooled. Preferences are allowed. What isn’t on offer is a reason the cosmos backs it.

k.f: If nothing matters, honesty doesn’t. He’s proud of a virtue he just deleted.
k.m: I’m not proud. I’m describing. You’re the one handing out medals.

k.f: Nihilism is very brave for a view that asks nothing of anyone.
k.m: It asks you to give up the one thing everyone wants to be true. That’s something.

t.t: “Pleasure is the only thing good in itself”

k.f: People want things besides pleasure: for their beliefs to be true, their friends to be real, their work to have happened. Those seem to matter in themselves.
k.m: Take away any experience of it and ask what those things add. A truth you never learn and a friend you never enjoy leave no trace in the life.

k.f: If pleasure were the only good, the best life would be a warm bath, and nobody’s written a biography of one.
k.m: Add a book, a friend and a view to the bath. All pleasures. The theory was never just the warm water.

k.f: Hedonism is the theory that the best person who ever lived was whoever had the best dessert.
k.m: The best life is the one that felt best to live. Say what’s wrong with that without mentioning how anything feels.

t.t: “Everything we want, we want for the pleasure”

k.f: People sacrifice their own pleasure knowingly, for children or causes. Saying they must be getting pleasure from it makes the claim true by definition.
k.m: The parent would be miserable doing otherwise. Motivation through one’s own feelings is a finding about how brains work, and it isn’t true by definition.

k.f: People run marathons. Explain that one with pleasure.
k.m: Ask a runner at the finish line whether it was worth it. They say it felt incredible.

k.f: “You only do nice things because it feels good” is something a person says once, at dinner, and is not invited back.
k.m: It’s true, and that’s why nobody wants to hear it at dinner.

t.t: “Pain is the only thing bad in itself”

k.f: Being deceived, betrayed or wasted seems bad for a person even if they never find out and feel nothing.
k.m: Being deceived is bad because of what it risks and how it feels to find out. A deception with no effect on any experience, ever, is hard to call a harm to anyone.

k.f: Exercise hurts and it’s good. Medicine tastes bad and it’s good. He’s 0 for 2 before breakfast.
k.m: Exercise and medicine are good because of how you feel later. You’ve made my argument with my examples.

k.f: So the worst thing that can happen to a life is a stubbed toe, as long as it’s a bad one.
k.m: A bad enough toe, for long enough, yes. You’ve obviously not had the right toe.

t.t: “The wise hedonist picks the calm, lasting pleasures”

k.f: Once pleasures are ranked by something other than amount, a second standard has come in, and it’s doing the real work.
k.m: The ranking is by amount over a lifetime. Calm pleasures win because they last and cost nothing afterwards, so one standard is doing all of it.
