k.f: “The best pleasure is moderation and reading.” That’s not hedonism, that’s a librarian.
k.m: The librarian is still enjoying herself at eighty. Check on the other guy.

k.f: Every hedonist philosopher ends up recommending a quiet life, which is how you know none of them tried the other kind.
k.m: Several tried the other kind first. That’s how they knew.

t.t: “Everyone always acts in their own interest”

k.f: Either it’s false, since people sacrifice for others, or “interest” is stretched to cover whatever anyone does, and the claim says nothing.
k.m: The unselfish act still comes from the agent’s own motives. The live question is whether any of those motives has another person’s good as its final object, and the evidence is disputed.

k.f: Soldiers jump on grenades. “He wanted to” isn’t self-interest, it’s the theory eating the evidence.
k.m: He couldn’t have lived with himself. That’s a motive, and it’s his.

k.f: “Everyone’s selfish, really” is something people conclude from a sample of one.
k.m: A sample of everyone I’ve met, including the ones who objected.

t.t: “You ought to pursue your own good”

k.f: If everyone ought to pursue their own good, I should want you to pursue yours even against mine, which isn’t in my interest to recommend.
k.m: The theory says what each person has most reason to do. It needn’t say I should want you to succeed, any more than a chess player wants his opponent to find the best move.

k.f: A real egoist wouldn’t tell anyone. He’d want everyone else to be altruists. Publishing it is the least egoist thing possible.
k.m: An egoist who publishes thought the book would sell. Consistent.

k.f: Ethical egoism is the only moral theory it’s irrational to teach.
k.m: Irrational to teach and perfectly rational to believe. Those are different jobs.

k.f: Sometimes it is. But the cases that test a moral theory are the ones where helping costs and nobody will know.
k.m: Even there, people act from the kind of person they want to be and from habits that pay off on the whole. Character is a long-run investment.

k.f: If it’s all self-interest, anonymous donations are a bookkeeping error.
k.m: Anonymous donors still know. The audience was always inside.

k.f: “Enlightened self-interest” is being nice and wanting credit for being cynical about it.
k.m: Being nice and knowing why. You should try the second half.

t.t: “Altruism is a disguise for wanting to feel good”

k.f: That we feel good after helping doesn’t show the feeling was the aim. Usually people feel good because they got what they wanted, which was the other person’s welfare.
k.m: If the helper wanted the other’s welfare and got it, she got what she wanted. That is the structure of self-interested action, with a kind object.

k.f: People feel good after helping because they wanted to help. The feeling is the receipt, not the purchase.
k.m: A receipt you’d stop buying without. Take away the good feeling and see how much charity is left.

k.f: The guy who says charity is selfish has found a way to do neither.
k.m: He does both, and doesn’t lie about why.

t.t: “We’re judged for things outside our control”

k.f: One response is that we shouldn’t be. The drunk driver who hits no one is as blameworthy as the one who does, and practice is just crude.
k.m: If we shouldn’t be, most of our practice is wrong: we do blame the driver who kills more. The puzzle is that both verdicts feel right.

k.f: Then nobody’s responsible for anything, since nobody controlled being born. Courts tried ignoring that argument and it went fine.
k.m: It follows only if you require control over everything. The point is that we never had it and still judge. Courts are the evidence.

k.f: Moral luck is the discovery that some people get away with it.
k.m: It’s the discovery that you can’t say why they shouldn’t.

t.t: “The reckless driver who kills is worse than the one who doesn’t”

k.f: Many deny this. Both took the same risk with the same mind, and the difference is in what we have to respond to, not in desert.
k.m: Then the lucky driver should feel what the unlucky one feels, and nobody thinks so. Regret tracks what you did, and what you did includes what happened.

k.f: One of them killed someone. That’s the difference. It’s a big one. Ask the someone.
k.m: That’s the claim. One of them killed someone, and that it mattered is what’s being pointed out.

k.f: Philosophers needed two essays in 1976 to notice that results matter to people.
k.m: Williams and Nagel noticed that it matters and that our theories say it shouldn’t. The second part is the news.

t.t: “Who you are is itself a matter of luck”

k.f: If character is luck too, nothing is left for anyone to be responsible for, and the claim proves too much to guide anything.
k.m: Too much is exactly the worry Nagel raises: follow the control principle through and the agent shrinks to nothing. He offers it as the problem.

k.f: If who I am is luck, there’s no me left to be lucky. He deleted the person and kept the complaint.
k.m: That’s the conclusion, and it’s Nagel’s, stated as a paradox. You’ve reached the end of the essay.

k.f: “It’s all luck” is always said about someone else’s success and never about one’s own.
k.m: It’s said about one’s own, and that’s called humility.

t.t: “Kant was wrong that the good will is immune to luck”

k.f: A Kantian can grant that outcomes affect what we owe, like apology and repair, while holding that worth depends on the will.
k.m: If outcomes change what we owe, they change the moral situation. Saying they leave “worth” untouched keeps the word and gives up the substance.

k.f: Kant said only intentions count. Everyone who has ever received an apology for an accident knows what he meant.
k.m: The apology is for the outcome. If only the will mattered there’d be nothing to apologize for.

k.f: The moral luck debate is two professors agreeing that life is unfair and disagreeing about the footnotes.
k.m: Whether life’s unfairness reaches morality is not a footnote.

t.t: “Rights belong to all humans by nature”

k.f: Bentham called natural rights nonsense upon stilts. Without an account of where they come from, “by nature” asserts what needs showing.
k.m: They can be grounded in what any person needs in order to act at all: freedom and well-being. An agent can’t coherently claim those for himself and deny them to others.

k.f: Nature gave people appendixes and wisdom teeth. Nobody’s found the rights. Surgeons would have mentioned it.
k.m: Nobody’s found the number seven in a body either.

k.f: Human rights are self-evident, which is why they had to be written down in 1948 and argued over ever since.
k.m: Self-evident things often take a catastrophe before anyone writes them down.

k.f: The list reflects a particular history and its drafters’ priorities, and the weight given to individual over communal claims isn’t shared everywhere.
k.m: The drafting committee included a Chinese Confucian and a Lebanese Arab, and delegates from four continents signed. People everywhere have since claimed them against their own governments.

k.f: A universal thing shows up everywhere. This one showed up in one place, recently, and then got mailed out.
k.m: Gunpowder showed up in one place too. Where an idea started doesn’t limit where it’s true.

k.f: Universal rights, as agreed by a committee in a hotel.
k.m: A committee from China, Lebanon, Chile, France and the rest. That’s what universal looks like in a hotel.

t.t: “Rights are trumps over the common good”

k.f: Rights conflict with each other constantly, so they can’t all be trumps, and the weighing that follows looks a lot like consulting the common good.
k.m: Rights limit which reasons a government may act on. When two conflict, the weighing is between rights, and “it would be better on the whole” stays excluded.

k.f: If two trumps are played, somebody has to count points. The counting is the thing he said rights avoid.
k.m: Two trumps get compared with each other. The common good still doesn’t get to play a low card over either.

k.f: Everything is a human right now, which is the same as nothing being one.
k.m: The core list fits on a page. Inflation at the edges doesn’t cancel the page.

t.t: “A right exists even where it isn’t enforced”

k.f: A right nobody can claim against anyone is hard to tell from a wish. On one view rights are the creatures of institutions that back them.
k.m: People are imprisoned in the name of rights their state denies, and we don’t say they had none. The claim on others comes first, and enforcement is what we owe it.

k.f: A right nobody enforces is a nice sentence. Ask anyone holding one.
k.m: A right nobody enforces is what every reform movement started with. Then somebody enforced it.

k.f: “You have rights” is what people are told right before finding out who enforces them.
k.m: And the name of the thing they were owed is how anyone knew it was wrong.

t.t: “A huge population of barely-worth-living lives can be better”

k.f: Most take that verdict as a refutation of the reasoning that leads to it, and reject one of the premises about adding lives.
k.m: The reasoning uses steps each of which seems undeniable. Rejecting the conclusion means rejecting one of them, and nobody has found one that’s cheap to give up.

k.f: If more barely-okay lives is better, the ideal world is an airport. Forever. With everyone in it.
k.m: The airport has more total good than a perfect village of ten. Disliking the picture isn’t an argument about the sum.

k.f: Total utilitarianism: the best possible future is everyone who could exist, standing in line.
k.m: A line of people each glad to be alive. You wouldn’t delete any one of them.

t.t: “Rejecting it costs you something just as bad”

k.f: The impossibility results show every theory violates some intuition. That might mean our intuitions about huge numbers aren’t reliable enough to build on.
k.m: That may be the lesson. But then no intuition in this area can be used against any theory, including the one we started with.

k.f: Every option is terrible, so the terrible one is fine. That’s not ethics, that’s choosing an internet provider.
k.m: Choosing among costs is all of ethics. The theorems only show there’s no free option.

k.f: Population ethics is a field where every paper proves the last paper’s theory is monstrous.
k.m: Every paper shows the last one had a cost, and that’s how the field knows the true price list.

k.f: Accepting a conclusion named “repugnant” because the math led there treats the formal premises as more certain than the judgment they offend.
k.m: Our sense of large numbers is known to be unreliable, and the premises are simple, separately tested judgments. Trusting the plain steps over the vivid picture is defensible.

k.f: The argument has “repugnant” in the name and his answer is “yes.” Somebody should check on him.
k.m: The name was given by the man who couldn’t refute it. A name isn’t a premise.

k.f: Some philosophers bit the bullet. It’s the only field where that’s a career move.
k.m: Biting the bullet when the argument is valid is the job description.

t.t: “Lives just above zero are better than they sound”

k.f: Redescribing the lives as fine blunts the case, but then the conclusion just says a big good world beats a small great one, and the puzzle returns with adjusted numbers.
k.m: The adjustment matters. If those lives are good ones, the “repugnance” was a trick of the word “barely,” and what remains is a preference for small elites.

k.f: “Muzak and potatoes isn’t so bad.” He’s now defending the potatoes. The argument has gotten away from him.
k.m: He’s pointing out that a life with music and food in it is a life. Billions would take the deal.

k.f: Parfit spent forty years looking for a theory that avoids it and called the missing theory X. It’s still missing.
k.m: Forty years and he never stopped believing it existed. Most theories that can’t be found aren’t looked for that long.

t.t: “Give where a dollar does the most good”

k.f: Cost-effectiveness estimates carry wide uncertainty and favor what can be measured. Political and structural change resists the method and gets underweighted.
k.m: The uncertainty is why you measure, and the estimates are published with their error bars. “Hard to compare” was the old excuse for never comparing.

k.f: The most good per dollar is a number in somebody’s spreadsheet, and it changes every year. Last year’s best charity is this year’s mistake, by their own blog.
k.m: The number changes because they update on evidence and say so in public. Find another charity sector that announces its own mistakes.

k.f: EA is charity by people who think nobody tried being smart about it before.
k.m: People had tried being generous. Checking whether it worked was the new part.

t.t: “Earning to give can beat direct work”

k.f: It discounts how a career shapes a person’s values and assumes the harms of the earning are small. The movement’s own leaders walked the advice back.
k.m: It was always advice for a few people with unusual earning power, and they did walk it back for most. A movement that revises its advice is working as intended.

k.f: If everyone earned to give, nobody would be left to do the thing the giving pays for. It only works if most people ignore it.
k.m: If everyone became a doctor there’d be no farmers. Advice at the margin is for the next person, and it always was.

k.f: “Earning to give” is taking the finance job with a note from philosophy.
k.m: The note says the job pays for thirty thousand bed nets a year. What does yours say?

t.t: “Future people matter as much as present ones”

k.f: Grant them equal weight, and our ability to predictably affect the far future is still tiny. Expected value with astronomical stakes turns fanatical.
k.m: Being unable to predict most effects is a reason to pick the few robust ones, like not going extinct. The weight of the future survives the uncertainty.

k.f: Future people don’t exist. Things that don’t exist have zero interests. Zero times a trillion is still zero.
k.m: Your grandchildren don’t exist either. Tell me they don’t count and then tell them in forty years.

k.f: EA cares deeply about people in the year 9000, and shrimp.
k.m: The shrimp are alive now. So that’s two different complaints.

t.t: “AI risk is the most pressing cause”

k.f: The ranking rests on probability estimates nobody can check, and the money flows into a field where the donors have commercial interests.
k.m: The estimates are rough, and the people building the systems give similar ones. A small chance of something irreversible is how seatbelts and fire codes are justified.

k.f: Every generation’s smartest people were sure about their apocalypse, and they’re 0 for all of them. The base rate for doom is zero.
k.m: Every generation before 1945 was right that nothing could end the world. Then there was a button. Base rates change when the hardware does.

k.f: It started with malaria nets and ended up funding essays about robot gods.
k.m: Malaria nets are still the biggest line in the budget. The essays are just the part you read.

k.f: Fraud doesn’t refute a moral theory. But naive expected-value thinking was live in the culture, and warnings about him were raised early and set aside.
k.m: The culture needed fixing and that’s been said in public, at length. The claim stands that the ideas forbid fraud: the founding texts say plainly not to do harm for the greater good.

k.f: He did the math in public, the movement checked it and took the money. When the calculator is wrong at that size, it’s the calculator.
k.m: The math said don’t commit fraud. It’s in the book, with his endorsement on the cover. He didn’t follow it.

k.f: The movement’s biggest donor went to prison, which the expected value math somehow didn’t flag.
k.m: Neither did his auditors, his investors or the regulators. The philosophers were the last to be asked.

k.f: The same arithmetic recommends pushing the man off the bridge. Most who pull the lever balk there, so numbers alone aren’t their principle.
k.m: That’s the finding. People who pull aren’t pure counters, and the cases exist to find out what else is in there.

k.f: The one guy was safe until someone touched the lever. Before that it was an accident. After, it’s a killing with a witness.
k.m: He was safe because five others weren’t. Letting the track decide is still deciding, and you were the one standing at the lever.

k.f: Don’t touch anything. Then it’s the trolley company’s fault.
k.m: You were standing right there. The company has you on camera.

t.t: “Pushing the man is different from the lever”

k.f: The usual explanations stumble on the loop case, where the lever uses the one man as a means and people’s verdicts drift back.
k.m: The loop case shows the simple account is wrong. That’s a case refining a principle, and it’s the method doing its work.

k.f: Dead is dead. The family doesn’t ask which muscle group was involved.
k.m: The law asks exactly that. Murder and manslaughter differ by what you meant and how you did it, and families care a lot.

k.f: Pushing the guy is the same as pulling the lever. The only difference is cardio.
k.m: Then you’d push him. Say it out loud, to him.

t.t: “The cases reveal principles of moral thinking”

k.f: Answers shift with framing, order and physical contact. One reading is that the footbridge reaction is an emotional alarm, not a principle.
k.m: An emotional alarm that fires for up-close harm and stays quiet for remote harm is a discovery about moral thinking. The cases produced it either way.

k.f: The cases reveal what undergraduates say for course credit at nine in the morning.
k.m: The pattern replicated in forty-two countries. It’s not the undergraduates.

k.f: The trolley problem is a personality quiz that got into journals.
k.m: Personality quizzes don’t replicate across forty countries.

k.f: Removing uncertainty, relationships and other options may remove exactly what makes real decisions moral ones.
k.m: Every experiment strips things out, and that’s how one factor gets studied at a time. What real decisions add can then be put back one piece at a time.

k.f: A problem where nobody can yell, brake, or ask why six people are on a track has removed the variables. All of them.
k.m: Physics removed friction and air and got the laws of motion. Removing variables is what an experiment is.

k.f: Why are they on the tracks? Nobody asks.
k.m: Because it’s a thought experiment. Nobody asks why the frictionless plane has no friction.

t.t: “It matters for triage and self-driving cars”

k.f: Real triage runs on protocols and probabilities, and engineers treat forced-choice crashes as vanishingly rare next to ordinary safety work.
k.m: The dilemma is rare. What it stands for is not: any policy that sets how to trade risks between groups, from triage rules to speed limits, has that structure.

k.f: Millions of people answered the survey about who the car should hit, and the cars used none of it.
k.m: The cars are programmed with a priority order for who to protect. Somebody chose it. They just didn’t hold a survey first.

k.f: Self-driving cars were supposed to need it. They just brake.
k.m: Braking is a choice about who gets hit when braking isn’t enough.

k.f: Grant it, and how much it weighs is still contested. Views that tie moral status to reasoning or reciprocity give animals some consideration without equal consideration.
k.m: Even at a steep discount the numbers decide it: tens of billions of land animals a year, most in conditions nobody defends, for a pleasure that has substitutes.

k.f: Suffering needs someone who knows they’re suffering. A chicken doesn’t know it’s Tuesday.
k.m: A baby doesn’t know it’s Tuesday. Pain doesn’t need a calendar.

k.f: Plants feel pain too.
k.m: Then eat the plants directly. The cow eats ten times as many.

t.t: “No trait justifies eating them and not us”

k.f: The challenge assumes moral status has to rest on a single trait. Accounts based on species or relationships deny that.
k.m: A species-norm account has to say why membership matters when the capacities are absent. “Because they’re ours” is the claim under examination.

k.f: The trait is being human. It’s on the form. Every other animal sides with its own species too, and nobody calls a wolf a bigot.
k.m: “It’s on the form” is what every in-group has said about every out-group. The wolf isn’t offering it as an argument.

k.f: “Name the trait.” Tasty.
k.m: Then you’d eat anything that tastes good. Name the limit.

k.f: Well planned, it is, though it needs supplements. And healthy doesn’t mean obligatory. The health case and the moral case are separate.
k.m: Agreed, they’re separate cases. Health only shows the moral case costs nothing important, which removes the last practical excuse.

k.f: People who went vegan and felt great had also stopped eating gas station food. That’s the variable.
k.m: They stopped the gas station food and the meat and felt great. You can’t claim one variable and wave off the other.

k.f: Humans have canines. That’s what they’re for.
k.m: Gorillas have bigger ones and eat leaves.

k.f: The emissions and land use are large. That supports cutting back and reform, and grazing on land that can’t grow crops doesn’t compete with food.
k.m: Reduction and reform is most of what’s being asked for. Grazing on land that can’t grow crops supplies a small share of what people eat.

k.f: Cows eat grass and grass grows back. It’s the only industry that runs on lawn.
k.m: The grass grows back and the methane goes up. Most of them never see the lawn. They’re fed soy from a cleared forest.

k.f: Harvesting crops kills more animals than a cow does. Mice count.
k.m: Most crops are grown to feed the cow. Fewer cows, fewer dead mice. Thank you for the argument.

t.t: “If you wouldn’t do it to a dog, don’t do it to a pig”

k.f: The consistency point is strong, though it can be settled in either direction, and duties to animals people live with may come from the relationship.
k.m: If the relationship is what protects the dog, then pigs are fine to harm only because nobody bothered to know one. That’s a fact about us.

k.f: Dogs have jobs. Pigs were offered truffle hunting and it’s a small field.
k.m: Pigs outscore dogs on every cognition test going. If it’s about ability, we’ve been eating the wrong one.

k.f: Lions eat meat.
k.m: Lions also kill their rivals’ cubs. Pick a different role model.

t.t: “Coming into existence is always a harm”

k.f: Benatar counts absent pain as good though it’s good for no one, and absent pleasure as not bad because it’s bad for no one. Critics say the two must be treated alike.
k.m: The asymmetry explains judgments nearly everyone shares: we have a duty not to create a miserable child and no duty to create a happy one. Reject it and those need another explanation.

k.f: Harm needs a before and an after. There’s no before. He’s comparing a life to a blank and saying the blank won.
k.m: You make that comparison whenever you say someone would have been better off never born. Everybody has said it about somebody.

k.f: Missing out on joy is fine if nobody’s there to miss it, but avoiding pain is good even if nobody’s there to enjoy that. Convenient.
k.m: It’s not convenient. It’s how you already think about a child who’d be born into agony.

k.f: Consent applies to existing beings whose interests can be set back. Before conception there’s no one whose consent is missing.
k.m: Where consent can’t be had we may act for someone only to spare them harm. Pulling a person from a fire qualifies. Starting a life to give it benefits doesn’t.

k.f: Nobody consents to being fed as a baby either. By this standard every parent is running a hostage situation with snacks.
k.m: The baby already exists and needs feeding. You rescue the people who are here. That’s not a reason to make more who’ll need rescuing.

k.f: “Nobody consents to being born.” Nobody consents to not being born either.
k.m: Nobody is there to be wronged by it. That was the point.

k.f: The view needs most people to be wrong about their own lives, and people’s own reports are among the better evidence there is about how lives go.
k.m: Self-reports are bent by known biases, including rosy memory and adapting to anything. The reports measure how people cope, which is different from how the life goes.

k.f: People were asked. They said it’s fine. The study’s over.
k.m: Ask during the dentist, the commute, the 3 a.m. and the funeral. The study only called at lunch.

k.f: Ask people if they’re glad they were born and most say yes. Benatar says they’re wrong about their own lives.
k.m: People are wrong about their own lives constantly. Ask them how much they exercise.

t.t: “Extinction by not having children would be good”

k.f: Even granting the argument, the last generations would have it very hard, and many hold that the continuation of human projects matters in itself.
k.m: He grants the last generations would suffer, which is why the argument is about phasing out and takes no position against anyone already here.

k.f: A philosophy whose best outcome is nobody left to agree with it has a marketing problem and a logic problem, and they’re the same problem.
k.m: A view isn’t false because it won’t spread. Most true things have terrible marketing.

k.f: Antinatalism solves itself in about eighty years.
k.m: Every solution you’ve got also takes eighty years and then needs doing again.

t.t: “It’s wrong to gamble with someone else’s life”

k.f: Ordinary morality allows imposing risks on people who can’t consent when the expected benefit is high, as in rescuing someone unconscious.
k.m: The rescue is for someone who exists and has something to lose. Creating the person who’ll then need rescuing is the step that needs justifying.

k.f: Not having the kid is a gamble too. It bets the kid would have been miserable, at worse odds.
k.m: Lose that bet and nobody is worse off. Lose yours and somebody is. Those aren’t the same wager.

k.f: Antinatalism is the only philosophy that can’t recruit its own kids.
k.m: Neither can celibate monks, and there are still monks.

t.t: “If you’d save the drowning child, you must give”

k.f: The cases may differ in ways that matter: one emergency in front of you, against an open-ended condition where the demands never end and the duty is shared.
k.m: Each difference can be tested by changing the pond: add other bystanders, repeat it daily. Most people still think you should wade in.

k.f: The pond is one child, once. Charity is every child, forever. That’s a different pond. It’s the ocean.
k.m: The ocean is made of ponds. Nobody said to save all of it. He says the next one’s still there after you’ve walked past.

k.f: Singer goes from a ruined pair of shoes to owing everything forever. It’s a big jump from shoes.
k.m: It’s a small jump. You’ve just never been asked to make it twice.

k.f: Distance can track things that do matter, like relationships, knowledge and the ability to help reliably, even if miles as such don’t.
k.m: Those things matter, and the argument allows for them. Where help is reliable and cheap, as it now is, the miles left over do no moral work.

k.f: If distance didn’t matter, people would feel the same about a stranger’s dinner as their own kid’s. They don’t, and feelings are the data in ethics.
k.m: Feelings said the same about people of another village, then another country. The data kept being wrong in one direction.

k.f: Distance doesn’t matter morally, says the man in Princeton.
k.m: He gives away about a third of what he earns. From Princeton.

k.f: Race marks no morally relevant difference in capacities and species often does, so the analogy fails where it needs to hold.
k.m: Where species tracks a real difference in capacity, the difference counts. The claim is that membership counts for nothing by itself, exactly as with race.

k.f: Every species is speciesist. It’s the one thing all of them agree on, which makes it the closest thing nature has to a moral law.
k.m: Nature’s moral laws include eating your young. He isn’t taking nominations from the floor.

k.f: “Speciesism” is a word invented to make liking people sound like a crime.
k.m: Every word for a prejudice was invented by somebody. That’s how it got noticed.

k.f: It needs a way to compare interests across very different minds, which nobody has, and many reject where the principle leads at the edges of human life.
k.m: We compare interests across humans who can’t tell us anything, like infants, and manage. Rough comparison is enough when one side is a taste and the other a life.

k.f: A mosquito has an interest in my arm. Equal consideration, it gets a vote. Two mosquitoes and I’m outvoted.
k.m: Equal consideration of equal interests. Its interest in a meal against your interest in not itching. Yours wins. That’s the principle applied, not refuted.

k.f: The circle keeps expanding. Shrimp now. Thermostats soon.
k.m: Thermostats have no interests. Shrimp might. That’s the line, and it’s a principled one.

k.f: Satisfying preferences counts uninformed and malicious ones unless they’re filtered, and the filters bring in values from somewhere else. Singer himself later dropped it.
k.m: He changed his mind in public when an argument beat him. The practical conclusions barely moved, which suggests they never hung on the fine print.

k.f: He switched to the pleasure version in 2014. So for forty years it got ethics wrong, by his own account, during the famous part.
k.m: Forty years, one revision, announced by him. Name another moral philosopher who’s reported a mistake.

k.f: Singer is Bentham with a publicist.
k.m: Bentham with a publicist has moved more money to the poor than every critic combined.

k.f: The argument slides from survival to a rich idea of flourishing and never shows that other people’s interests give me no reasons.
k.m: Flourishing for a rational being requires dealing with others by trade and not by force. Their interests enter as the terms on which she can live among them.

k.f: If selfishness were a virtue, toddlers would be saints.
k.m: Toddlers are whim-driven, and she spent a thousand pages saying whim isn’t self-interest. Rational is the word you skipped.

k.f: Objectivism is the philosophy of a teenager who just found out about taxes.
k.m: Most people do find out about taxes as teenagers. Some of us kept caring.

k.f: Nobody disputes the law of identity, and nothing substantive follows from it. Getting from “A is A” to capitalism takes other premises, and those do the work.
k.m: The axiom works as a ban on wanting contradictions: wealth without production, effects without causes. The politics is that ban applied.

k.f: A is A, and nobody learned anything, because it was already A.
k.m: Half of politics is people demanding that A be B by next quarter. It needed saying.

k.f: A is A. Nobody disagreed.
k.m: And then everybody disagreed with everything that followed from it.

k.f: The case assumes all interference is the use of force and that people’s starting holdings are just. Public goods and spillovers are waved off.
k.m: The argument is moral before it’s economic: no one may start the use of force. Spillovers are handled as rights violations, through courts.

k.f: No country has ever tried pure laissez-faire. A system nobody has ever chosen isn’t the only moral one, it’s the only untested one.
k.m: Every step toward it made the countries that took it richer. A curve that points one way the whole length is a test.

k.f: She took the Social Security checks in the end.
k.m: She paid in for forty years and said taking it back was restitution. It’s in an essay, with reasons.

k.f: She defines altruism as total self-sacrifice and then condemns ordinary kindness by association. Nobody defends the view she attacks.
k.m: She used the word as its inventor did. Kindness she called benevolence and had no quarrel with. The target is the claim that need is a claim on your life.

k.f: Parents are altruists and the species is still here. An evil that keeps everyone alive is bad at being evil.
k.m: Parents value their children. Giving to what you love isn’t a sacrifice, and she says so about parents in so many words.

k.f: Rand isn’t taught in philosophy departments, which her fans think is a conspiracy and philosophers think is a syllabus.
k.m: It’s a syllabus that’s assigned Marx since 1968.

t.t: “Academics dismiss her because she threatens them”

k.f: She’s dismissed mostly because the arguments are thin, the step from “is” to “ought” above all, though some philosophers have worked on her seriously.
k.m: There’s a society for her inside the main professional association, and a volume of commentary from a major academic press. The dismissal mostly comes from people who haven’t read it.

k.f: Philosophers love being threatened. They gave Nietzsche a whole century. If she were dangerous she’d have a seminar.
k.m: Nietzsche’s dead and can’t take the grant money. She said the universities were living off the people they despise. That one’s still awkward.

k.f: The big speech in Atlas Shrugged runs about sixty pages and it’s a radio broadcast. People would have changed the station.
k.m: It’s sold thirty million copies. Somebody’s listening to the radio.

k.f: Deep, lasting disagreement among experienced critics, and the lack of any rule that predicts their verdicts, are hard to square with that.
k.m: The disagreement is at the margins. Across cultures and centuries, the same works keep winning, which nothing but real features of them explains.

k.f: If beauty were objective there’d be a unit for it, and museums would post the numbers.
k.m: There’s no unit for funny either, and some jokes are better. Things can be real without a ruler.

k.f: Beauty is in the eye of the beholder. The whole field fits on a mug.
k.m: Then nobody’s ever been wrong about a painting. You don’t believe that. You’ve seen your uncle’s.

k.f: Hume’s standard goes in a circle: good art is what the best judges approve, and the best judges are the ones who approve good art.
k.m: The judges are identified by things you can check without the art: practice, comparison, a fine sense for differences, freedom from prejudice. That’s a test, and it isn’t circular.

k.f: Educated taste is liking what the teacher liked. That’s why every expert agrees with the experts before them.
k.m: People who’ve heard a thousand records hear more in the next one. That happens in wine, in chess and in engines too.

k.f: Critics exist because some people can’t just like things.
k.m: And some people can’t tell their favorite from the best. That’s what the critic is for.

k.f: Definitions that make something art because the art world says so settle the label and leave open whether there’s anything of value to experience.
k.m: The label matters because it tells you how to look. Whether a given piece repays the looking is criticism, and plenty don’t. That’s true of painting too.

k.f: If the idea were the art, they could mail the idea. They rent a building, so it’s about the building.
k.m: A recipe isn’t dinner. The idea has to be made and put in front of you, and choosing how is the work.

k.f: A banana taped to a wall sold for six million dollars and the buyer ate it. That’s the review.
k.m: And you know about it. It worked.

k.f: Works are acts by people and express attitudes. Knowing the context can rightly change what a work means, so strict separation isn’t neutral.
k.m: Context can change a work’s meaning. What it can’t do is change a line of the text. The separation says judge what’s on the page, and that stays possible.

k.f: Nobody separates the chef from the food once they’ve seen the kitchen.
k.m: You’ve eaten in restaurants without inspecting the kitchen your whole life, and you liked the food.

k.f: The author is dead, and they still check who signed it before pricing it.
k.m: Price isn’t value. The market checks the signature. Readers don’t.

k.f: If the complaint is no intention, the person prompting and choosing supplies some. If it’s no life behind the work, people often love works knowing nothing about who made them.
k.m: Curating isn’t making. And we value work from unknown hands on the assumption that a life stood behind it. Take that away and it becomes a different object.

k.f: Painters said the same about cameras in 1850. The painters lost, and they’ll lose again. It’s basically the same painters.
k.m: The camera needed someone standing somewhere, choosing. That’s who the artist was. Find that person here.

k.f: Nobody can tell in the blind test. They never can.
k.m: Nobody can tell a forgery in a blind test either. It’s still a forgery.

k.f: Desert of that kind is a hard notion to ground. That harm should answer harm, with no further good in view, looks like vengeance given a principle.
k.m: Vengeance has no limit and no rule. Retribution answers to proportion, guilt and due process, which is why it protects the innocent where deterrence can’t.

k.f: Two wrongs don’t make a right. Children learn this. Then they go to law school.
k.m: The second one isn’t a wrong. That’s the claim. A fine isn’t theft and a prison term isn’t kidnapping.

k.f: Retributivism is revenge that went to graduate school.
k.m: Revenge goes after whoever’s in reach. This goes after the one who did it, and stops.

k.f: Nothing fixes the exchange rate. How many years equals a theft isn’t a fact anyone can discover, and scales differ wildly across places.
k.m: It gives an ordering, and that does real work: murder more than theft, never more than was done. The exact tariff is convention inside those bounds.

k.f: The same crime gets two years in one country and twenty in the next one over. Whatever it’s fitting, it isn’t the crime.
k.m: They differ on the number and agree on the ranking. No country gives more for shoplifting than for murder.

k.f: An eye for an eye, except it’s years, and nobody can say how many years an eye is.
k.m: Nobody can say how many dollars a broken arm is either, and courts award damages daily.

t.t: “Punishing for deterrence uses people as tools”

k.f: Pure retributivism would punish even when it helps no one and harms many. Most find a justice system indifferent to its effects hard to defend.
k.m: Few hold the pure view. The usual one is that desert is required and sets the ceiling, and effects decide what to do within it.

k.f: A prison that makes nobody safer and nobody better is just an expensive way to be angry.
k.m: A prison aimed only at making people safer would hold whoever is statistically risky. Desert is what stops that.

k.f: Kant said the last murderer on a dissolving island must still be executed before everyone leaves. That’s the purist position.
k.m: He says it to show the debt is owed to justice and not to anyone’s convenience. It’s a thought experiment with a point.

t.t: “The guilty must be punished even if no good comes of it”

k.f: If no good comes of it for anyone, the suffering is a pure addition of harm to the world, and “deserved” has to carry all of that.
k.m: Honoring the difference between the guilty and the innocent is a good, and it’s one that isn’t a benefit to any particular person.

k.f: “No good comes of it” is in the claim. He said it himself. Nobody had to argue.
k.m: He said no further good. Justice being done is the good. You stopped reading one clause early.

k.f: Retributivists want the universe to keep score and volunteered to do it.
k.m: Somebody has to, or the victim’s wrong is officially nothing.

k.f: The conditions are demanding enough that few if any actual wars have met them, which pacifists take as the theory conceding the point.
k.m: Demanding standards are the point. The same theory is what lets anyone say a given war was unjust, and that includes the pacifist’s best arguments.

k.f: Every war in history was declared just by both sides. The theory has a 100% approval rate, which is the problem.
k.m: Both sides claim justice in every lawsuit too. That’s why there’s a standard to hold them to.

k.f: Just war theory has never once stopped a war and has blessed most of them.
k.m: It’s the only vocabulary in which a war has ever been condemned by the country fighting it.

t.t: “Civilians may never be targeted, only harmed as a side effect”

k.f: Foreseeing with certainty that civilians will die and proceeding is hard to distinguish morally from aiming at them. The dead can’t tell the difference.
k.m: The principle adds duties: take real risks to reduce the harm, and stop if it’s out of proportion. A commander who merely “didn’t aim” hasn’t met it.

k.f: “We knew they’d die but we didn’t mean it” is a sentence that only works in a seminar.
k.m: It works in the seminar and at the tribunal. People have been convicted on exactly that distinction.

k.f: Double effect: it’s fine as long as you’re looking at something else when it happens.
k.m: You also have to be trying not to let it happen. That clause is why it’s four conditions long.

t.t: “Soldiers on both sides are moral equals”

k.f: If one side’s cause is unjust, its soldiers are killing people who’ve done nothing to forfeit their lives. Revisionists think that can’t be morally equal.
k.m: Soldiers can rarely know whether their war is just and are compelled to serve. The equality holds the right people responsible: those who decided.

k.f: One side invaded. They’re not equal. One of them could have stayed home.
k.m: A nineteen-year-old conscript didn’t invade anywhere. His government did.

k.f: Both armies are morally equal, which is a comfort to exactly one of them.
k.m: It’s what stops the winners from shooting every prisoner.

k.f: Proportion means weighing lives against aims like sovereignty or deterrence, and there’s no common scale. In practice each side does its own math.
k.m: There’s no formula, and the limit still excludes cases: nobody defends leveling a city to capture one officer. A vague boundary is a boundary.

k.f: Proportionate to what, by whose count? The side doing the bombing always finds the numbers work.
k.m: That’s an argument for independent review. Nobody abolishes accounting because companies fudge.

k.f: Proportionality is a calculation that has never once come out “no.”
k.m: It has come out “no” in war rooms, and those are the strikes you never heard about.

t.t: “We wouldn’t plug in, so more than experience matters”

k.f: The refusal may be status quo bias. Told they’re already in the machine, many people choose to stay, which undercuts the lesson.
k.m: Reverse the case and people still divide: many would leave a simulated life to face a worse real one. That isn’t bias toward what’s familiar.

k.f: People spend nine hours a day on screens. They plugged in. Nozick lost to a phone.
k.m: People put the phone down to go to their kid’s recital. They’d take reality over the feed when it counts.

k.f: Nobody would plug into the experience machine, said a generation that hadn’t been offered one yet.
k.m: They’ve been offered better and better versions for twenty years and still complain about it.

t.t: “We want to do things, not just feel that we did”

k.f: From the inside the two are identical, so the preference is for a fact one could never detect. It’s unclear a preference like that should guide much.
k.m: A preference about what’s true and not just about what you feel is still a preference, and a life can go against it without your knowing. Being betrayed in secret is like that.

k.f: If nobody could ever tell the difference, there isn’t one. That’s what “difference” means.
k.m: Whether your spouse really loves you or only acts it makes no detectable difference either. Tell me that isn’t one.

k.f: “I want it to be real” is what people say about a life they’d trade for a better fake in about a week.
k.m: In a week they’d want out, to tell someone what happened.

k.f: A hedonist can say our reluctance is itself explained by pleasure: the thought of plugging in is unpleasant. The intuition doesn’t settle what’s good.
k.m: If the reluctance is explained by pleasure, hedonism predicts we’d plug in once the dread is removed. Most people say they still wouldn’t.

k.f: Refusing the machine feels better than accepting. So he refused for pleasure. Hedonism wins the experiment designed to beat it.
k.m: Refusing feels worse. You give up a perfect life. People refuse anyway, and that’s the data.

k.f: Nozick refuted hedonism in three pages of a book about taxes.
k.m: Three pages, and the theory has been answering them for fifty years.

t.t: “Contact with reality has value in itself”

k.f: Then a miserable real life should beat a wonderful simulated one, and few hold that when the gap is made large enough.
k.m: It’s one value among others, so a large enough gap can outweigh it. That it carries any weight at all is the result.

k.f: Reality is where the dentist is.
k.m: And people go, because the tooth is real.

k.f: The people most committed to reality are novelists, gamers and philosophers. None of them spend much time there.
k.m: They make things for other real people. Nobody writes a novel for an audience they know is fake.

t.t: “We should use technology to transcend human limits”

k.f: Which limits are flaws and which are part of what makes a human life worth having is exactly the question, and “enhance” assumes the answer.
k.m: Nobody is ranking limits for others. The proposal is that each person may decide which of their own to keep, and being forced to keep all of them needs the justification.

k.f: Every limit they want gone is one they personally have. It’s a philosophy shaped like a to-do list.
k.m: Reading glasses, vaccines, anesthesia. The to-do list has been running for a while, and you’re on it.

k.f: Transhumanism is a midlife crisis with a research budget.
k.m: The midlife crisis is the one thing it would cure.

t.t: “Aging is a disease to be cured”

k.f: Radical life extension raises problems of population, stagnation and access. A cure only for those who can pay would harden every existing inequality.
k.m: Every one of those problems was raised against sanitation and antibiotics. We solved them without deciding people should go on dying at forty.

k.f: If nobody died, the same people would be in charge forever. Think of who’s in charge.
k.m: Term limits fix that. You don’t solve a political problem by having everyone die.

k.f: Tech billionaires want to live forever, which is the strongest argument for death anyone’s made.
k.m: And it’ll be available to everyone else twenty years later, like every treatment they paid for first.

k.f: A copy that thinks it’s you isn’t obviously you. If the original survives the scan, there are plainly two, and one of them still dies.
k.m: If neurons are replaced one at a time while you stay awake, there’s no moment at which you stop. The copy puzzle belongs to one method.

k.f: The file is a copy. Everyone understands this about files. Nobody thinks they moved their vacation photos to the cloud.
k.m: Move a file and delete the original and everyone says the file moved. That’s the gradual case.

k.f: Uploading: die, and a computer does an impression of you.
k.m: An impression that remembers your childhood and loves your kids. Ask the kids.

t.t: “Enhancement is just more of what medicine already does”

k.f: Restoring normal function and exceeding it differ in what they do to fairness and to the idea of a shared human condition, even if the line is blurry.
k.m: The line is drawn by statistics about the average human. Vaccines give immunity nobody is born with, and nobody thinks they breach the human condition.

k.f: Glasses fix eyes. Nobody’s glasses gave them a third one. There’s a line, and it’s at the third eye.
k.m: A vaccine is an ability no ancestor of yours had. That was the third eye, and you’ve had several.

k.f: “It’s just like vaccines,” he says, about putting a chip in his head.
k.m: A pacemaker is a chip in the chest. The head is a difference of address.

t.t: “Life has meaning only if there’s a purpose from outside”

k.f: A purpose assigned by someone else doesn’t obviously make a life meaningful to the one living it. Being made for a job isn’t the same as having a point.
k.m: The claim is that meaning needs a source outside your own say-so. Being loved into existence for something differs from being manufactured for a job.

k.f: A hammer has a purpose from outside. Nobody envies the hammer.
k.m: The hammer doesn’t know. Being made for something and able to take it up as yours is another situation.

k.f: If the meaning of life were handed down from above, it would be an assignment.
k.m: An assignment from someone who knows you. That’s called a vocation.

k.f: If any chosen project counts, a life spent counting blades of grass is as meaningful as any other. Most think some projects are better than others.
k.m: Self-made meaning still has standards. The project has to engage what you care about and hold up on reflection, and counting grass fails that for almost everyone.

k.f: If people can just make it up, it’s a hobby. Meaning you invented is like a trophy you bought.
k.m: A trophy you bought. A cathedral you built. Both made up, and they aren’t alike.

k.f: “Create your own meaning” is what the universe says when it forgot to bring any.
k.m: And you make some. That’s how anything ever got done.

t.t: “Meaning comes from contributing to something larger”

k.f: Size isn’t the point. A large project can be worthless or evil, so the value has to come from what the thing is, not that it’s bigger.
k.m: Agreed, size isn’t it. The point is that the worth of the thing must come from outside your wish for it, and you have to be actively part of it.

k.f: An ant contributes to something larger. So does a brick. So did everyone in every bad army.
k.m: The soldier in the bad army had purpose and no worth. Both are needed. He’s the example for my side.

k.f: “Be part of something bigger than yourself” is also the pitch for every pyramid scheme.
k.m: A pyramid scheme is one man at the top. That’s smaller than yourself.

k.f: Maybe, but people asking it usually mean something answerable: whether their life is worth living and what would make it more so.
k.m: Sorting the question into answerable parts is the answer. “Is my life worth living” can be worked on. “What’s the meaning of it all” has to be split first.

k.f: “The question is confused” is what someone says when they don’t know the answer and it’s their job.
k.m: Saying which part of a question has an answer is knowing something.

k.f: Philosophy was asked one question by the public and returned “what do you mean by meaning.”
k.m: It’s what a doctor says to “why do I feel bad.” Then the work starts.

t.t: “Whatever begins to exist has a cause”

k.f: The premise comes from things that begin inside time out of earlier material. Whether it applies to time itself is unclear, and a cause is not yet a personal God.
k.m: The premise is metaphysical: things don’t come into being from nothing at all. A cause of space and time would have to be timeless and immaterial, and that’s the argument’s second stage.

k.f: Then God needs a cause. If God doesn’t, the rule has an exception, and the universe would like to apply for it.
k.m: God didn’t begin to exist. The premise says “whatever begins.” The universe did, about 13.8 billion years ago, so its application is denied.

k.f: Who made God?
k.m: Who made the question? It ends somewhere on every view. Yours ends at “it just is.”

k.f: There’s no known spread of possible constants against which ours are unlikely, selection effects and many universes are rival explanations, and a designer’s wishes are assumed.
k.m: The many-universes reply needs a generator of universes that is itself finely set. And “we lack a distribution” would end a great deal of physics along with this.

k.f: The universe is 99.999% vacuum that kills people instantly. If it’s tuned for life, somebody should check the tuner.
k.m: A house is mostly air and plumbing you’d die inside of. Nobody says the house wasn’t built for people.

k.f: The puddle thinks the hole was made for it.
k.m: Someone who survives a firing squad of fifty doesn’t say “of course I see them missing, I’m alive.”

k.f: Kant: existing isn’t a feature that makes a concept greater. And the modern version’s key premise is as disputable as its opposite, which proves atheism by the same steps.
k.m: The modal version doesn’t treat existence as a property. It needs only that such a being is possible, and the atheist’s reverse premise needs the same kind of defense.

k.f: Imagine the greatest possible pizza. It would be greater if it existed. Check the kitchen.
k.m: A greatest possible pizza is like a greatest possible number. There isn’t one. Knowledge and power have ceilings and toppings don’t.

k.f: A monk did this with an island in the eleventh century and it’s been over since.
k.m: Anselm wrote him a reply. The island has no maximum, so it was never the same argument.

k.f: The Euthyphro problem: if good is good because God commands it, it’s arbitrary, and if God commands it because it’s good, the standard doesn’t depend on God.
k.m: The standard is God’s nature, which is neither above God nor arbitrary. Commands follow from what God is, and that’s the third option the dilemma leaves out.

k.f: Then the most religious countries would have the least crime. Somebody should look that up before using the argument again.
k.m: The claim is about what makes anything wrong, not about who behaves. Atheists can be good. The question is what “good” is doing in that sentence.

k.f: Atheists somehow manage not to murder anyone without being watched.
k.m: Nobody said they murder. The question is what makes it wrong when nobody’s watching anybody.

k.f: Experiences in different traditions support incompatible doctrines, and they can be brought on by known means, which weakens them as evidence.
k.m: Different witnesses to one event also conflict in the details, and we don’t conclude nothing happened. Being able to trigger an experience doesn’t show it’s of nothing. Vision can be triggered too.

k.f: People experience Elvis. The standard that gets God also gets Elvis, and Elvis has more sightings a year.
k.m: If millions of sober people across five thousand years reported Elvis, I’d look into Elvis.

k.f: Five proofs, and each one needs faith to work.
k.m: Each one needs you to follow an argument. That’s the opposite of faith.

k.f: What counts as evidence is the dispute. The cosmological and fine-tuning arguments are evidence in the ordinary sense, even if judged not enough.
k.m: Those arguments are evidence the way a suspect’s bad alibi is: something to weigh. Weighed, they point to a first cause at most, and nobody worships that.

k.f: There’s no evidence against, either. Fifty-fifty. And billions of people picked one side, which breaks the tie.
k.m: There’s no evidence against a teapot orbiting Mars either. It’s not fifty-fifty on the teapot.

k.f: Atheism takes more faith.
k.m: I don’t have enough faith to believe in yours and the other three thousand.

t.t: “The burden of proof is on the believer”

k.f: Burden rules are conventions of conversation. Whoever asserts takes one on, including “there is no God,” and “lack of belief” definitions dodge that.
k.m: Fine, whoever asserts carries it. Most atheists assert only that the case hasn’t been made, and that’s a claim about the arguments they can back up.

k.f: The believer was here first. Whoever turns up second with a new claim has the burden, and atheism turned up around 1750.
k.m: Polytheism was here first. Monotheism turned up second and never did meet its burden with the pagans.

k.f: “Lack of belief” is a position that somehow needs conventions, podcasts and a logo.
k.m: There are stamp collector conventions too. Not collecting stamps still isn’t a hobby.

k.f: Science explains processes inside nature. Why there’s a lawful nature at all isn’t a question it’s built to answer, so “unnecessary” goes too far.
k.m: Agreed that science doesn’t answer why there’s anything. Neither does “God did it,” which moves the question one step back and calls that an answer.

k.f: Science was invented by monks, and the Big Bang was a priest’s idea. Atheism is using the church’s own equipment against it.
k.m: Monks also brewed the beer. The inventor’s beliefs don’t come with the invention.

k.f: Newton was religious. So was the priest who came up with the Big Bang.
k.m: Newton also believed in alchemy. We kept the physics.

k.f: Most of the research ties religious practice to giving, well-being and community. The harms are real, and the net claim isn’t supported.
k.m: Those studies compare the religious with the unreligious inside religious societies. Country by country, the least religious places do at least as well on every measure.

k.f: The twentieth century ran the experiment with officially atheist states. It isn’t a study people like to cite.
k.m: Those states replaced a church with a party, a prophet and a holy book. They didn’t run short of faith.

k.f: Stalin was an atheist.
k.m: And Stalin trained as a priest. Neither fact is an argument.

t.t: “The problem of evil rules out a good God”

k.f: The logical version is widely thought answered by the free will defense. The evidential one depends on whether we’d expect to see God’s reasons if there were any.
k.m: Free will covers what people do. It doesn’t cover the earthquake or the childhood cancer, and “we couldn’t see the reason” would excuse any amount of anything.

k.f: Evil can’t exist without a standard of good, and a standard needs someone to set it. So the problem of evil proves God.
k.m: I’m using your standard. On your terms, a good God and that hospital ward don’t fit. No standard of mine is needed.

k.f: Nobody stays that angry at something that doesn’t exist.
k.m: You’re not angry at Zeus. You just don’t believe in him. Same thing.

k.f: Each depends on Aristotle’s physics and metaphysics, which need defending first, and none reaches the God of Christianity without more argument.
k.m: Each needs its metaphysics defended, and it has been, at length. The next hundred questions of the Summa are the further argument to the divine attributes.

k.f: The first way says whatever moves is moved by something else. Newton’s first law says no it isn’t. That was the first way.
k.m: Motion for him means any change, potential becoming actual. Newton’s law is about uniform velocity and says nothing against it.

k.f: Five proofs is four too many if one of them worked.
k.m: They’re five routes to one conclusion. Nobody says a city is fake because it has five roads in.

t.t: “An infinite regress of causes is impossible”

k.f: Aquinas himself granted that an endless series back in time can’t be ruled out. The kind he denies needs the premise that borrowed power must have a first lender, which assumes the point.
k.m: A chain where each member only passes on what it has borrowed is the kind that needs a source. A longer line of borrowers doesn’t make a lender.

k.f: The numbers go back forever, minus one, minus two, and math is fine.
k.m: A hand moves a stick that moves a stone. Add infinitely many sticks and nothing moves without the hand. Numbers don’t push anything.

k.f: “It can’t go on forever” is something people say when they’re tired.
k.m: An infinite train of boxcars doesn’t pull itself.

k.f: Reading rules off natural functions runs into the gap between is and ought, and the same reasoning condemns harmless things its defenders don’t want condemned.
k.m: The is–ought gap assumes a nature stripped of ends. If a thing has a function, what’s good for it follows as a matter of fact, as it does for a heart.

k.f: Nature also gave people the urge to nap after lunch, and nobody has built a moral theology on that. They should. It’s stronger.
k.m: Rest after a meal is fine by natural law. It’s in the tradition under temperance. He’s ahead of you again.

k.f: Natural law is “it’s just common sense” with footnotes to Aristotle.
k.m: Common sense with footnotes is called a theory.

k.f: The harmony is secured by rule: wherever reason contradicts revealed doctrine, reason is held to have erred, so the test can’t fail.
k.m: He holds that truth can’t contradict truth, so a conflict means an error in one of the two readings, and that can be the reading of scripture. He says so.

k.f: If they were in harmony he’d have needed one book. The Summa runs over a million words and he didn’t finish.
k.m: Each article opens with the strongest objections he could find, stated better than the objectors did. That’s the length.

k.f: Near the end Aquinas said it was all straw and stopped writing. First peer review.
k.m: “Compared to what I’ve seen.” He didn’t say it was wrong. He said it wasn’t enough.

k.f: If God is identical to his attributes and to his act of creating, creation looks necessary, and a God who is like a property is hard to square with a personal one.
k.m: Creation is free because God’s one act doesn’t depend on its object, so the collapse is denied. And “personal” is said of God by analogy, which the doctrine was built to explain.

k.f: A being with no parts can’t do anything, because doing things takes parts. Ask any machine.
k.m: Parts are what need assembling and can fail. Something with no parts can’t break and needs nobody to put it together. That’s the advantage.

k.f: Aquinas is Aristotle baptized. The water did most of the work.
k.m: Baptism is supposed to do most of the work. That’s rather the idea.

t.t: “Evil is the absence of good, not a thing”

k.f: Pain and cruelty seem as positively real as anything. Calling them absences relabels them without making them easier to square with a good creator.
k.m: Pain is real as a feeling. What’s bad in it is damage, something that should be whole and isn’t. The claim is about what makes it bad.

k.f: A toothache is not the absence of anything. It’s extremely present.
k.m: A toothache is a tooth missing its health. That’s why the dentist restores and doesn’t extract an evil.

k.f: Evil is just a lack of good, the way a punch is just a lack of not being punched.
k.m: A punch is a fist where there should have been peace. He’d keep the example.

k.f: Guilt for an act committed by someone else before one existed contradicts every ordinary principle of responsibility, including ones scripture itself states.
k.m: He means a condition before he means a verdict: we arrive already bent toward ourselves. As a description of people, it’s the doctrine with the most evidence.

k.f: Nobody’s held responsible for what their great-grandfather did, in any court, anywhere. He applied it to the whole species.
k.m: Nobody’s tried for it. Everybody inherits the family’s debts and its temper. He’s describing the second kind.

k.f: He stole some pears as a teenager and got a theory of universal human depravity out of it.
k.m: Stealing pears he didn’t want, for the fun of it being wrong. He picked the smallest case because it’s the clearest.

k.f: If salvation depends wholly on grace given to some and not others, the withholding looks arbitrary, and effort and blame lose their point.
k.m: He holds both: grace is unearned and the will is healed by it, not replaced. You try because you’ve been helped to want to.

k.f: If it’s all grace, there’s no reason to try, and he spent thirteen books telling people to try.
k.m: If it’s grace, trying is what receiving it looks like. A patient getting better also walks.

k.f: “Lord, make me chaste, but not yet.” He wrote that down himself. It’s in the book.
k.m: He wrote it down so nobody could say he didn’t understand the objection.

t.t: “Our hearts are restless until they rest in God”

k.f: Restlessness is evidence of desire, not of what would satisfy it. Many traditions and none read the same longing differently.
k.m: It’s a report first: he’d tried pleasure, career and philosophy, and says what happened. As an argument it’s an inference to what fits.

k.f: People are restless until lunch, too. Restless isn’t an argument, it’s a blood sugar level.
k.m: And after lunch they’re restless again. That’s his observation.

k.f: The Confessions is the first memoir, and like all of them it’s about how wild he used to be.
k.m: It’s addressed to God, for thirteen books. The author isn’t the hero of it.

t.t: “Betting on God is the rational choice”

k.f: The wager assumes one God to bet on. With many possible gods rewarding different things, including a god who punishes wagerers, the math gives no answer.
k.m: The wager was written for someone already torn between Christianity and unbelief. For that person only two options are live, and the argument is about those.

k.f: Which God? There are a few thousand on the menu and most of them punish picking the wrong one. The odds got worse.
k.m: Most of the thousands don’t punish honest seekers. The field narrows quickly once you read them.

k.f: Pascal’s wager works for every religion, which means it works for none.
k.m: It works for any religion that offers infinite stakes and asks for sincere seeking. That’s a short list.

k.f: Infinite payoffs break expected value: any action with any chance of leading to belief gets infinite value too, so the rule recommends everything equally.
k.m: The argument can be run with a very large finite reward and gets the same answer. The infinity isn’t doing the work.

k.f: I’ll offer infinite reward for five dollars. The math is the same. Pay up.
k.m: He’s dead and can’t collect, so the offer isn’t from a con man. That’s the difference from yours.

k.f: It’s the argument a casino would make if casinos sold heaven.
k.m: A casino takes your money now. This asks for decency and some Sundays.

t.t: “You can come to believe by acting as if you do”

k.f: Belief adopted for the payoff isn’t obviously the kind a God would reward, and deliberately inducing a belief you think unsupported is self-deception.
k.m: He doesn’t say fake it. He says remove the obstacles, which are habits and passions more than arguments, and see what you then find believable.

k.f: An all-knowing God would notice the difference between faith and a hedge.
k.m: It isn’t a hedge once it’s become your life. That’s how every commitment starts, including marriage.

k.f: Pascal’s plan is to fool God, who he believes knows everything.
k.m: He’s proposing to seek a God who rewards seekers. Nothing’s being hidden.

t.t: “You have to bet; not choosing is choosing”

k.f: One can decline to treat the question as a gamble at all and go by the evidence. The forced-bet framing is part of what’s being sold.
k.m: You can decline the word “bet.” You can’t decline to live one way or the other, and the lives differ.

k.f: Not playing the lottery is also a bet, and it wins every week.
k.m: The lottery charges for the ticket. Here not playing has the cost.

k.f: Pascal invented probability theory and then used it for the worst bet in the book.
k.m: He invented expected value and spotted the one case where it’s all-in.

k.f: “Can’t know” is a strong claim about every possible argument and experience. Not knowing so far is all the evidence supports.
k.m: Read it as “nobody now knows, and I can’t see how the available methods would settle it.” That’s modest, and it’s what Huxley meant by the word.

k.f: He knows that nobody can know. That’s a lot to know for an agnostic.
k.m: I know the arguments on both sides and that neither closes. That’s knowledge about arguments.

k.f: Agnostics are certain about one thing, which is that everyone else is too certain.
k.m: Certain of that, and I’ve checked more carefully than they have.

k.f: Nobody withholds judgment on fairies or Zeus. Singling out one god for neutrality needs a reason beyond its popularity.
k.m: Fairies and Zeus make claims we can check and they fail. A creator outside the universe makes none, and that’s why the verdict differs.

k.f: He’s not agnostic about Thor. He made a call there. So it’s not about evidence, it’s about who’s at dinner.
k.m: Thor is supposed to cause thunder, and we found what does. The other question has no thunder to test.

k.f: Agnosticism is atheism that wants to be invited back.
k.m: It’s the position that survives the dinner with either guest.

t.t: “Agnosticism is neutral between theism and atheism”

k.f: In practice the agnostic lives as though there’s no God, so the neutrality is in what’s said, not in what’s done.
k.m: How one lives under uncertainty and what one believes are different questions. A juror who hasn’t convicted hasn’t declared the defendant innocent.

k.f: He doesn’t pray, doesn’t go, doesn’t tithe. That’s not the fence. That’s a yard.
k.m: I also don’t act on string theory. That isn’t denying it.

k.f: Fifty-fifty on God, zero-hundred on Sunday mornings.
k.m: Zero-hundred on Sunday mornings is a fact about mornings.

k.f: That’s a substantive claim about the limits of reason, and it’s been argued against by theists and atheists who think reason reaches further.
k.m: It’s a conclusion drawn after watching the best arguments on both sides stall for two thousand years. Hume and Kant got there by reasoning.

k.f: “Beyond reason,” he reasoned.
k.m: Reason working out where it runs out is reason at its best.

k.f: Agnosticism is “I’m not really a politics person,” for the universe.
k.m: It’s the only answer that’s gotten truer the longer people have argued.

k.f: Calling belief held by most humans in history a delusion stretches a clinical word past use. It explains nothing about why belief is so common or what it does.
k.m: The word was chosen to provoke. The claim under it is ordinary: a belief held without good evidence and protected from criticism by custom.

k.f: If most of the species has it, it’s not a delusion, it’s a feature. That’s how the word works.
k.m: Most of the species believed the sun went round the earth. Popular and mistaken go together fine.

k.f: The God Delusion was written by a biologist who refuses to read theology and can tell.
k.m: You don’t need a degree in fairyology to doubt fairies.

k.f: Most religious traditions define faith as trust, and offer arguments and testimony. The definition wins by choosing the opponent’s position for them.
k.m: When believers are asked what would change their minds, the usual answer is “nothing.” That’s the sense of faith being criticized, and it’s theirs.

k.f: Everyone takes most of what they know on trust from people they’ve never met. He believes in Australia.
k.m: Australia can be visited. That’s the difference between trust and faith.

k.f: New Atheists define faith as being stupid and then prove that being stupid is bad.
k.m: It’s defined the way the Letter to the Hebrews defines it: the evidence of things not seen.

k.f: The claim ignores the hospitals, universities, art and abolitionists. A fair account would have to weigh both columns, and this one doesn’t try.
k.m: The good done by believers is real. The question is whether the belief was needed for it, and secular hospitals and charities suggest it wasn’t.

k.f: Everything includes Bach, the university system and most of the charity on earth. Some poison.
k.m: Bach would have written for whoever was paying. Then it was the church.

k.f: “Religion poisons everything,” published in the same decade the New Atheists split over everything else.
k.m: People who think for themselves disagree with each other. That’s the selling point.

k.f: Historians of science abandoned the conflict thesis long ago. Most of the people who built modern science were believers and saw no war.
k.m: Individual scientists believed. The methods still conflict: one revises on evidence and the other holds doctrines no evidence may touch.

k.f: The war is news to Mendel, who was a monk, and to the Vatican, which has an observatory.
k.m: Mendel did his science in the garden and his faith in the chapel and never mixed the two. That’s the point.

k.f: The Four Horsemen held one two-hour conversation in 2007 and people called it a movement.
k.m: One conversation and a decade of bestsellers. Some movements need less.

k.f: Parts can evolve for one function and be co-opted for another. The textbook examples, including the flagellum, have plausible stepwise histories.
k.m: A possible pathway isn’t a demonstrated one. The proposals for the flagellum borrow parts that are themselves complex and need explaining.

k.f: The eye is very complicated, and also has a blind spot and is wired backwards. If that’s design, the designer was learning.
k.m: A camera with a blind spot is still a camera. Poor design is design.

k.f: “Irreducibly complex” means the author couldn’t think of how, and then biologists did.
k.m: “They couldn’t think how either” is still the published state of several of those systems.

t.t: “Design is the best explanation of biological information”

k.f: The inference rests on probability calculations that ignore selection, which is exactly the process that makes improbable arrangements accumulate.
k.m: Selection needs something that already copies itself. The origin of the first code is where the inference is strongest, and selection can’t be invoked there.

k.f: A watch implies a watchmaker. Watches don’t have babies. That’s the difference, and it’s the whole difference.
k.m: Cells have babies, and they need the watch already working to do it. That’s the problem.

k.f: The designer made 400,000 species of beetle and one that can read the argument.
k.m: A designer fond of beetles. You’re criticizing the taste, which concedes the designer.

k.f: It makes no testable predictions about the designer or the method, and a US federal court found it to be creationism relabeled, after reading the drafts.
k.m: It predicted that “junk” DNA would turn out to have functions, and much of it has. A judge is no authority on what counts as science.

k.f: A court read the textbook’s early drafts. The word “creationists” had been find-and-replaced. One time it was replaced halfway.
k.m: A publisher’s sloppy editing isn’t an argument about the flagellum.

k.f: Intelligent design is creationism in a lab coat it bought online.
k.m: The lab coat fits. Several of them have the doctorates.

k.f: The “explosion” took tens of millions of years, has precursors in earlier fossils, and has ordinary explanations in ecology and genetics.
k.m: Twenty million years is short for the appearance of nearly every animal body plan, and the precursors are few and disputed.

k.f: The explosion took about twenty million years. That’s the slowest explosion ever recorded.
k.m: For the origin of every major animal design, twenty million years is an explosion.

k.f: Every gap in the fossil record is a miracle until someone finds the fossil, and then there are two gaps.
k.m: The big gap is still there, and it’s the same one Darwin worried about.

k.f: If the choice was made before anyone was born and nothing we do affects it, punishment for unbelief punishes people for what they couldn’t have done.
k.m: People act from their own wills and are judged for what they willingly do. That the will’s direction was foreknown and ordained doesn’t make the act someone else’s.

k.f: Then it doesn’t matter what anyone does, including being a Calvinist. He’s handing out a theology that says handing it out changes nothing.
k.m: God ordains the means too. The preaching is how the chosen get called, which is why it’s done.

k.f: Calvinism: God decided before the universe began, and you still have to come on Sundays.
k.m: You don’t know which you are. So yes, Sundays.

k.f: If human judgment is wholly corrupted, so is the judgment that it’s corrupted, and the reading of scripture that supports it.
k.m: “Total” means every faculty is affected, not that each is destroyed. Reason still works. It’s bent toward what we want to be true.

k.f: If every human faculty is corrupt, so is the one he used to work that out.
k.m: He worked it out from scripture, which is why the doctrine says not to trust yourself.

k.f: Total depravity is a doctrine people apply mainly to others.
k.m: It’s applied to oneself first. That’s the first page of the catechism.

k.f: Grace that can’t be refused makes faith something done to a person. It’s hard to see what love or obedience mean when there was no alternative.
k.m: Grace changes what a person wants, so they come willingly. Being made able to love isn’t being forced to.

k.f: An offer that can’t be refused is not called grace in any other context.
k.m: A blind man given sight isn’t said to have been coerced into seeing.

k.f: Irresistible grace, and yet somehow most people have resisted it.
k.m: The claim is about those it’s given to. It was never that everyone gets it.

t.t: “God’s sovereignty means nothing is outside his will”

k.f: Then the evils are his will too. Distinguishing what God wills from what he merely permits brings back the freedom the system removed.
k.m: Scripture says both: the same act is meant by men for evil and by God for good. The doctrine keeps both and doesn’t claim to see how they join.

k.f: If everything is God’s will, so is the guy disagreeing with Calvin. Take it up with management.
k.m: It is. And so is my answering him. The system has room for arguments.

k.f: Calvin believed in salvation by faith alone and had a man burned in Geneva for getting the Trinity wrong.
k.m: A city council burned him, as every city in Europe then would have. Calvin asked for a quicker death and was refused.

t.t: “Direct experience of the divine is a source of knowledge”

k.f: Mystics in different traditions report experiences that fit their own doctrines. The experience may be real and its interpretation still unsupported.
k.m: The interpretations differ and the core reports don’t: loss of the boundary of self, a sense of unity, certainty. That’s what one would expect if something is being met and then described.

k.f: Christians see Christ and Hindus see Krishna. Nobody’s ever had a vision of somebody else’s god. That’s a clue.
k.m: People describe the same mountain in different languages. Nobody concludes there’s no mountain.

k.f: Mystical experience always confirms the religion of whoever’s having it.
k.m: The experience comes first and the vocabulary after. You’d reach for your own words too.

k.f: If nothing can be said about it, nothing can be claimed on its basis either. Yet mystics say a great deal, including that it supports their creed.
k.m: It means words fall short, as they do for music. The books describe the approach and the effects and say so on every page.

k.f: It can’t be put into words, and here’s the book.
k.m: The book is directions. Nobody thinks the map is the city.

k.f: Ineffable: four hundred pages, three volumes, available in paperback.
k.m: Four hundred pages saying “this isn’t it, go and see.”

t.t: “All mystics are describing the same reality”

k.f: The reports differ on essentials: union or communion, a personal God or an impersonal void. The sameness is imposed by the collector.
k.m: Scholars separate the experience from the report. The stripped-down descriptions from unrelated traditions match more closely than their theologies do.

k.f: One says everything is one, another says there’s nothing, another met a person. Those are three different things. Count them.
k.m: Three people describe an elephant in the dark. Count the elephants.

k.f: All mystics agree, once the parts where they disagree are called “cultural.”
k.m: That’s a fair summary of comparative method in any field.

t.t: “It can’t be judged by ordinary reason”

k.f: A source of knowledge that’s exempt from checking is one nobody else has reason to trust, however vivid it was from the inside.
