k.m: It can be judged by its fruits, which is the traditions’ own test: what the person is like afterwards. That’s a public check.

k.f: “You can’t judge it rationally” is also the defense for every bad decision made at 3 a.m.
k.m: The decision at 3 a.m. doesn’t leave people kinder for forty years.

k.f: The same states are available from fasting, drums, or a mushroom, and the mushroom is faster.
k.m: The mushroom route gets the same reports. That suggests there’s something there to get to.

k.f: Without a self, karma and rebirth have nobody to carry them. The answer is causal continuity, and then responsibility across lives is as puzzling as before.
k.m: A flame passed from candle to candle is neither the same flame nor a different one. Continuity without an owner is the teaching itself.

k.f: If there’s no self, nobody is enlightened, because there’s nobody to be. The Buddha achieved something for no one.
k.m: Right. Enlightenment is the end of the idea that somebody needed to achieve something. You’ve stated the doctrine as an objection.

k.f: No self, but somebody keeps getting reborn.
k.m: A wave keeps arriving too. No particular water travels.

k.f: A lot of suffering, like pain, loss and injustice, doesn’t come from craving, and a life without attachments also lacks much of what makes lives good.
k.m: The first arrow is pain and the second is what the mind adds: resistance, grasping, the story about it. The teaching is aimed at the second arrow.

k.f: Wanting to end desire is a desire. So the path is powered by the thing it’s getting rid of, like a car that runs on having no car.
k.m: A raft is for crossing the river. You leave it on the far bank. The desire for the path gets dropped last, and the texts say so.

k.f: The cure for wanting things is wanting nirvana.
k.m: And when you get there you put that one down too. It’s a ladder.

k.f: Historical Buddhism has rebirth, heavens and hells, merit, relics, prayer and monasteries. The “philosophy” reading is a modern Western edit.
k.m: Fair, historically. The arguments about self, causation and suffering stand without the cosmology, and the tradition has always graded its own teachings by level.

k.f: It has monks, temples, hells, saints, and a founder born out of his mother’s side. That’s the full set.
k.m: Monks, temples and saints is also a description of a university.

k.f: Buddhism is a religion in Asia and a personality in California.
k.m: And Christianity is a religion in Rome and a personality in Texas.

k.f: What trained meditators find is shaped by the doctrine the training teaches. Agreement among them may show shared instruction.
k.m: Then compare across traditions with different doctrines. They report the same instabilities of attention and the same passing of sensations, described in rival vocabularies.

k.f: Staring at the inside of your eyelids reveals the inside of your eyelids.
k.m: You’ve looked at them for ten seconds. Try ten days and report back.

k.f: Mindfulness went from ending rebirth to getting through a quarterly review.
k.m: The Buddha taught kings, merchants and soldiers who went back to work. It was always for people with jobs.

k.f: If everything is empty, so is the doctrine. Its defenders accept that, and critics have long replied that a thesis which denies its own standing can’t refute anything.
k.m: He says he holds no thesis, and that emptiness is empty too. It works like medicine that leaves the body along with the illness it cleared.

k.f: If nothing has intrinsic existence, emptiness doesn’t either, so things are full again. It cancels.
k.m: Empty means dependent on other things. Emptiness depends on there being things. So it’s empty, and nothing fills back up.

k.f: Schopenhauer read two translations, and Western Buddhism has been him ever since.
k.m: He read two translations and still got the first noble truth right.

t.t: “The Dao that can be told isn’t the eternal Dao”

k.f: A teaching that disowns statement can’t be assessed or told apart from having no content. The text goes on to make many definite claims anyway.
k.m: It says the told Dao isn’t the constant one. It doesn’t say telling is useless. The words are a finger pointing, and the chapters keep saying so.

k.f: Then the first line is wrong, because it just told it. The book refutes itself in line one and keeps going.
k.m: The first line is a warning label. You read the label and then complained there’s a product.

k.f: The Dao can’t be put into words, and there are 81 chapters of words about it.
k.m: Five thousand characters. It’s the shortest scripture there is. He was trying.

k.f: As advice it can’t fail. Success shows the flow, failure shows forcing, and nothing tells trained spontaneity from doing nothing.
k.m: It’s a claim about skill: the cook’s knife that never dulls because it goes through the gaps. The difference between forcing and fitting is visible in any craft.

k.f: Nothing was ever built by not forcing. The Great Wall was a lot of forcing.
k.m: The Great Wall didn’t keep anyone out. Water got around it. That’s the example.

k.f: Wu wei is procrastination with a lineage.
k.m: Procrastination is forcing yourself not to. Different thing entirely.

k.f: That the ideas come in pairs doesn’t show the things are balanced or that preferring one is a mistake. Health doesn’t need disease.
k.m: The point isn’t that all preferences are mistakes. It’s that pushing one side to its limit produces the other, as with strength that becomes brittleness.

k.f: By that logic the cure for being poor is that rich people exist. It’s been tried.
k.m: High needs low the way a door needs the empty part. The emptiness is the bit you use.

k.f: Yin and yang is “it is what it is” with a logo.
k.m: It is what it is. You say that like you’ve found a flaw.

k.f: The parable is a survival plan for one person under bad rulers. Made general, it rides free on everyone who does carry a load.
k.m: Zhuangzi’s target is usefulness on other people’s terms. The tree gives shade and shelter. It just can’t be made into someone’s coffin.

k.f: The useless tree lives longest because nobody wants it. That isn’t wisdom, that’s being picked last.
k.m: Picked last and still standing. The ones picked first are furniture.

k.f: Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly, and people have been pretending it’s a hard question since.
k.m: It is a hard question. You’ve had 2,300 years.

k.f: The ideal village keeps people ignorant and at home. As politics it has no account of defense or disputes beyond hoping they won’t come up.
k.m: The ideal is a ruler whose people say “we did it ourselves.” As a limit on meddling it’s the oldest statement of an idea that later got very popular.

k.f: “The best ruler does nothing.” Every country has tried a ruler who did nothing. They have a different word for it.
k.m: A ruler who does nothing and has things run well is called a good ruler. The ones you’re thinking of did plenty, all of it for themselves.

k.f: Daoism is anarchism for people who nap.
k.m: Naps are good. That was in the argument.

k.f: Ritual trains conformity just as easily. The Mohists objected early that elaborate rites waste resources and serve whoever is at the top.
k.m: He says ritual without feeling is empty, repeatedly. The claim is that shared forms are how feeling gets trained and shown. Even the Mohists kept funerals.

k.f: If ritual made people good, the most ceremonial institutions would be the most honest. Think about weddings, and then the DMV.
k.m: The DMV has procedure, which is ritual with the meaning taken out. That’s what he warned about.

k.f: Confucius is “sit up straight” as a civilization.
k.m: Sit up straight, look at people when they talk, show up for the dead. It’s held up.

t.t: “Filial piety is the root of virtue”

k.f: Putting family loyalty first collides with impartial justice. The Analects praises a son who covers for his father’s theft.
k.m: The same text has him tell sons to remonstrate with a father who does wrong. The sheep passage is about whether a child should be the state’s informant.

k.f: Parents are assigned by lottery. A morality rooted in whoever you happened to get is astrology with chores.
k.m: Everyone gets a family before they get a theory. Morality has to start where people start. Yours begins with strangers and never arrives home.

k.f: Confucius said a good son covers for his dad stealing a sheep. It’s in the book.
k.m: He said the son doesn’t testify against his father. Most legal systems now agree. It’s called privilege.

k.f: Counting on a ruler’s virtue offers no remedy when he lacks it. The Legalists’ complaint was that institutions have to work with ordinary people.
k.m: He wanted both. Laws alone make people evasive, and laws plus rulers worth copying give them a sense of shame. The Legalist state lasted fifteen years.

k.f: He tried it. He went from state to state for fourteen years offering to be the moral example, and nobody hired him.
k.m: Nobody hired him, and then his students ran the civil service for two thousand years. Slow start.

k.f: Confucius spent fourteen years looking for a government job and didn’t get one. Then he taught.
k.m: And then he taught. That’s where the two thousand years came from.

t.t: “Harmony comes from everyone filling their role”

k.f: An ethics of roles has trouble criticizing the roles. Ruler over subject and husband over wife are built in.
k.m: Roles bind upward too: a ruler who fails his role stops being a ruler. Mencius drew the conclusion that such a man may be removed.

k.f: Every role-based harmony has one man at the top explaining that harmony means staying where you are.
k.m: He told the men at the top that the name “ruler” has to be earned. That’s why none of them hired him.

k.f: “Know your place” doesn’t get deeper by being 2,500 years old.
k.m: Your place includes telling the ruler he’s wrong. It’s in the job description.

t.t: “The Analects is a guide to living well”

k.f: It’s a collection of sayings put together over generations, tied to lost contexts and often opaque. Most of the guidance comes from later commentary.
k.m: A book of remembered conversations is the form the teaching took, because it was about situations. The opacity is what any context-bound advice looks like out of context.

k.f: It’s a list of things a teacher said, written down by students who liked him. Every teacher has one. Most are on Rate My Professors.
k.m: The ones on Rate My Professors didn’t get an examination system built on them.

k.f: Half the things Confucius said, he didn’t. The other half are “respect your elders.”
k.m: And you can quote two of them, which is two more than most philosophers get.

t.t: “Only Brahman is real; the world is appearance”

k.f: If the world is illusion, so are the scriptures, the teacher and the argument. The system has to climb a ladder it says isn’t there.
k.m: The tradition has two levels of truth. Teacher and scripture are real at the everyday level and are used to reach the higher one, like a thorn to remove a thorn.

k.f: If the world is illusion, so is the book that says so. It’s an illusion telling an illusion about illusion.
k.m: A dream tiger can wake you up. The book is one of those.

k.f: The world is unreal, said the teacher, and then looked both ways.
k.m: At the everyday level traffic is real. He never said to ignore it.

t.t: “The self is identical with the absolute”

k.f: If individual selves are really one, it’s unexplained who is ignorant and who gets liberated. Ignorance can’t belong to Brahman or to nobody.
k.m: Ignorance has no beginning and no owner you can find. Asking whose it is, is like asking where the darkness went when the lamp was lit.

k.f: If I’m already the absolute, there’s nothing to do, and the course is twelve years long.
k.m: Nothing to do, and twelve years to notice it. Seeing what’s already the case can take that long.

k.f: You are God, and so is the guy who cut you off in traffic. Enlightenment is being fine with that.
k.m: Being fine with that is the hard part. That’s why it’s called a path.

t.t: “Ignorance is what makes us see many where there is one”

k.f: Ignorance needs someone to have it. Locating it in Brahman makes the absolute deluded, and locating it in the individual assumes the many it was to explain.
k.m: It’s called indescribable for that reason: it can’t be put in either place. The school names the difficulty and builds it into the teaching.

k.f: Whose ignorance? If there’s only one thing, it’s the one that’s confused. The absolute has a problem.
k.m: From the absolute’s side there never was any. The problem appears only from where you’re asking.

k.f: Maya is the answer to every objection. That’s an objection.
k.m: It’s an objection the tradition wrote down first, a thousand years ago, and answered at length.

t.t: “Liberation is realizing what you always were”

k.f: A change that changes nothing is hard to tell from no change. If knowledge alone frees, it’s unclear why the knowledge is so rarely enough.
k.m: The change is the falling away of a mistake. A man who thought a rope was a snake changes a great deal when he sees it, and the rope doesn’t.

k.f: If I always was it, nothing happened. He’s charging for a receipt.
k.m: A receipt for something you had and were terrified you’d lost. People pay a lot for that.

k.f: Advaita is the oldest way of saying “it was inside you all along.”
k.m: It’s the oldest way of saying it because it keeps being what people find.

k.f: The tradition that says so has one of the largest literatures in Buddhism, with lineages, commentaries and canonical records of what masters said.
k.m: The texts are records of people being pointed past texts. A library of fingers pointing at the moon isn’t a claim that the moon is made of fingers.

k.f: A tradition outside words with ten thousand koans, written down, with official answers.
k.m: Ten thousand ways of saying “not this.” It takes that many.

k.f: Zen says truth can’t be written, across about four hundred years of writing.
k.m: Four hundred years of writing down what can’t be written. Persistence counts.

t.t: “Koans break the grip of conceptual thinking”

k.f: Koan practice is highly conventional. Standard responses are taught and checked, which is a curriculum, not an escape from concepts.
k.m: The standard responses are the floor. A teacher can tell a memorized answer from one that’s been seen through, and that’s what the interview is for.

k.f: There are answer books. Monks pass them around. It’s conceptual thinking with a cheat sheet.
k.m: Monks who use the cheat sheet get sent back. The teacher has read it too.

k.f: What is the sound of one hand clapping? There’s a traditional answer. It’s on the exam.
k.m: And reciting it fails the exam.

k.f: If sitting is already enlightenment, nothing distinguishes the master from the novice, and the long training and certification have no point.
k.m: Practice and realization are one, on that view. The training exists because sitting with nothing extra, no aim and no escape, is the hardest thing a person does.

k.f: If sitting is enlightenment, everyone at the DMV has attained it.
k.m: Everyone at the DMV is trying to be somewhere else. That’s the difference.

k.f: Zen is doing nothing in an extremely specific way for thirty years.
k.m: Thirty years to do one thing without adding anything. You try it for ten minutes.

t.t: “Zen is pure experience, free of dogma”

k.f: Historical Zen is a monastic institution with rituals, hierarchy and doctrine. The dogma-free version was assembled for export in the twentieth century.
k.m: True of the institution. The teaching inside it keeps undercutting its own forms, which is why the tradition tells stories about burning the statues.

k.f: It has robes, ranks, a founder, chanting and a guy who hits people with a stick. That’s a full religion.
k.m: A full religion that tells you to kill the Buddha if you meet him.

k.f: Zen arrived in America as “no rules,” which was news to the monasteries.
k.m: The monasteries have rules so that nothing else has to be decided.

k.f: As a law of nature it has no mechanism and no evidence. As a moral claim it implies that those who suffer earned it, which few can accept looking at a sick child.
k.m: Read psychologically it needs no cosmic machinery: acts form habits, habits form character, and character meets its own results. That’s the oldest layer of the teaching.

k.f: Bad things happen to good people on the news every night. The law has a lot of exceptions for a law.
k.m: The law doesn’t say when. A seed doesn’t come up the day it’s planted.

k.f: Karma is “what goes around comes around,” with a schedule nobody can check.
k.m: The schedule is the length of a habit.

t.t: “We are reborn according to our deeds”

k.f: Without memory or continuity of character, it’s unclear in what sense the one reborn is the one who acted, or why the consequences are just.
k.m: The same puzzle holds within one life. The child who earned the scar isn’t the adult who carries it, and we don’t call that unjust.

k.f: If I can’t remember it, somebody else did it. I’m doing his time.
k.m: You don’t remember being three, and you still have that kid’s teeth and his fear of dogs.

k.f: Everyone who remembers a past life was royalty. Nobody was the guy who carried the royalty’s water.
k.m: In the texts most past lives are as animals and servants. Royalty is the Western edition.

k.f: Any outcome can be explained by an unobservable past life, so the explanation risks nothing. It has also served to justify leaving hierarchies alone.
k.m: The teaching says the reverse about helping: another’s suffering is your chance to act well, and what you do about it is your own karma.

k.f: It explains everything, in the sense that nothing could show it wrong. So does “a wizard did it.”
k.m: It explains the past and leaves the next act entirely to you. A wizard doesn’t do that.

k.f: “They must have done something in a past life” is the oldest way of not helping.
k.m: That reading is condemned in the texts. Not helping is an act with results.

t.t: “There are cases of children recalling past lives”

k.f: The case collections rely on testimony gathered after families had talked, in cultures that expect such memories. Controlled verification is absent.
k.m: The strongest files have statements written down before the families met, and details later verified. Few, and they exist.

k.f: The memories show up in countries that believe in rebirth and nowhere else. Souls apparently respect borders.
k.m: They get reported where reporting them doesn’t cost you your reputation.

k.f: The evidence for reincarnation is anecdotes, and the anecdotes have reincarnated many times.
k.m: Each anecdote has a name, an address and a file. That’s called a case series.

k.f: Deception matters, but logistics, numbers and industry decide most wars. A theory centered on cleverness flatters the reader.
k.m: Logistics gets two of the thirteen chapters. Deception is how the smaller force makes numbers matter less, which is who the book was for.

k.f: Wars are won by the side with more trucks. There’s no chapter on trucks.
k.m: There’s a chapter on supply. He says an army without its baggage train is lost.

k.f: The Art of War is thirteen chapters of “be smarter than the other guy.”
k.m: Every plan that works is that. The book says how to check whether you are.

t.t: “The supreme art is to win without fighting”

k.f: It’s an attractive ideal with few instructions attached. Opponents who could be beaten without fighting weren’t much of a problem to begin with.
k.m: The instructions are there: attack the enemy’s plans first, then his alliances, then his army, and cities last. It’s an order of priorities.

k.f: If you can win without fighting, the other side was losing anyway. He’s taking credit for the weather.
k.m: Arranging things so the other side is losing before the fight is the skill. That’s the weather he’s taking credit for.

k.f: “Win without fighting” is great advice, right up there with “buy low, sell high.”
k.m: “Buy low” is also correct. Almost nobody does it.

k.f: True and nearly empty. It tells a commander to have good information without saying how, which is the entire difficulty.
k.m: The book says how: use spies, measure terrain, count provisions, watch the dust. The maxim is the heading and the chapters are the content.

k.f: “Have all the information” is not strategy. It’s what strategy is for when that didn’t happen.
k.m: It’s what strategy is, and there’s a chapter on getting it, with five kinds of spy.

k.f: Know yourself, know your enemy, and you’ll never lose. Unfalsifiable: if you lost, you didn’t know.
k.m: It says you’ll never be in peril. Losing a battle and being ruined are different, and he’s careful about it.

t.t: “Its lessons apply to business and life”

k.f: The maxims are general enough to fit anything, which is why they fit quarterly sales as easily as siege warfare.
k.m: It applies wherever there’s an opponent, limited resources and uncertainty. The business readers go wrong by skipping the half about restraint.

k.f: A book that applies to war, marketing, dating and golf is a horoscope.
k.m: A horoscope doesn’t tell you to count your supplies before you start.

k.f: Sun Tzu may not have existed, which is the one piece of deception that definitely worked.
k.m: Thirteen chapters appearing from nowhere and fooling everyone for 2,500 years would be the best campaign in the book.

t.t: “Act without attachment to the fruits of action”

k.f: Complete indifference to results would make it impossible to choose between actions, since their results are how they differ.
k.m: It says to give up the claim on results. You still aim the arrow as well as you can, and you don’t make your peace depend on where it lands.

k.f: If the results don’t matter, there’s no reason to do one thing over another. He’s detached all the way to the couch.
k.m: You do it because it’s yours to do. That’s a reason, and it gets people off couches.

k.f: Do your job and don’t think about the outcome. Management loves this book.
k.m: Management quotes one verse. The book has seven hundred.

k.f: The duty in question comes from birth into a class. The ethic tells each person to stay in their assigned role, which is what its critics have always pointed out.
k.m: The same text says the divisions follow qualities and conduct, and reformers from inside the tradition have read it against birth for centuries.

k.f: “Better your own duty done badly than another’s done well.” Convenient for whoever handed out the duties.
k.m: It was said to a prince who wanted to resign and become a monk. Convenient for nobody in the scene.

k.f: The Gita’s answer to “should I do this?” is “what were you born as?”
k.m: It answers “what are you fitted for and what’s in front of you?” Read on a chapter.

t.t: “Arjuna must fight, though it means killing his kin”

k.f: The argument that the soul can’t be killed, so killing isn’t really killing, would excuse any killing whatever.
k.m: That verse is one argument of many. The main one is that he’s a soldier in a war he didn’t seek, all negotiation has failed, and walking away abandons the people depending on him.

k.f: “Nobody really dies, so go ahead” is an argument that works for every war and every murder. It proves too much by a lot.
k.m: Krishna tried to prevent the war first and failed. It’s the argument for after diplomacy.

k.f: A man doesn’t want to kill his family, and God talks him into it. That’s the plot.
k.m: A man is frozen on the worst day of his life and someone tells him how to act without hatred. That’s the plot.

t.t: “There are many paths to the same goal”

k.f: Paths of knowledge, devotion and action rest on different pictures of what’s ultimately real. Calling them one goal papers over the difference.
k.m: The paths suit temperaments: the thinker, the lover, the worker. One mountain and several trails is the plain reading.

k.f: If every path gets there, there’s no reason to take the hard one, and the book is eighteen chapters of the hard ones.
k.m: The path that’s easy for you is hard for someone else. That’s why there are three.

k.f: Oppenheimer quoted it at the bomb test. That’s the most famous application.
k.m: He quoted the verse about time. He read it in Sanskrit, and reported that it helped.

t.t: “Paying attention to the present moment reduces suffering”

k.f: The measured benefits are modest, about what other active treatments give, and the early studies were small and poorly controlled.
k.m: “About as well as other treatments” for depression relapse, with no drug and no side effects, is a good result. The early hype was the problem.

k.f: The studies say it works about as well as going for a walk. The walk is free and gets somewhere.
k.m: A walk where you notice the walk is the practice. You’ve described it.

k.f: Mindfulness is noticing that you’re stressed, for ten minutes, on an app with a subscription.
k.m: Ten minutes of noticing is ten more than most people manage.

k.f: What was removed is the ethics and the goal. A technique meant to end attachment was repurposed to make people better at their attachments.
k.m: The clinical programs were designed to carry the ethics implicitly and reach people who’d never enter a temple. Whether that worked is fair to debate.

k.f: They kept the breathing and dropped the part about giving everything up. That’s keeping the wrapper.
k.m: People who start with the breathing often go looking for the rest. It’s a door.

k.f: Mindfulness was designed to end the self, and got sold as self-care.
k.m: Seeing what the self is up to turned out to be good for it.

k.f: Sometimes thoughts deserve judgment, and distress is a signal about one’s situation. Non-judgment can turn a real problem into a private attitude adjustment.
k.m: Not judging is a method for the cushion. You see the thought clearly first, and what to do about it is decided afterwards, better informed.

k.f: “Don’t judge your thoughts” is a judgment about thoughts. He failed in the instructions.
k.m: It’s an instruction for twenty minutes. You get your opinions back afterwards.

k.f: If your job is making you miserable, mindfulness will help you notice that calmly and stay.
k.m: People who see clearly that the job is making them miserable tend to leave.

k.f: Offered by employers, it puts the burden of coping on the individual and leaves the conditions causing the stress as they were.
k.m: Both can be true: fix the conditions and teach the skill. People under stress that won’t be fixed this year still have to get through this year.

k.f: The company that causes the stress pays for the class about the stress. It’s cheaper than fixing anything.
k.m: Teach it and fix things. The class wasn’t the reason nothing got fixed.

k.f: Corporate mindfulness: breathe through the layoffs.
k.m: Breathing through a layoff beats not breathing through it.

t.t: “God is dead and we must create our own values”

k.f: If values are made by will, nothing ranks the creator’s above the herd’s except the creator saying so. Revaluing values presupposes a standard.
k.m: He ranks them by a standard he does state: whether a way of valuing strengthens life or sickens it. You can dispute it, and it isn’t “because I said so.”

k.f: Created values are called preferences. He announced the death of God and replaced it with a mood board.
k.m: A preference is what you have about soup. A value is what you’d reorganize a life around. He knew the difference, and that was the whole worry.

k.f: “God is dead.” Nietzsche’s dead too, and God has more followers.
k.m: He predicted the followers. He said the shadow would be shown in caves for centuries.

t.t: “Master morality is healthier than slave morality”

k.f: The Genealogy is speculative psychology and word history presented as history, and that a morality grew from resentment says nothing about whether it’s right.
k.m: He agrees origins don’t settle validity and says so. The history is there to break the assumption that these values have always been obvious.

k.f: The slaves won. By his own standard, winning is what the strong do. So slave morality is master morality and the book is over.
k.m: Winning by making strength ashamed of itself is the thing he was describing. You’ve summarized the book and called it a refutation.

k.f: Nietzsche fans have never once pictured themselves as the herd.
k.m: He says the reader is the herd. In the preface. You were warned.

t.t: “He was no proto-Nazi; his sister distorted him”

k.f: The editing was real and he despised nationalism. Still, the praise of rank and breeding and the contempt for equality are his own, and they made the theft easy.
k.m: His aristocratism is of spirit and is aimed at Germans above all. He broke with Wagner over antisemitism and called nationalism a sickness. The theft needed forgery.

k.f: When that many people misread a writer the same way, that’s the reading.
k.m: They had to delete and rearrange him to get that reading. A reading that needs scissors is not the reading.

k.f: Misunderstood by everyone except whoever’s explaining him.
k.m: And the people who “understood” him had to edit the books first.

k.f: As psychology it can’t be tested, since any motive can be redescribed as power. As metaphysics it rests mostly on notebooks he didn’t publish.
k.m: In the published books it’s mostly a psychological hypothesis, offered against the idea that people chiefly seek pleasure or survival. He put it forward as an experiment.

k.f: Sloths. A whole animal that refutes it.
k.m: A sloth owns its niche so completely that nothing bothers to compete. That’s power with no wasted motion.

k.f: The will to power is a self-help book the author decided not to publish.
k.m: The book of that name was assembled by his sister. He’d abandoned the project.

t.t: “Live so you’d will it all again”

k.f: As cosmology it fails, and as a test it’s empty. A contented tyrant passes, and it can’t tell better lives from more self-satisfied ones.
k.m: It isn’t a test of whether a life is good. It’s a test of whether you affirm yours, and a tyrant who passes has shown something about himself.

k.f: If everything recurs exactly, nobody remembers, so nothing changes, so it’s the same as not recurring. He invented a thought experiment with no difference in it.
k.m: If nobody could tell, the only question left is whether you’d say yes. That’s the difference. It’s in you.

k.f: He printed forty copies of the last part of Zarathustra and found seven people to send it to.
k.m: Seven readers. Now there’s a shelf of him in every bookstore, and you’re the one counting.

k.f: Passionate inwardness doesn’t discriminate between its objects. The fanatic has the “how” as fully as the knight of faith.
k.m: He doesn’t say sincerity makes a belief correct. He says that for the questions of how to live, the relation you take is part of what’s being asked.

k.f: If truth were subjectivity, being really into something would make it true. Sports fans would win every game.
k.m: Fans don’t stake their lives on it. Passion in his sense is what’s left when being wrong would cost you everything.

k.f: “Truth is subjectivity” is “that’s my truth” in Danish.
k.m: “My truth” asks nothing of you. His asks for all of it.

t.t: “The leap of faith is beyond reason, not against it”

k.f: If nothing rational constrains the leap, there’s no reason to leap toward Christianity over anything else. The choice is arbitrary by design.
k.m: The leap isn’t picking a creed off a shelf. It’s what’s left when the evidence runs out and living still requires a decision, which is everyone’s position.

k.f: A leap with no reasons is called falling.
k.m: Falling is what happens when you didn’t choose. He’s describing the half-second before, when you could still step back.

k.f: The leap of faith is jumping to the conclusion and calling the jump the point.
k.m: You jumped to that one.

t.t: “Abraham shows the ethical can be suspended”

k.f: If a private command from God can suspend ethics, nothing tells the knight of faith from a murderer. Kierkegaard states that problem and doesn’t solve it.
k.m: Right, and that’s the book. It was written to make faith terrifying again for readers who thought they had it for the price of a pew.

k.f: A man who hears a voice telling him to kill his son and saddles the donkey isn’t suspending the ethical. He’s a case file.
k.m: That’s what his own pseudonym says: either he’s a murderer or the ethical isn’t the highest. He doesn’t let you off with the first.

k.f: Fear and Trembling is 150 pages defending a man the police would like a word with.
k.m: The author can’t sleep over it either. That’s the title.

k.f: Lonely conviction has no better record than shared judgment. Science and law use public checking because individuals fool themselves.
k.m: The claim is narrower: a crowd can’t repent, love or die for you. Where the task is becoming a self, numbers have no vote.

k.f: The crowd is who decided Kierkegaard was important. He’d have to throw that out.
k.m: The crowd also laughed him out of Copenhagen in the papers for a year. He’d tell you which verdict he trusts.

k.f: He published under a dozen fake names so he could disagree with himself and still win.
k.m: None of the names agree with each other. That was the method.

t.t: “Aesthetic, ethical, religious: the stages of life”

k.f: The ranking is asserted from inside the religious stage. From the other two, the “higher” one looks like a different choice, not a higher one.
k.m: He doesn’t argue you up the ladder. Each stage breaks down by its own standards, in boredom or in guilt, and the next is a choice.

k.f: Three stages, and the last one is the author’s. Every stage theory ends where the man writing it lives.
k.m: He wrote the first stage so well that people still stop there. Hardly a man rigging it for his own side.

k.f: Kierkegaard is for people who want to be religious without going to church or agreeing with anyone there.
k.m: He spent his last year attacking the church by name. He had the agreeing-with-no-one part covered.

k.f: People arrive with a biology, a temperament and a situation they didn’t choose. Sartre’s later work conceded how much of that he’d underplayed.
k.m: Biology gives a situation. It doesn’t give its meaning: whether a limp is a tragedy, a fact or a dare is not in the leg.

k.f: Babies exist and don’t choose anything for years. So for the first while, essence is winning.
k.m: For the first years somebody else is choosing for them. Somebody always is. That’s the point.

k.f: Existence precedes essence. Genetics would like a word.
k.m: Genes gave you a temper. What you do when you’re angry is still yours.

k.f: Freedom to interpret a situation isn’t freedom to change it. Calling a prisoner free in Sartre’s sense drains the word of what people care about.
k.m: He means there’s no fact about you that makes the choice for you. The prisoner decides what the walls are to him, and that’s the freedom nobody can take or give.

k.f: If people were radically free, nobody would be at work on a Monday.
k.m: They chose the paycheck over the alternative. That’s a choice with a commute.

k.f: He said a man is always free, and he said it from a café.
k.m: He wrote in the café because the apartment had no heat. During the occupation.

t.t: “Bad faith is lying to yourself about your freedom”

k.f: The account needs a person to know the truth in order to hide it from themselves, the paradox Sartre raises against Freud and doesn’t clearly escape.
k.m: It works because we are both a set of facts and more than them. One half can be played off against the other, and no second inner person has to be fooled.

k.f: The waiter is acting like a waiter because it’s his job. Sartre watched a man work and diagnosed him.
k.m: He isn’t faulted for working. He’s faulted for a little too much flourish, as though being a waiter were all he could ever be.

k.f: Bad faith is whatever the other person is doing.
k.m: Yes. And you can only see it in them because you know the move.

k.f: The line dramatizes his view that relations are a contest of stares, which leaves love and solidarity unexplained. He later reached for Marxism to fill the gap.
k.m: He said later that it means our relations are hell when they’re poisoned, since we know ourselves through others’ eyes. It was never a recommendation of solitude.

k.f: Solitary confinement is the punishment prisons use on people who are already in prison. Hell is the opposite of other people.
k.m: Solitary is a punishment because the others are still there, deciding it. You’ve found the play’s plot.

k.f: Hell is other people, said the man who was never once alone at a table.
k.m: All three people in the play want to leave the room and none of them does. He understood tables.

t.t: “We choose our values with no outside standard”

k.f: In his own lecture he says that in choosing I choose for all mankind, which imports a Kantian universality his premises don’t support.
k.m: The universality isn’t a law from above. It’s that choosing shows what you take a human being to be, like it or not.

k.f: With no standard, choosing is the same as flipping a coin. He made a philosophy out of heads.
k.m: A coin doesn’t answer for the result. You do. That’s the whole difference and it’s the theory.

k.f: Total freedom, total responsibility, and then he spent the fifties making excuses for the Soviet Union.
k.m: He got that wrong, and by his own philosophy it’s his to answer for. That’s the philosophy working.

t.t: “Life is absurd: we want meaning from a silent universe”

k.f: Nagel: the absurd comes from our ability to step back from our lives, and calls for irony more than revolt. The silence only disappoints a demand nobody has to make.
k.m: Irony is one response. He’s asking whether a person can live with the question open, without pretending it’s closed, and irony may be one way of doing that.

k.f: The universe isn’t silent. It has thunder, birds, traffic. He meant it doesn’t talk to him specifically.
k.m: It doesn’t answer the question you asked it. That’s what silent means.

k.f: Camus noticed nothing matters and wrote five books about it mattering.
k.m: Nothing mattering in the end and things mattering now aren’t the same claim. The five books are about the second.

k.f: Nothing in the argument shows that scorn is the fitting response and not despair or resignation. “Must” is rhetoric.
k.m: “Must” means it’s the only picture that leaves him anything. Despair hands the rock the win.

k.f: Sisyphus has job security, clear goals and exercise. He’s doing better than most readers. That’s a comparison, not a philosophy.
k.m: He owns the walk back down. That’s the hour Camus cares about, and it’s better than most readers get.

k.f: One must imagine Sisyphus happy. One doesn’t have to. He’s pushing a rock.
k.m: Then he’s unhappy and still pushing a rock. You’ve made it worse and changed nothing.

t.t: “The answer to the absurd is revolt”

k.f: Revolt against a condition that can’t change is hard to tell from the change of attitude he rejects in religion. He calls one a leap and the other lucidity.
k.m: The difference is what you claim. Religion says the condition is other than it looks. Revolt says it’s exactly as it looks and declines to approve.

k.f: Revolting against the universe is yelling at weather.
k.m: You carry an umbrella and you don’t say thank you to the rain.

k.f: Camus’s answer to the absurd is to keep going, which is what everyone was doing.
k.m: Doing it knowing is the difference. It’s a small one. It’s the only one on offer.

k.f: He refused the label, but the themes, the period and the circle are theirs. The difference rests mostly on his declining Sartre’s politics.
k.m: It’s more than a label. They hold that we make our essence and he holds there’s a human nature worth defending, which is why he wouldn’t excuse the camps.

k.f: He sat with the existentialists, wrote about the same thing at the same tables, and fought with them like family. That’s membership.
k.m: Sitting at the table isn’t signing the manifesto. He’s the one who got up.

k.f: Camus spent years explaining he wasn’t an existentialist to people who didn’t care which kind of sad Frenchman he was.
k.m: He cared. It cost him every friend he had in Paris.

k.f: Meursault kills an Arab the novel never names and barely registers. Later readers took that silence as the book’s own blind spot.
k.m: The silence is the narrator’s, and the book is a portrait of that blankness. An author who grew up poor in Algiers knew what he was showing.

k.f: A man shoots someone, and the lesson is that the court was rude about his mother’s funeral.
k.m: The court convicts him for not crying at the funeral. That’s in the transcript, and that’s the point.

k.f: The Stranger is about a guy who shot a man because it was sunny, and people put it on their dating profiles.
k.m: It’s a hundred pages. They could finish it before the second date.

t.t: “Camus was right and Sartre was wrong”

k.f: The Rebel’s history of ideas is sweeping and thin, which was the original criticism, and his own stance on Algeria struck many as evasion.
k.m: The history is thin and the judgment was right: no future paradise justifies present murder. On Algeria he refused both sides’ terror, and that’s a position.

k.f: Sartre got the students, the funeral and the school of thought. Being right is supposed to come with something.
k.m: Sartre got the students. Camus got the verdict of everyone who later counted the dead.

k.f: Camus was a goalkeeper. It’s the one position where the job is to stand there while things happen.
k.m: A goalkeeper is the one who can’t blame anyone else.

t.t: “The question of Being has been forgotten”

k.f: “Being” may not name anything to ask about. On the classic objection, the question comes from treating “is” as a noun.
k.m: He begins with that objection. The claim is that we already understand “is” well enough to use it everywhere and can’t say what we understand.

k.f: Nobody forgot it. Nobody asked, because “what is is” isn’t a question, it’s a stutter.
k.m: You used it twice in that sentence without trouble and can’t define it. That’s the question.

k.f: Heidegger asked what “is” is for 400 pages and didn’t finish the book.
k.m: The unfinished half is why it’s still being read.

k.f: That ordinary language can’t carry the thought is a claim that certifies itself. Good expositors restate much of it plainly, which suggests the difficulty wasn’t required.
k.m: The paraphrases use the tradition’s vocabulary, which carries the assumptions he’s digging out. Something is lost each time, even where it helps.

k.f: If it could only be said that way it couldn’t be translated, and most of his fans read him in English.
k.m: It’s been translated twice into English and the translators fought over every term for decades. That’s what “can’t be said otherwise” looks like.

k.f: Heidegger is hard to read because he’s hiding.
k.m: He invents a word and defines it on the same page. Hiding is the reverse of that.

t.t: “His politics are separate from his philosophy”

k.f: His own notebooks tie the antisemitism to his history of Being, and he never took it back. Separation has to be argued passage by passage, not assumed.
k.m: Agreed that it must be argued passage by passage. Done that way, the analysis of everyday existence in the 1927 book stands without the politics, and Levinas and Arendt built on it.

k.f: A philosophy of resolve and destiny, by a man who used it once and picked that. The field test is the result.
k.m: Then judge Frege by his diaries and Aristotle by his slaves. The rule can be applied. Just apply it to everyone.

k.f: Being and Time is about authenticity, by a man who joined the party in 1933 and paid dues until 1945.
k.m: It’s a 1927 book. His students who had to flee kept teaching it.

t.t: “We are being-in-the-world, not subjects facing objects”

k.f: The account of skilled, unreflective coping is valuable, but it’s description. It doesn’t show the subject and object picture is wrong for science or reflection.
k.m: It doesn’t say the detached view is false. It says that view is derived, a special way of standing back from a world we were already at work in.

k.f: Hammers. His main example of how humans exist is a hammer, and he never built anything.
k.m: The hammer you don’t notice until it breaks. That’s the example, and you’ve never thought about your keyboard either until today.

k.f: Dasein is “person” with a toll booth.
k.m: “Person” already sneaks in a mind inside a body. The toll is for not doing that.

t.t: “Technology turns the world into a stockpile”

k.f: The critique is too sweeping to guide anything. He infamously said mechanized farming and far worse were the same in essence.
k.m: The remark was grotesque. The analysis is narrower than “technology bad”: it’s about a way of revealing in which everything shows up as stock to be optimized.

k.f: He wrote that in a hut with a stove, a road and a publisher.
k.m: The stove was for heat. He didn’t think of the forest as a wood supply measured in units. That’s the distinction.

k.f: The technology essay is “phones bad” for people with a reading group.
k.m: “Phones bad” is about the phone. His is about why you check it as if you were inventory.

k.f: Read one way it blesses whatever exists, and read the other way it’s nearly empty. Hegel’s own gloss doesn’t settle which.
k.m: “Real” translates his word for what has worked itself out fully, and he separates it from whatever merely exists. A bad state exists and falls short of that.

k.f: Traffic is real.
k.m: Traffic exists. He said so himself, and it’s the distinction: what merely exists against what’s actual.

k.f: Hegel proved the Prussian state was the goal of history while being paid by the Prussian state.
k.m: He’d lost a job under censorship already. The preface is aimed at the people who wanted the state stormed and the people who wanted it worshipped.

k.f: The story is selected to fit. Whole continents are set outside history, and every regression is renamed a moment.
k.m: The geography is indefensible. The thesis survives it: that slavery has gone from unquestioned to unthinkable is hard to describe in any other way.

k.f: History is one thing after another. He drew an arrow on it, and the arrow pointed at Berlin.
k.m: The arrow points at the principle that everyone is free. Berlin was only where he was standing.

k.f: History ended in 1806. Then again in 1989. It keeps ending near whoever’s writing.
k.m: He said the principle had been reached, not that events were over. The rest is other people.

k.f: Popper’s complaint: if contradictions are welcome, no criticism can bite. And the famous three-step formula isn’t even his, which shows how loosely the method is specified.
k.m: He doesn’t assert that P and not-P. A position pressed far enough undermines itself in a specific way, and the next one is what’s needed to fix that.

k.f: From a contradiction anything follows. So a method that runs on contradictions can prove anything, and did.
k.m: Explosion is a rule of formal logic. He’s describing what happens when a concept is applied, and that follows no such rule.

k.f: Thesis, antithesis, synthesis. He never said it, and it’s still the clearest thing with his name on it.
k.m: He never said it because it’s a cartoon of it. That it’s clearer tells you about cartoons.

k.f: Each step is supposed to be necessary, and commentators can’t agree on what the argument for most of them is.
k.m: Each shape of consciousness is tested by its own standard, and fails by it. The reader is supposed to check each step, which is why it can be disputed at all.

k.f: A path where every step is necessary doesn’t need 600 pages of the guide explaining why no other way was possible.
k.m: It’s 600 pages because he shows each wrong turn failing. A map with only the right road isn’t a proof.

k.f: Schopenhauer scheduled his lectures against Hegel’s to prove a point, and nobody came. He was still right about Hegel.
k.m: Schopenhauer was right about nobody coming.

k.f: A position that can only be criticized after accepting its whole framework is protected from criticism by design.
k.m: Every system asks to be read whole before it’s judged. The test is whether, once inside, it explains more than its rivals, and plenty of readers left unconvinced.

k.f: If nobody can be said to understand a writer after two hundred years, the simplest explanation involves the writer.
k.m: Marx understood him well enough to turn him over. Understanding isn’t the problem. Liking it is.

k.f: Hegel supposedly said only one man ever understood him, and even he didn’t.
k.m: It’s a joke told about every difficult writer. It was told about Kant first.

k.f: He says the thing in itself can’t be known through experience and then identifies it through inner experience, which is still experience in time.
k.m: He concedes it: inner experience still has the form of time, so the will is the thing in itself under its thinnest veil. He claims that much and no more.

k.f: The will is blind and has no goals, and somehow it built eyes.
k.m: Eyes are what blind striving looks like after a few hundred million years. He said that forty years before Darwin.

k.f: Schopenhauer looked inside himself, found wanting things, and decided that’s what the universe is made of.
k.m: He looked inside, found wanting, and then found it in the plant, the magnet and you. Check for yourself.

t.t: “Life is suffering; pleasure is only relief”

k.f: The claim that pleasure is merely the absence of pain is false to experience. Learning and music, his own example, aren’t relief from a prior lack.
k.m: Even granting some positive pleasures, the ledger is his real argument: wants are many and lasting, satisfactions brief, and boredom fills what’s left.

k.f: If pleasure were only no pain, a nap and a concert would be the same thing.
k.m: You nap because you were tired and go to the concert because you were bored. Two lacks, two reliefs.

k.f: The great pessimist ate well, played the flute every day and lived to 72.
k.m: A man who expected the worst and arranged a tolerable life anyway. That’s the philosophy applied.

k.f: Grounding compassion in everyone being one will makes concern for others a disguised concern for oneself.
k.m: Egoism needs a wall between me and you. If the wall is appearance, the self that egoism serves is what has gone, and the concern is left.

k.f: If everyone is the same will underneath, helping someone else is helping myself. So compassion is selfishness with extra steps, and he proved egoism.
k.m: Selfishness with the self removed is called kindness.

k.f: The philosopher of compassion loved his poodles and couldn’t stand people.
k.m: He left his estate to disabled soldiers and their families.

t.t: “Art, above all music, releases us from the will”

k.f: If we are will through and through, will-less contemplation is unexplained. The escape hatch contradicts the system.
k.m: He says it’s rare and brief, and takes an excess of intellect over what the will needs. An exception at the margin doesn’t contradict the rule.

k.f: People want to hear music. Wanting is will. So the release from the will is powered by the will, like a diet of cake.
k.m: You want it before it starts. During it, for a few minutes, you don’t want anything. That’s the release.

k.f: Schopenhauer’s solution to existence is a nice evening in.
k.m: A nice evening in is most of what anyone gets. He just said so.

t.t: “Denying the will is the way out”

k.f: The will denying itself is either one more act of will or impossible on his premises, and he made no attempt to live it.
k.m: He says he describes sainthood and doesn’t practice it, any more than a sculptor of beautiful figures must be beautiful. The possibility is what he argues for.

k.f: Wanting to stop wanting. Buddhism had this bug first, and at least they noticed.
k.m: It isn’t achieved by wanting. It comes from seeing through the thing, and the wanting quiets down. He’s explicit that it can’t be forced.

k.f: He recommended renouncing the world from a comfortable apartment, on an inheritance.
k.m: He said a philosopher doesn’t have to be a saint. He was right about himself as usual.

k.f: If meaning is whatever one chooses, no choice can be better than another, and the seriousness the movement demands has nothing to rest on.
k.m: The choice isn’t unconstrained. It’s made in a situation, in front of others, and you answer for it. What’s denied is a ready-made answer handed down.

k.f: If I get to make it up, I pick “naps.” That’s as valid as his, by his rules, and he hates that.
k.m: Pick naps and then live it, in front of everyone, for forty years. The seriousness comes from that part.

k.f: Existentialism is being a teenager, but in French and with citations.
k.m: Teenagers ask the question. The French kept asking it past twenty, which is the difference.

k.f: Authenticity says be true to yourself and is silent on what self. A committed fanatic is as authentic as anyone.
k.m: It was never the whole ethic. It’s the condition for having one: owning your choices instead of crediting them to your role, your nature or your orders.

k.f: Plenty of terrible people were being completely themselves. That was the problem.
k.m: They were being what their party, their rank and their mob told them to be. That’s the opposite.

k.f: “Authentic” is what people call themselves right before being rude.
k.m: That’s sincerity, and it’s cheap. Authenticity is admitting you chose to be rude.

k.f: Anxiety has ordinary causes, and reading a mood as a disclosure of metaphysical truth is a choice the argument doesn’t justify.
k.m: The claim is about a particular mood with no object, different from fear of something. That it sometimes has a chemical trigger doesn’t tell you what it shows.

k.f: Anxiety reveals too much coffee. It’s revealed that for years and nobody built a philosophy on it.
k.m: Coffee gives you jitters about nothing. Now ask why “about nothing” is unbearable.

k.f: They took a bad mood and gave it a Danish name and a German name.
k.m: Two names because two languages noticed the same thing separately.

t.t: “Existence can’t be captured by any system”

k.f: The claim is general and systematic, and the major existentialists wrote very large books laying out structures of existence.
k.m: The big books describe structures every existence has, like being in a situation and facing death. They leave the content to each person, and that was the claim.

k.f: “No system can capture it,” Being and Nothingness, 700 pages, with a table of contents.
k.m: Seven hundred pages on why no page can live it for you. He was thorough.

k.f: Existentialism rejected systems and then had required reading.
k.m: Required reading that tells you nobody can do your reading for you.

k.f: The descriptions that result differ from one phenomenologist to the next, with no agreed way to tell whose account of experience is right.
k.m: The descriptions get corrected against each other, as observations do. Merleau-Ponty’s account of perception displaced Husserl’s on specific points.

k.f: Everyone went back to the things themselves and came home with a different thing.
k.m: They came back with different parts of the same thing and argued about how they fit. That’s a field.

k.f: Phenomenology is describing a coffee cup for forty pages and calling it rigor.
k.m: The forty pages show how much you were taking for granted about the cup. That’s the rigor.

t.t: “Bracket the natural attitude and describe pure experience”

k.f: Whether anyone can suspend their assumptions on command is doubtful, and there’s no check on whether it was done. Husserl’s own students mostly gave it up.
k.m: Full suspension may be impossible, and he came to say so. Even a partial one shows how much of what we “see” is assumption.

k.f: “Set aside all your assumptions” is an assumption about what can be set aside.
k.m: It’s a working assumption that gets tested by trying it. That’s allowed.

k.f: The epoché is closing your eyes and saying you’ve stopped assuming things.
k.m: Try it for one minute. You’ll find out how much you never stopped assuming.

k.f: Moods, pains and dizziness don’t obviously point at anything. The thesis holds for many mental states and is stretched to cover the rest.
k.m: Moods are about the world as a whole: in boredom everything shows up as flat. They have a wider object.

k.f: A headache isn’t about anything. It’s just there, being a headache.
k.m: A headache is of your head, as hurting. Ask where it is and you’ll point.

k.f: Intentionality: the discovery that when you think, you think about stuff.
k.m: And that nobody had said how. That part took the next hundred years.

k.f: A science has shared methods and results others can check. A century on, phenomenology has schools and founders, and no body of settled findings.
k.m: The results exist and went elsewhere: the lived body, the horizon of perception and the structure of time-consciousness are now standard in cognitive science.

k.f: A science where every practitioner gets different results from the same experiment is called a hobby.
k.m: Psychologists and roboticists use the results. Being absorbed by other fields is what success looks like.

k.f: Husserl kept restarting the whole project from scratch every few years. That’s how the rigorous science was going.
k.m: He restarted because he found the earlier version wasn’t rigorous enough. That’s the standard he was applying.

k.f: Putting ethics before any account of what exists or what we can know leaves the ethical claim with nothing to be checked against.
k.m: The claim is that the demand another person makes on me doesn’t wait for my theory of what they are. It’s checked against every encounter you’ve had.

k.f: Ethics can’t be first. Somebody has to exist before anybody owes them anything. Order of operations.
k.m: Someone asks you for help before you’ve worked out your metaphysics. That’s the order he means.

k.f: Levinas put ethics before everything, including clarity.
k.m: The clarity comes when someone needs something from you. It’s in the text less.

t.t: “The face of the Other commands me”

k.f: If the command comes before all concepts and reasons, there’s no way to say what it asks or to weigh one face against another.
k.m: He’s describing where obligation starts. He isn’t offering a decision procedure. Weighing claims comes with the third person, and he says that’s where justice and institutions begin.

k.f: The face says “do not kill,” apparently. Mostly faces say “do I know you?”
k.m: “Do I know you?” is already an answer to someone. You were addressed before you decided.

k.f: His whole ethics is making eye contact.
k.m: Try refusing someone while looking at them. Then tell me it’s nothing.

t.t: “My responsibility to the Other is infinite”

k.f: An obligation without limit can’t be met and can’t guide a choice between claims. Something infinite in every direction recommends nothing in particular.
k.m: Infinite means it’s never discharged, so you can’t say “I’ve done my share” and stop. The guiding is done by justice, which compares and limits.

k.f: Infinite responsibility to each of eight billion people. He’s behind.
k.m: Behind is the correct self-assessment. He wrote the philosophy of knowing you are.

k.f: “I am infinitely responsible for everyone” has never once gotten a dish washed.
k.m: It’s why you feel bad about the dish.

t.t: “Western philosophy reduces the Other to the Same”

k.f: The charge sweeps two and a half millennia into one gesture. Any tradition can be made to look uniform at that distance.
k.m: It’s a claim about a tendency: to understand is to fit a thing into what’s already known. He names exceptions, Plato’s Good beyond being and Descartes’s idea of the infinite.

k.f: All of Western philosophy made the same mistake, and one man noticed. That’s usually not how that goes.
k.m: He credits Plato and Descartes with noticing first. He says so repeatedly.

k.f: Levinas says philosophy erases difference, in prose where every sentence sounds the same.
k.m: He lost his family to people who were certain they’d understood who the Other was. He’s entitled to a theme.

t.t: “It would have been better never to have been born”

k.f: The claim compares existing with a state in which there’s no one to be better off. And he lived to 84 without acting on it.
k.m: He grants there’s no one to be better off. The remark is a judgment from inside life on what it costs, and living to 84 was his evidence.

k.f: Better for whom? There’s no one in the other column. He’s comparing his life to an empty chair and losing.
k.m: The empty chair has never had a bad night.

k.f: Cioran thought being born was the catastrophe and lived to 84 in Paris on a nice street.
k.m: He said the idea of an exit was what let him stay. The nice street doesn’t contradict it.

k.f: “Disease” assumes a healthy state for comparison, and the only vantage from which to make the comparison is the supposedly diseased one.
k.m: It’s a figure for excess: awareness beyond what living requires, which no other animal carries. The comparison class is everything else alive.

k.f: If consciousness is a disease, so is the thought that it’s a disease. It’s a symptom reviewing itself.
k.m: Every doctor is a symptom reviewing symptoms. It works for them.

k.f: He diagnosed consciousness as an illness using consciousness, and didn’t get a second opinion.
k.m: He asked the mystics and the Stoics. They concurred and prescribed more of it.

t.t: “Lucidity means seeing that everything is futile”

k.f: Pessimism is presented as clear sight and optimism as illusion, with no argument that the dark mood is the accurate one.
k.m: He doesn’t prove it and says proof belongs to systems. He reports what’s left when the consolations are examined one at a time.

k.f: Being miserable isn’t the same as being right. Lots of people manage only one.
k.m: He was funny about it, which the merely miserable never are.

k.f: Cioran is what happens when insomnia gets a book deal.
k.m: Seven years of insomnia and the best French prose of the century. Some people get neither.

t.t: “Only the aphorism is honest; systems lie”

k.f: A scattered form protects claims from having to cohere. That’s convenient, and it isn’t the same thing as honesty.
k.m: An aphorism can be judged on the spot, with nothing around it to lean on. A system lets a weak step hide behind the strong ones.

k.f: A man who never writes more than three sentences in a row can’t be caught contradicting himself. That’s the method.
k.m: He contradicts himself constantly and says that’s the honest record of a mind.

k.f: Aphorisms: for when an argument would take effort.
k.m: A good one takes longer than the chapter you’d write instead.

k.f: People without belief hold and act on moral norms, and belief has licensed plenty. Whatever grounds morality, the psychology doesn’t go the way the line predicts.
k.m: The claim concerns justification. People behave decently on inherited habits, and he’s asking what happens over generations once the ground is seen to be gone.

k.f: Then with God, nothing bad would have been done by believers. Somebody should check the record on that.
k.m: Believers who did evil broke their own law and knew it. That’s a different condition from having none to break.

k.f: “Without God everything is permitted” is said in the novel by a character, and people quote it like he signed it.
k.m: He gave it to his most intelligent character and couldn’t fully answer him. That’s honesty.

t.t: “Reason alone leads to the Grand Inquisitor”

k.f: The novels dramatize what rationalists do in Dostoevsky’s imagination. A story built to show a view failing isn’t evidence that it fails.
k.m: He gave the other side its strongest speech. Readers still argue over whether the Inquisitor is answered, which a rigged book wouldn’t allow.

k.f: He wrote the atheists himself and then they lost. That’s not an argument, that’s being the author.
k.m: He wrote the Inquisitor so well that atheists quote it. An author rigging the game doesn’t arm the other side.

k.f: Every rationalist in Dostoevsky goes mad or kills someone. It’s a pattern, and the pattern is the novelist.
k.m: He’d watched the real ones in the 1860s. Some of them did.

k.f: Much suffering crushes people and teaches nothing. Finding redemption in it risks telling the wretched their condition is good for them.
k.m: He never says suffering is good. He says a person can refuse or accept the truth it shows them, and Ivan’s objection about children stays in the book unanswered.

k.f: If suffering redeemed, the worst places on earth would be full of saints. They’re full of suffering.
k.m: He doesn’t say it redeems on contact. Raskolnikov suffers for five hundred pages and it does nothing until he stops lying.

k.f: Suffering ennobles, wrote a man who gambled away the rent and wrote about that too.
k.m: He wrote that down as well. He’s the least excused person in his own books.

k.f: He shows that people can act against their interest out of spite, which is a fact about perversity, not a refutation of a theory about what’s good.
k.m: It hits the premise that people act for their advantage once they see it. If they’ll wreck their interest to prove they aren’t piano keys, the planned society fails.

k.f: A man doing something stupid to prove he’s free has proved one of those two things.
k.m: One of the two, and it wrecks every plan built on people doing what’s good for them.

k.f: Notes from Underground is the first blog.
k.m: The first blog, and the comments section, in one voice.

k.f: If all knowledge is an effect of power, so is that claim. Critics pressed that the critique needs a standard of truth or freedom it refuses to state.
k.m: He never says knowledge is nothing but power. He says the two come together, in clinics and prisons and surveys, and that what gets studied depends on who can be made to hold still.

k.f: If power made knowledge, the most powerful people would know the most. Check on that.
k.m: The powerful don’t know the most. They decide what counts as knowing: who gets examined, filed and graded. That’s the claim.

k.f: Power is everywhere, which is a nice way of saying he couldn’t find it.
k.m: He found it in the timetable, the exam and the case file. You were looking for a villain.

k.f: Historians have challenged the evidence, including the mass confinement he describes, and showing a category was built doesn’t show the condition isn’t real.
k.m: He doesn’t say the suffering is unreal. He says where the line fell, and who policed it, has a history. The archival fights are over dates.

k.f: Broken legs were also categorized by institutions with power. Still broken.
k.m: A broken leg has been a broken leg in every century. Homosexuality was a sin, then a disease, then neither. Only one of those needs a historian.

k.f: Historians checked the footnotes. That’s why he’s shelved in philosophy.
k.m: The historians checked them and then started writing history his way.

k.f: The model prison was never built as designed, and treating schools, hospitals and prisons as one diagram flattens real differences in consent and exit.
k.m: It’s a diagram. Its principle is being visible without knowing when you’re watched, so you watch yourself. That needs no round building.

k.f: Schools are like prisons except for the going home at three, the no bars, and wanting your kid to get in.
k.m: You want your kid to get in. Having a subject want it is how the thing works.

k.f: The Panopticon is his big example and nobody ever built one.
k.m: Nobody had to. There’s a camera on your street and a rating on your profile.

k.f: Chomsky’s reply in their debate: without some idea of human nature there’s no basis for calling any arrangement unjust, including the ones Foucault opposed.
k.m: His reply was that the idea of justice Chomsky appeals to was itself shaped by the society it would judge. That’s a caution about the standard, and not a refusal to oppose anything.

k.f: Discourses are made by humans. Whatever makes them come out the same way every time is the nature.
k.m: They come out the same every time? Read two centuries apart on madness or sex and say that again.

k.f: Chomsky asked what would be better and what would justify it, and he wouldn’t say.
k.m: He said the task was to criticize institutions that look neutral. He then went and organized on behalf of prisoners.

k.f: Showing that a practice has ugly, accidental origins invites suspicion and can’t by itself show the practice should go. Some norm is doing unacknowledged work.
k.m: Genealogy removes a practice’s claim to be natural and necessary. Once it looks optional, the people subject to it can ask whether they want it.

k.f: A critic with no standards is a guy saying “interesting” in a suspicious voice.
k.m: “Interesting” in a suspicious voice is how every reform started. Somebody noticed the thing wasn’t inevitable.

k.f: Foucault is the most cited author in the humanities, which by Foucault makes him the regime.
k.m: He’d agree, and tell you to write the genealogy of it.

k.f: Read as “meaning always needs context” it’s a mild claim few deny. The radical reading is the one that made it famous, and defenders move between the two.
k.m: The mild reading is the right one and he said so many times. That it’s uncontroversial once stated correctly isn’t a mark against it.

k.f: Rent.
k.m: The lease is a text. So are the notice and the law that backs it. You picked the example with the most paperwork.

k.f: “There is nothing outside the text,” and he still cashed the checks, which are outside it.
k.m: A check is a text with a signature, and he wrote a whole essay about signatures.

k.f: That meaning depends on differences and context doesn’t make it indeterminate. People communicate reliably, and the theory has to explain that away.
k.m: He doesn’t deny that people communicate. He denies that any context can be closed for good, which is why contracts get litigated and scripture has commentaries.

k.f: If meaning were endlessly deferred, nobody would have understood that sentence, and his fans claim to.
k.m: You understood it well enough for now. Ask again in a hundred years. That’s “deferred.”

k.f: Deconstruction is finding out the dictionary defines words with other words.
k.m: And then finding out what follows from that. You stopped at the dictionary.

k.f: Some pairs are ranked for good reason, like true and false or valid and invalid. The method assumes in advance that ranking is illegitimate.
k.m: He doesn’t say every ranking is wrong. He shows that the first term keeps needing the second to define itself, so the ranking isn’t the simple thing it claimed to be.

k.f: On and off is a binary with a hierarchy, and every light switch is fine.
k.m: “On” is defined by a circuit that includes “off.” You can’t have the top without the bottom. The switch is his example, working.

k.f: The Sokal paper got in. That was the peer review.
k.m: Sokal fooled an unrefereed journal. The same trick has since worked on physics and medicine journals.

k.f: “The grand narratives are over” is a story about the whole of modernity. The contradiction was pointed out immediately.
k.m: He called it a report on what had already happened to belief, and he qualified it later. Describing a loss of faith isn’t founding a new church.

k.f: A story about how all the big stories ended is the biggest story.
k.m: A weather report that the big storms are over isn’t a big storm.

k.f: Postmodernism says there’s no truth, and gets upset when it’s misquoted.
k.m: It says truths have histories. People who repeat “there’s no truth” are the ones misquoting.

k.f: That defense puts the writing beyond checking. Where plainer statements of the ideas exist, they seem to lose little except the aura.
k.m: Where the claim is that ordinary phrasing hides an assumption, writing in ordinary phrases would repeat it. The style is an argument, and you can judge it as one.

k.f: If the difficulty were the point, the books explaining him clearly would be destroying him. They outsell him.
k.m: The guides sell because readers want to get to him. Nobody writes a guide to a writer who’s finished.

k.f: Foucault reportedly said a French book needs ten percent nonsense to be taken seriously. Derrida went for a higher score.
k.m: That story comes from Searle, who was not a neutral party.

k.f: That doesn’t say what makes one created concept better than another. Novelty and “interest” replace truth as the test, which critics find evasive.
k.m: The test is what a concept lets you do: which problems it makes thinkable. He says a concept is good the way a tool is good, and that’s a standard.

k.f: Creating concepts is also what conspiracy forums do. Output isn’t the standard.
k.m: Conspiracy forums recycle one concept, the hidden hand. Making a new one is the hard part.

k.f: Deleuze said philosophy is making up concepts. At least he was upfront.
k.m: He was. The others say they’re discovering what they invented.

k.f: Difference looks like a relation between things that can already be told apart. Making it basic takes a “difference in itself” that’s hard to state without identities creeping back.
k.m: The view from identity treats difference as what’s left after comparing two finished things. His claim is that the things are produced by differing, like a gradient before there are two sides.

k.f: Different from what? There. That’s identity. It was already in the question.
k.m: Different from what it was a moment ago. No second thing required.

k.f: Difference and Repetition says it’s different every time, and repeats that.
k.m: Each time it comes back it’s changed. That’s the title, and you read it.

k.f: The contrast is itself a neat pair of the kind it rejects, and real knowledge, in classification, proof and causal explanation, is often usefully tree-shaped.
k.m: He says trees and rhizomes turn into each other and the pair isn’t a ranking. It’s a way of noticing when a branching model is being forced on a network.

k.f: A rhizome is a root. It’s ginger. He replaced the tree with a different plant and called it the end of trees.
k.m: Ginger has no trunk and no top, and any piece grows a new plant. That’s the property. He picked the right vegetable.

k.f: The rhizome has no beginning, middle or end, which also describes reading it.
k.m: It’s written so you can start on any chapter. That was announced on page one.

k.f: Throwing out lack leaves no room to criticize any desire. The book says desire can desire its own repression and can’t say why that’s bad.
k.m: He criticizes desires by what they do: whether they connect and expand or close down. That’s a standard, and it replaces “lack” with “blockage.”

k.f: Hunger. A desire that is one hundred percent lack, three times a day.
k.m: Hunger builds farms, kitchens, trade routes and cuisines. It’s the most productive thing people have.

k.f: Anti-Oedipus has a thousand machines in it and none of them do anything.
k.m: They produce. That’s the entire point of calling them machines.

t.t: “The math and science references are rigorous”

k.f: Sokal and Bricmont documented uses of calculus and physics that are trivial or wrong. Calling them metaphors concedes they do no technical work.
k.m: The borrowed terms are used as concepts. He says philosophy takes from science without doing science. Judge the concept by its use.

k.f: If the math were right, mathematicians would cite it. Citations from the math department: zero.
k.m: Mathematicians have read him and written books on his use of the calculus. Zero is not the count.

k.f: A body without organs is a bag.
k.m: A bag is organized. Read it again.

t.t: “Ideology is strongest where we think we’re outside it”

k.f: The claim can’t lose: belief confirms ideology and disbelief confirms it more. Nothing could count as being free of it, his own account included.
k.m: The claim is specific: we now know very well and act as if we didn’t. That can be checked against behavior, and it describes how most people use their phones.

k.f: Then the people who think they’re in it are outside it. So the most ideological person in the room is whoever read Žižek.
k.m: Reading Žižek and feeling safely outside is the exact move he describes. So yes. He’d agree and include himself.

k.f: Everything is ideology except the guy pointing.
k.m: He says he’s in it too. That’s most of the act.

k.f: The method applies the same three-step to films, toilets and elections. A tool that fits everything explains nothing in particular.
k.m: The same structure turning up in many places is what a theory of ideology predicts. The test is whether each reading shows something the film’s makers would recognize.

k.f: Lacan can’t be tested and Hegel can’t be read. Adding them doesn’t fix either.
k.m: Hegel can be read, and you’ve used the word “alienation” this week.

k.f: Žižek explains capitalism using a movie he’s describing from memory, wrong.
k.m: Wrong about the plot, right about why you liked it.

k.f: Often the example stands in for the argument. The paradoxical reversal is asserted, and the audience’s laugh is taken as agreement.
k.m: A joke that works shows the structure it relies on. If you laughed, you already saw the mechanism, and the explaining comes after.

k.f: If jokes carried arguments, comedians would be the theorists. Some of them think so too.
k.m: The good comedians are theorists. Ask one how a joke about class works and you’ll get twenty minutes.

k.f: Žižek has written the same book forty times, and the toilets are in all of them.
k.m: He says he repeats himself. It’s the only way to find out what you actually think.

k.f: The positive program is thin to absent. Calls to “think” and to refuse are offered where a politics would go.
k.m: He says the old program failed and the first duty is not to rush into the next one. Refusing to supply a blueprint on demand is a position about blueprints.

k.f: A serious communist charges less for tickets.
k.m: He takes capitalism’s money to attack capitalism. That’s the contradiction he lectures on, performed live.

k.f: The most dangerous philosopher in the West, available for corporate events.
k.m: Dangerous and booked. That’s what the system does to everything, as he keeps saying.

k.f: The line is hard to draw when the provocation lands opposite the audience’s expectation every time, whatever the topic.
k.m: The reversal is the method when the audience’s expectation is the ideology. It fails as argument only if the reversed claim can’t be defended, and he usually tries.

k.f: Saying the opposite of what the room expects, in every room, is called a bit.
k.m: If the opposite is true in every room, the rooms have a problem.

k.f: “It’s precisely the opposite” works on any sentence. That’s the method, and so on.
k.m: And so on, and so on. He knows.

k.f: Science accepts plenty of unconscious processing. Freud’s unconscious of repressed wishes is a further, specific claim with weak support.
k.m: The modern findings cover the core: motives people can’t report, defenses, the long reach of early attachment. The specific mechanisms have been revised, as in any field.

k.f: If it’s unconscious nobody can check, including the analyst. He’s guessing, at an hourly rate.
k.m: The analyst can’t check, and the patient can: something shifts when the guess is right. That’s the test, session by session.

k.f: Freud discovered that people don’t know why they do things and then told them it was their mother.
