k.m: And when you rolled your eyes just now, whose voice was that in?

t.t: “Repression and the Oedipus complex are real”

k.f: The Oedipal theory rests on a handful of case histories that Freud shaped, and evidence from other cultures and from child development doesn’t support it.
k.m: The literal family drama is the weakest part. The general claim survives: a child’s first loves and rivalries leave a pattern that later ones repeat.

k.f: Most people have checked how they feel about their mother, and it’s fine.
k.m: “It’s fine” is the most examined sentence in the history of the couch.

k.f: The Oedipus complex is one man’s situation, generalized.
k.m: Sophocles had it packing theaters two thousand years before Freud.

k.f: That’s the classic objection. If acceptance and denial both confirm, the interpretation risks nothing.
k.m: Good practice never took a “no” as confirmation. An interpretation is tested by what follows it: new memories, a change in the symptom, or nothing.

k.f: Heads he’s right, tails the patient’s in denial. That’s not a method, it’s a coin he owns.
k.m: He doesn’t own the coin. The patient can leave. They mostly come back, and that’s also data.

k.f: If the patient agrees, it’s true. If the patient disagrees, it’s really true.
k.m: Freud wrote the paper saying yes and no both prove nothing. You’re attacking a position he rejected in 1937.

k.f: Uncontrolled case reports can’t separate suggestion from discovery. That the therapy helps about as much as others doesn’t validate the theory behind it.
k.m: The long-term outcome studies now exist, and the gains from this kind of therapy keep growing after it ends. That’s a measurable difference.

k.f: Clinical experience also supported bloodletting. The clinicians were very experienced.
k.m: Bloodletting never had a patient say “that’s it” and stop having the symptom.

k.f: Freud’s famous cures mostly weren’t. Somebody followed up.
k.m: The follow-up on the pills isn’t flattering either.

k.f: The formulas and knot diagrams have no fixed content. Critics, and some sympathetic readers, found the mathematics decorative.
k.m: The formulas are shorthand for teaching, and he said they weren’t mathematics. The rigor is in reading Freud line by line against what patients say.

k.f: Lacan said the unconscious is structured like a language, and then didn’t use one.
k.m: He meant it’s made of substitution and combination, like metaphor and metonymy. He used French, heavily.

k.f: Lacan charged full price for five-minute sessions and called it technique.
k.m: A session ends when something has been said. Sometimes that takes five minutes. Sometimes it takes you ten years.

k.f: Audiences interpret, resist and repurpose what they consume. The picture of passive masses was asserted from above, with little study of actual audiences.
k.m: Audiences reinterpret what they’re sold and still buy the next one. The claim is about the form, standardized and pre-digested, and that survives lively fans.

k.f: People watched a lot of movies and then had the 1960s. The conformity machine had a recall.
k.m: The sixties were on vinyl by 1969 and in commercials by 1975. He predicted the second part.

k.f: Adorno heard jazz and concluded civilization was over.
k.m: He heard the dance-band jazz of 1930s radio, the product he was writing about.

k.f: If reason as such leads to domination, the critique, which is an exercise of reason, has no ground to stand on. Habermas made this point against his own teachers.
k.m: The book says so itself: it’s reason criticizing a narrowing of itself into mere calculation, for the sake of the wider kind. Habermas built on that.

k.f: They used reason to show reason is a trap. So either the argument’s a trap or it isn’t true.
k.m: They used one kind of reason against another. There’s more than one, and that was the argument.

k.f: Dialectic of Enlightenment: two men in California explaining that everything is fascism, including the weather.
k.m: Two refugees from the real thing, noticing what it had in common with the radio. They’d earned the comparison.

k.f: Building the desired political result into the method means the theory can’t discover that it’s wrong about what would free anyone.
k.m: The aim is fixed only as less needless suffering. What would bring that about is left open to inquiry, and they revised their own answers repeatedly.

k.f: A theory that knows its conclusion before it starts is called a position.
k.m: Medicine knows it wants the patient well before it starts. Nobody calls that bias.

k.f: They theorized revolution for forty years, and when students actually occupied the institute, Adorno called the police.
k.m: He thought their tactics would bring a backlash, and he said so in advance. It did.

k.f: A theory that licenses suppressing views the theorist judges regressive hands a weapon to whoever holds power, whichever direction they face.
k.m: The essay argues that formal neutrality favors whoever already owns the megaphones. Who decides is its weak point, and he admits as much.

k.f: Tolerance means only tolerating the correct side. He needed a whole essay because it doesn’t sound good short.
k.m: It says tolerance that treats the megaphone and the leaflet alike isn’t neutral. That takes more than a sentence.

k.f: Marcuse figured out that free speech is oppression unless he’s the one talking.
k.m: He was talking about a few broadcasters owning nearly every channel. That detail usually goes missing.

t.t: “We live in simulation; the real has disappeared”

k.f: The claim trades on the difference between the real and its images to announce that there’s no difference. If it were true it couldn’t be stated.
k.m: It can be stated because it’s a matter of degree. Models now precede the events they describe: polls, forecasts, brands. He names the tipping point.

k.f: If the real had disappeared, he couldn’t know what was missing. He’s describing the thing he says is gone.
k.m: He’s describing the missing thing from memory, like everyone over forty.

k.f: Baudrillard announced that reality was over and kept accepting real money for it.
k.m: The money’s a number on a screen, backed by confidence in other numbers. He’d take the example.

t.t: “Signs now refer only to other signs”

k.f: People still get wet in the rain. That media shape perception doesn’t show that nothing lies behind the images.
k.m: The rain is real. What it means to you, a ruined event or a trending storm with a name, arrives pre-packaged, and that layer is what he’s describing.

k.f: A stop sign refers to stopping. People who treat it as referring to other signs are in the hospital.
k.m: People stop for the sign with no car in sight. They’re obeying the sign.

k.f: Hyperreality is noticing that Disneyland is fake and then not stopping.
k.m: He says Disneyland is there to make the rest look real by contrast. Noticing it’s fake is the first step and he took the second.

t.t: “The Gulf War did not take place”

k.f: Read as media criticism it says the public saw a staged version. Read as written, it’s false and offensive to the people it happened to.
k.m: The essays came out before, during and after. The thesis is that what the West experienced was a televised event with a fixed outcome, and he says the dead were real.

k.f: There were casualties. They took place.
k.m: He says so. The claim is that for the audience it wasn’t a war, it was programming, and for one side it was a slaughter.

k.f: He said a war didn’t happen while it was on television, and his defenders say you have to read it carefully.
k.m: You do have to read it. It’s forty pages.

t.t: “The Matrix is based on his work”

k.f: He said the film misunderstood him. On his view there’s no outside to escape to, which is the film’s entire plot.
k.m: Right, and his fans say the same. The film’s error is instructive: it imagines a real world you could wake up into.

k.f: Baudrillard said The Matrix got him wrong. The movie made more sense, so that checks out.
k.m: The movie made more sense because it kept the door marked “exit.”

k.f: The book appears in The Matrix for four seconds, hollowed out, used as a box. Fair.
k.m: The filmmakers opened the book, put the money in it and didn’t read it. He couldn’t have staged it better.

t.t: “The unconscious is structured like a language”

k.f: The slogan borrows linguistic terms loosely, and working linguists don’t recognize the borrowed concepts in the use he makes of them.
k.m: He means it works by substitution and displacement, as jokes and slips do. Freud’s own examples are wordplay, and that’s the evidence.

k.f: Languages have grammar and can be learned. Nobody has ever learned to speak unconscious.
k.m: You speak it fluently every time you say the wrong name.

k.f: Lacan said the unconscious is structured like a language, specifically one that only he spoke.
k.m: Several thousand analysts trained in it. It’s a crowded language.

k.f: The developmental claim was made with almost no evidence, and children blind from birth form a sense of self without mirrors.
k.m: The mirror is the example. The claim is that the self is first met from outside, as an image held together by someone else’s gaze, and a parent’s face will do.

k.f: People had selves before mirrors were invented. Ponds are not that reliable.
k.m: A mother’s face did the job before glass. He says the mirror can be a person.

k.f: A baby looks in a mirror, and from that he got a theory of everything and fifty years of seminars.
k.m: From a baby delighted by its reflection six months before it can walk. It’s a good observation.

t.t: “Desire is the desire of the Other”

k.f: The phrase supports several incompatible readings, and the theory doesn’t choose. What can’t be pinned down can’t be tested or applied.
k.m: The readings are meant together: we want what others want, we want to be wanted, and we want from a place others shaped. It’s compressed, on purpose.

k.f: I want a sandwich. Nobody else is involved.
k.m: You want the sandwich you saw in an ad, at the place your friends go. Somebody else is involved.

k.f: Every Lacanian sentence means three things and is defended with whichever one wasn’t attacked.
k.m: It means three things because desire does.

k.f: A category defined as what can’t be said or imagined does no explanatory work and can’t be wrong.
k.m: It names the point where the patient’s story breaks down, in trauma or repetition. Clinically, that’s where the work is.

k.f: If it resists symbolization, stop writing about it. He wrote about it for thirty years.
k.m: Thirty years circling a thing that can’t be said is called an analysis.

k.f: The Real is whatever the theory can’t explain, renamed as the theory’s deepest concept.
k.m: Every theory has a remainder. His is the only one with a chapter on it.

t.t: “There’s a collective unconscious shared by all humanity”

k.f: Shared themes in myths are explained by shared biology, common life situations and contact between cultures. An inherited store of images adds nothing testable.
k.m: He agrees it’s biological: inherited patterns of response, the way a chick fears a hawk’s shadow. “Collective unconscious” is his name for the shared equipment.

k.f: Every culture has stories about mothers because everybody has a mother. No psychic underground required.
k.m: Everybody has a mother, and every culture tells the same six stories about her. That’s the thing to be explained.

k.f: Jung found the same symbols in every culture, having gone looking for them.
k.m: He went looking, in patients who’d never read a myth and dreamed one anyway.

k.f: The archetypes are vague enough to fit any story or dream, and no finding could count against their presence.
k.m: They’re patterns of situation: threat, guide, betrayal, return. Screenwriters and game designers use them because audiences respond on schedule.

k.f: A wise old man, a trickster, a mother. That’s not the structure of the psyche, that’s casting.
k.m: It’s casting that works in every country without translation. Ask why.

k.f: Archetypes are zodiac signs for people who went to graduate school.
k.m: Zodiac signs don’t predict what scares a three-year-old.

k.f: With enough events, striking coincidences are expected. Calling them meaningful describes how they feel and adds no connection between them.
k.m: He called it a hypothesis about meaning and said it wasn’t causation. Its use is clinical: what a coincidence means to the patient tells you about the patient.

k.f: Thinking of someone right before they call happens. So do the nine thousand times they didn’t call.
k.m: The nine thousand didn’t arrive on the day it mattered. That’s what he’s pointing at.

k.f: Synchronicity is noticing a coincidence and refusing to do the math.
k.m: He co-wrote it with a Nobel physicist, who didn’t think it was arithmetic.

t.t: “Individuation is the goal of psychological life”

k.f: The stages and their end state come from his own experience and his reading of alchemy. There’s no evidence that minds develop along that path.
k.m: The map is his. That midlife turns people from achievement toward meaning is among the better-replicated findings in the psychology of aging.

k.f: He based the map of the human soul on his own dreams and some medieval chemistry books.
k.m: He used his own dreams, his patients’ and the alchemists’, who he argued were describing the same process in other symbols.

k.f: Jung gave us the Myers-Briggs. That’s the testable part, and it failed.
k.m: He disowned being typed. Introvert and extravert are his, and they held up.

t.t: “Meaning comes from differences within a system”

k.f: That signs contrast with each other doesn’t show the world plays no part in what they mean. Words are also used to pick things out.
k.m: The world supplies the things and the system supplies the cuts. Where one language has a single word and another has two, the difference is in the system.

k.f: “Cat” means cat because of cats. The differences help. The cats help more.
k.m: Cats help, and then English has “cat” and “kitten” where another language cuts elsewhere.

k.f: Structuralism is the theory that a dictionary could be written without anyone going outside.
k.m: A dictionary does define every word with other words, and it works.

k.f: The sound is arbitrary. What follows from that is modest, and it was stretched into the claim that categories and facts are arbitrary too.
k.m: It’s modest and it’s the foundation: no sound has a natural meaning, so meaning has to come from the system. Stretching it was other people’s doing.

k.f: The word “poison” is arbitrary. The poison isn’t. He confused the label with the bottle.
k.m: The label is arbitrary and what counts as “poison” versus “medicine” is a line the language draws. Ask a pharmacist about dose.

k.f: Saussure never wrote the book. His students assembled it from lecture notes after he died. The foundation is somebody’s homework.
k.m: Students assembled the Gospels too.

t.t: “Myths and kinship share universal deep structures”

k.f: The analyses can’t be replicated: different analysts find different structures in the same myth, with no procedure for deciding between them.
k.m: The kinship work made testable claims about which marriage systems can exist, and anthropologists argued over the data for decades. That’s replication being attempted.

k.f: He found binary oppositions in every myth. Give anyone two columns and a myth and they will too.
k.m: Two columns and a myth, and then predicting the variants found in the next valley. He did that part.

k.f: Lévi-Strauss reduced world mythology to raw and cooked, and people let him.
k.m: Raw and cooked is nature and culture, which every society marks. He picked the kitchen because every society has one.

t.t: “The subject is an effect of structures”

k.f: If people are produced by structures all the way down, the theorist is too, and the theory is one more effect with no claim to have seen the truth.
k.m: A theorist shaped by structures can still describe them, as a native speaker can write a grammar. Being inside a system doesn’t stop you mapping it.

k.f: Then the structures wrote his book, and they should get the royalties.
k.m: The royalties go where the contract says. That’s a structure.

k.f: Structuralism abolished the author, and every structuralist put their name on the cover.
k.m: The name on the cover is a legal function. One of them wrote a famous essay on exactly that.

t.t: “It’s easier to imagine the end of the world than the end of capitalism”

k.f: That says something about imagination and film budgets. People imagined alternatives constantly, and the hard part was showing they’d work.
k.m: The claim is about what’s publicly thinkable: no party, film or mainstream program presents an alternative as live. The bookstores are the niche he describes.

k.f: People imagine the end of capitalism all the time. There are whole bookstores. What’s hard is the second chapter.
k.m: The second chapter is missing from all of them, and that’s his point.

k.f: “Capitalist realism” is a name for not having a plan.
k.m: It’s a name for why nobody has one. A diagnosis isn’t a prescription.

k.f: A theory on which every protest is absorbed and every success is co-optation can’t be told apart from one where things simply aren’t that bad.
k.m: He doesn’t say resistance is impossible. He says its usual forms were already priced in, and asks what a form that isn’t would look like.

k.f: If all resistance gets absorbed, so did the book. It’s sold by a multinational and comes with free shipping.
k.m: He says exactly that about his own book, in the book.

k.f: Capitalist Realism is eighty pages on how nothing can be done, and it sold very well.
k.m: It sold to people who felt that and had no word for it. That’s what books are for.

t.t: “Culture has stalled: nothing new, only retro”

k.f: Every generation’s critics say this about the music after their youth. Novelty is easier to see in retrospect and in scenes one isn’t part of.
k.m: His test is concrete: play a record from 1975 to someone in 1955 and it would shock them. Play one from 2015 in 1995 and it wouldn’t.

k.f: Every forty-year-old thinks music stopped being new when he was twenty-five. He wrote it up.
k.m: He was listening to new music weekly and writing about it. The claim came from someone keeping up.

k.f: Hauntology is being sad that the future from old TV shows didn’t arrive.
k.m: Sad that a future was promised, budgeted for and cancelled. That’s a political fact.

t.t: “Mental distress is political, not just personal”

k.f: Social conditions matter, but making every case a symptom of the economy tells people nothing useful about their own, and it isn’t supported in that strong form.
k.m: He doesn’t say every case. He says treating a mass rise in distress as millions of private chemical accidents is itself a political choice.

k.f: Unhappiness predates capitalism by a few thousand years. The Book of Job has no employers in it.
k.m: Job’s troubles came from on high, were nobody’s fault he could find, and he was told to look within. Good example.

k.f: Everything is capitalism’s fault, a claim that’s very available on mugs.
k.m: The mugs are how you know the claim got absorbed. He covered that.

t.t: “Speed capitalism up to push through it”

k.f: Nothing shows that intensifying a system produces its successor and not just more of it, or a collapse nobody would choose.
k.m: The left version says: take the productive forces capitalism built, the automation and the logistics, and push them past what it can use. It’s a plan about technology.

k.f: “Make it worse until it gets better” has been tried by every gambler.
k.m: It’s what every technological transition has been. Nobody reformed their way from horses to engines.

k.f: Accelerationism: the plan is to floor it and find out what the wall is made of.
k.m: We know what the brake is made of. It’s the same people it was last time.

t.t: “Capital is an inhuman intelligence using us”

k.f: Markets are aggregates of human choices under rules humans set. Treating the aggregate as an agent with aims is a metaphor promoted to a theory.
k.m: A process that sets its own goals, routes around obstacles and reshapes its parts is an agent on any definition used for other systems.

k.f: Capital doesn’t want anything. It’s money. He got scared of a spreadsheet.
k.m: It decides where you live and what you study. For a spreadsheet it has a lot of say.

k.f: Nick Land wrote that capitalism is an alien intelligence from the future, and people in tech said “finally, someone gets it.”
k.m: They’d been building it and wanted to know what it was.

t.t: “Technology’s growth can’t and shouldn’t be steered”

k.f: Technologies have been steered, slowed and banned many times. “Inevitable” tends to be said by those who’d profit from nobody trying.
k.m: Each of those was slowed in some places for some time. The claim is about the whole system under competition: what one group declines, another builds.

k.f: Human cloning, chemical weapons, lead in gasoline. Steered. It happens constantly.
k.m: Steered until somebody else needed it. Look at where each of those stands now.

k.f: e/acc is “you can’t stop progress” from people who own the progress.
k.m: The people who own the last round of progress are the ones asking for the pause.

k.f: Speed and safety trade off in every engineered system. Asserting that caution is always the greater danger is a slogan, not an analysis.
k.m: Delay costs lives too: cures arriving later, poverty lasting longer. A ledger that counts only the risks of acting is missing a column.

k.f: Every engineer who ever lived would like a word about “slowing down is the risk.”
k.m: Engineers ship. The ones who never ship aren’t called careful.

k.f: The movement that wants to accelerate everything has been mostly posting for ten years.
k.m: Posting while the thing gets built by people who read the posts.

k.f: Most overwork still has an employer, a mortgage or a visa behind it. Describing it as self-exploitation takes the pressure off whoever’s applying it.
k.m: The boss is real. What’s new is how many people with no boss in the room still can’t stop, and call it passion.

k.f: People aren’t exploiting themselves. They have a boss. He can be reached by email, at midnight, that’s the issue.
k.m: The email arrives at midnight and you answer it because you want to be the kind of person who does.

k.f: The Burnout Society is sixty pages, because the reader is too tired for more. He knows his market.
k.m: Sixty pages is the form the argument takes about attention. He means it.

k.f: The essays assert broad cultural diagnoses without evidence, and the opposite claim, that secrecy protects abuse, has at least as much support.
k.m: He’s writing essays in a tradition that argues by concepts. The claim is that trust means not needing to see everything, and a demand for total visibility admits it’s gone.

k.f: Opaque institutions have an excellent record, he said, naming none.
k.m: Friendship, the confessional, the ballot booth. Some good things work because nobody’s watching.

k.f: Han is against transparency and proves it with his prose.
k.m: It’s clear, short sentences with no footnotes. You’ve confused opaque with uncited.

k.f: “The Other has disappeared” is the sort of sentence that can’t be checked. People online meet more strangers and more disagreement than any generation before.
k.m: More strangers, fewer others: the feed shows you people sorted to resemble you or to enrage you. An Other is someone you didn’t select.

k.f: The internet is nothing but other people. That’s the complaint everyone actually has.
k.m: Other people as content. That’s what he means by abolished.

k.f: He writes that we’ve lost the capacity for contemplation, in books designed to be read on a train.
k.m: Short enough to finish on the train and long enough to make you put the phone away for it.

t.t: “We’ve lost ritual and the ability to linger”

k.f: Nostalgia for a slower, more ritual past rarely specifies when that was or who got to enjoy the lingering.
k.m: He isn’t asking for the past back. He’s noting that repeated shared forms did something for attention and belonging that nothing has replaced.

k.f: The people who had time to linger had servants. Somebody else was not lingering.
k.m: The servants had festivals, sabbaths and saints’ days, which was more shared time off than you get.

k.f: Byung-Chul Han publishes the same short book about once a year. It’s a ritual.
k.m: One short book a year, the same themes, turned slightly. He practices what he describes.

t.t: “History is the history of class struggle”

k.f: Much of history is driven by religion, nationalism, technology, disease and accident. Reducing those to class takes a new side-assumption each time.
k.m: He doesn’t claim class is the only cause. Other struggles take the shape that material interests allow, and the long sweep from feudalism to capitalism fits that.

k.f: The longest wars in history were between people of the same class over which church. He’d read about them.
k.m: Follow the church’s land and the princes’ revenues through those wars and say that again.

k.f: Marx said the workers would rise up. The workers bought houses.
k.m: With a mortgage. He covered that. It’s called a chain.

k.f: Economics dropped the labor theory of value for good reasons, since value depends on demand. Exploitation has to be restated without it, as later Marxists tried.
k.m: The exploitation claim survives without it: one group owns the means of production, the other must sell its time, and the surplus goes to the first.

k.f: A mud pie takes labor. A lot of it, if it’s a big one.
k.m: He says in chapter one that useless labor creates no value. You’ve refuted page ten with something on page eleven.

k.f: Marx never worked in a factory. His friend owned one.
k.m: He read every factory inspector’s report in the British Museum for thirty years. The inspectors are the ones in the footnotes.

k.f: The predictions didn’t come about: deepening misery, falling profits, revolution in the richest economies. The theory was adjusted each time to survive.
k.m: The crises came on schedule. What he missed was how far the state would go to manage them, and that’s a revision the theory can take.

k.f: It’s been about to collapse since 1848. A prophecy on its 180th extension is a lifestyle.
k.m: 1873, 1929, 1973, 2008. It keeps having the heart attack and getting the paddles.

k.f: Late capitalism has been late for a hundred and fifty years.
k.m: And it’s still the best description of last quarter.

k.f: Marx left little institutional design, so regimes filled the gap. That every attempt took a similar turn is evidence about the theory, not only about the attempts.
k.m: He expected revolution in rich industrial countries with a majority working class. It was tried in poor agrarian ones under siege, which he said couldn’t work.

k.f: It’s been tried in about forty countries. At some point the sample is the result.
k.m: All forty were poor, rural and at war. The sample has one kind of country in it.

k.f: “That wasn’t real communism” is the only part of the theory that’s been tested every time.
k.m: “That wasn’t real capitalism” is what gets said after every crash.

k.f: If ideas are fixed by class position, so is Marxism, a theory written by middle-class intellectuals. The thesis is either too weak to matter or false.
k.m: He says ideas are conditioned, and that members of a class can see past its interests when its position is crumbling. He names himself as an instance.

k.f: Marx was middle class and lived on a factory owner’s money. So by his own theory Capital is factory-owner ideology.
k.m: A factory owner’s money paying for a book against factory owners isn’t the ideology you’d expect. That’s the anomaly the theory explains.

k.f: Engels paid for Capital out of the family mill’s profits. Surplus value has its uses.
k.m: Yes. Best use of surplus value on record.

t.t: “Justice is what we’d choose behind the veil of ignorance”

k.f: The outcome depends on what’s stipulated about the choosers. Other theorists’ equally ignorant parties pick average utility. The veil illustrates a view more than it argues for one.
k.m: The veil is a device for showing what fairness requires, and he says so. The stipulations are argued for one by one, since they express conditions people accept on reflection.

k.f: Nobody was ever behind a veil. It’s a contract nobody signed, by people who don’t exist, in a room that isn’t there.
k.m: It’s a test, like asking how you’d cut the cake if someone else picked first. You don’t need to have cut it.

k.f: Behind the veil of ignorance everyone turns out to be a Harvard professor.
k.m: A Harvard professor who concluded Harvard professors shouldn’t get more unless the janitor does better for it.

k.f: The rule is extremely risk-averse, and Nozick’s objection is that keeping any such pattern requires constant interference with free transfers.
k.m: Extreme caution fits a one-time choice of basic institutions with your whole life at stake. And the principle applies to the basic structure, leaving individual transfers alone.

k.f: So if the poorest get one more dollar, any inequality is fine. He wrote the mission statement for every billionaire’s foundation.
k.m: “Any inequality” has to be the arrangement that leaves the poorest best off out of all the possibilities. One dollar almost never passes.

k.f: Rawls proved that justice is roughly the Democratic platform of 1971.
k.m: No Democratic platform has ever come close to it.

t.t: “The state should be neutral about the good life”

k.f: Neutrality is itself a commitment, to autonomy and individualism, that many reject, and no state is neutral in its effects.
k.m: He dropped neutrality of effect. The claim is neutrality of justification: basic law shouldn’t rest on one contested account of the good life.

k.f: A state that’s neutral about what’s good can’t say why neutrality is good.
k.m: It can say why. People who disagree about the good still have to share a state, and neutrality is the term each can accept.

k.f: Liberal neutrality: every way of life is welcome that’s already liberal.
k.m: Welcome so long as it doesn’t use the police to make the others join. That’s the one condition.

t.t: “Laws must be justifiable to all reasonable citizens”

k.f: “Reasonable” is defined to leave out those who reject liberal premises, so the agreement is built into the entry conditions.
k.m: “Reasonable” means willing to offer terms others could accept and to admit that sincere people disagree. It leaves out those who’d impose, whatever their doctrine, liberals included.

k.f: Reasonable people are the ones who agree. So it’s justified to everyone who already said yes.
k.m: Reasonable people agree to look for terms. They don’t agree on the answer. That gap is the whole theory.

k.f: “Reasonable” does so much work in Rawls it should have tenure.
k.m: It’s defined in the text. Twice. It earned tenure.

k.f: If my talents and efforts aren’t mine in the sense that matters, it’s unclear what self is left to have rights at all.
k.m: He doesn’t say talents aren’t yours. He says no one deserves their starting place, so the rules for rewarding talent need a justification other than desert.

k.f: If nobody deserves their talents, nobody deserves credit for a theory of justice.
k.m: He agreed. He said his career was mostly luck and wouldn’t take credit for it in interviews.

k.f: A Theory of Justice is 600 pages, and the later books are him taking some of it back.
k.m: A theorist who revises under criticism. You say that as if it’s a flaw.

t.t: “Without a sovereign, life is nasty, brutish and short”

k.f: Anthropology finds stateless societies with norms, reciprocity and ways of settling disputes. His state of nature is a model of civil war, not of human origins.
k.m: Those societies are small and their homicide rates, where measured, run high. His claim is about strangers at scale with nothing to enforce agreements.

k.f: People lived without states for two hundred thousand years. If it was that bad there’d be nobody left to write Leviathan.
k.m: They lived in bands of fifty where everyone was a cousin. Try it with eight million strangers.

k.f: Hobbes was afraid of everything and built a philosophy so it would be the government’s job.
k.m: He lived through a civil war. The fear was a field observation.

t.t: “Rational people would give a sovereign all power”

k.f: Locke’s reply: nobody escapes polecats by handing themselves to a lion. Unchecked power recreates the insecurity it was meant to end.
k.m: Divided power is how the war he lived through began: two authorities each claiming the last word. A lion is one danger and a pack is many.

k.f: Nobody rational signs a contract with no exit clause. He described the worst lease in history and called it reason.
k.m: The exit clause is the state of nature. You can always go back. People don’t.

k.f: Hobbes’s solution to “people are dangerous” is to give one of them everything.
k.m: One you can predict beats a thousand you can’t.

k.f: That’s either false, since people sacrifice for others, or made true by redescribing every motive as self-interest, which empties it.
k.m: He needs less than egoism: only that enough people may be dangerous and nobody can tell which. Distrust alone gets the argument going.

k.f: Then Hobbes only wrote the book for himself, and there’s no reason to believe it.
k.m: He wrote it for his own safety and yours. They happened to coincide. That’s the book.

k.f: Hobbes thought people were wolves, and he’d only met Englishmen.
k.m: You lock your door at night. Who do you think is out there, by your account?

k.f: If nothing obliges before the covenant, nothing obliges anyone to keep it. His answer to the man who breaks it when it’s safe has never convinced many.
k.m: His answer is that the man who breaks faith can’t be let into any group that knows it, so he’s betting his life on never being found out.

k.f: A promise only counts if promises already count. He needed the thing to build the thing.
k.m: Promises count once there’s something to make them count. That’s the thing being built.

k.f: The social contract: nobody saw it, nobody signed it, everybody owes.
k.m: You renew it every day you call the police instead of a cousin.

k.f: The trade assumes the sovereign delivers order. Absolute regimes have been major sources of violence against their own subjects.
k.m: He never says the sovereign is safe. He says the alternative is worse, and the worst modern death rates do come from places where the state collapsed.

k.f: The most orderly place there is, is a cemetery.
k.m: A cemetery is what you get without order. That was his whole point.

k.f: Leviathan is a very long way of saying “do what you’re told.”
k.m: It’s a long way of saying what happens when nobody can tell anyone anything.

t.t: “Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains”

k.f: The noble savage doesn’t fit the evidence on violence in societies without states, and he admitted the state of nature may never have existed.
k.m: He says outright that the state of nature is a hypothesis for separating what’s natural from what’s made. The claim it supports is that existing chains are no fact of nature.

k.f: Babies are born unable to hold their own heads up. “Free” is a stretch.
k.m: He means no one is born a subject or a master. The baby’s neck was never the claim.

k.f: Man is born free, and Rousseau left all five of his at the orphanage.
k.m: He said so himself, in print, with shame. The argument doesn’t depend on his being fit to make it.

k.f: With no procedure to tell the general will from the majority’s, or from a ruler’s claim to speak for it, the doctrine licenses coercion in the people’s name.
k.m: He gives conditions: general laws only, no factions, informed citizens, rough equality. Where they fail he says the vote doesn’t express it. Those are demanding standards.

k.f: If it’s always right there’s no need to vote, and that’s where everyone who used the idea ended up.
k.m: It’s found by voting. The vote is the procedure. People who skipped the voting weren’t using his idea.

k.f: “Forced to be free” is a sentence a person wrote down and kept.
k.m: It means the law you gave yourself can be enforced on you. Every speed limit does it.

k.f: That the arts and sciences ruined morals is argued from selected history. Trends in health, literacy and violence point the other way.
k.m: The later books refine it. Progress in knowledge and comfort is real, and it came with dependence, vanity and inequality. He’s asking about the cost.

k.f: He wrote that for an essay contest, at a desk, with a pen, and took the prize.
k.m: He won an essay contest by saying essay contests make people worse. He knew. That’s the joke, and he was in on it.

k.f: Rousseau said society ruins people, and every society that took him in came to agree, about him.
k.m: They took him in, lionized him, then threw stones at his house. That’s about what he predicted.

k.f: Inequalities of status and power exist among foragers with little property, and property rights also support the investment that reduces want.
k.m: He separates natural differences from the kind that needs other people’s agreement. Status among foragers isn’t rent, debt or inheritance.

k.f: The first man to fence a plot also grew more food on it. That part gets left out.
k.m: And then needed guards for it. More food and the first guard arrived in the same season.

k.f: Voltaire read it and said it made him want to walk on all fours.
k.m: Voltaire made a joke. That was his method with everything he couldn’t answer.

k.f: The “natural” education is stage-managed in detail by a tutor who arranges the child’s whole world. The freedom is an appearance.
k.m: The tutor arranges the world so the child meets things before words about them. All teaching arranges something, and this kind hides the hand so the child reasons.

k.f: Kids following nature eat dirt.
k.m: Eating dirt once is how a child learns about dirt. That’s the method.

k.f: He wrote the great book on raising children, having declined to try it.
k.m: He says in the book that a man who can’t do a father’s duty has no right to be one. He knew who he meant.

t.t: “It’s better to be feared than loved”

k.f: He adds: only if both can’t be had, and above all avoid being hated. His other book praises republics where rulers depend on the people.
k.m: Yes, that’s the actual view, and it’s better than the slogan: fear without hatred, cruelty used once and briefly, and the people’s support as the only real fortress.

k.f: Feared rulers get poisoned. Loved ones get statues. He didn’t run the numbers.
k.m: Loved rulers get poisoned by the people closest to them. He ran the numbers on Rome, emperor by emperor.

k.f: Machiavelli wrote the manual on keeping power after losing his job.
k.m: He lost it for serving a republic loyally. Then he wrote down what he’d seen.

t.t: “Politics should be judged by results, not private morality”

k.f: Results for whom is the question. If only the prince’s safety counts the view is self-serving, and if the common good counts it’s a morality after all.
k.m: He means the survival of the state and the safety of the people in it. A ruler with clean hands who loses the city has failed the people he was responsible for.

k.f: If results are the standard, his own were prison and unemployment. By Machiavelli, don’t read Machiavelli.
k.m: He kept Florence’s republic alive for fourteen years with no army and no money. The exile came when someone else’s troops arrived.

k.f: The Prince is a cover letter. He didn’t get the job.
k.m: The best cover letter ever written. Still read after five hundred years.

t.t: “The Prince is realism, not a defense of tyranny”

k.f: The reading on which it’s secretly satire has little support in the text. The book advises on taking and holding power, whatever his republican sympathies elsewhere.
k.m: Agreed, it isn’t satire. It describes what holding power requires so that it can be done with the least cruelty. The moralizing manuals around it described nothing.

k.f: When a book has to be explained as secretly meaning the opposite, the book said it.
k.m: It means what it says: this is how it’s done. Not liking that is different from finding a secret meaning.

k.f: Every guy who says The Prince is satire owns it in hardcover.
k.m: In hardcover, and so do the people who say it’s evil. Somebody’s reading it.

k.f: His own model undercuts it. Cesare Borgia is ruined by his father’s death and one misjudgment, and Machiavelli has to call it bad luck.
k.m: He says fortune rules about half of what we do. Borgia is the example of how much skill achieves and where it stops, and the chapter says both.

k.f: His model prince was Cesare Borgia, who lost everything within about a year. That’s the case study.
k.m: He built a state out of nothing in three years and was undone by falling ill the week his father died. That’s the half that’s fortune.

k.f: Cesare Borgia followed the advice before it was written and died at 31 in an ambush.
k.m: At 31 he’d done more than most dynasties.

k.f: Hard-headed description of power is older than him, and his method is anecdote from Roman history and recent memory, not anything systematic.
k.m: The step was the question he asked: what actually happens, and what follows from it. Earlier writers described rulers as they ought to be.

k.f: Science has data. He had stories about Romans.
k.m: Cases are data. He compared Rome, Sparta, Venice and Florence on the same questions, which is the method.

k.f: Machiavelli is the favorite philosopher of men who manage six people.
k.m: And of the six people. They read it to see what he’s up to.

t.t: “Mix your labor with something and it’s yours”

k.f: Nozick’s question: if I pour my tomato juice into the sea, do I own the sea or lose my juice? Why mixing labor yields ownership is never shown.
k.m: The labor argument comes with limits he states: enough and as good left for others, and nothing taken to spoil. The juice case ignores the first.

k.f: I painted a fence once. I don’t own the fence. I asked.
k.m: You were paid for the fence. You sold the labor. That’s in the theory.

k.f: Locke’s theory of property is that whoever got there first and did some gardening owns it forever.
k.m: Whoever worked it and left enough for others. The second clause does a lot.

t.t: “Government rests on the consent of the governed”

k.f: Almost nobody has consented. Tacit consent by staying put, as Hume said, is like saying a man pressed onto a ship consents by not jumping overboard.
k.m: Tacit consent is his weak point. The standard it sets isn’t: a government that couldn’t be justified to the people under it has no claim on them.

k.f: Nobody asked me. Nobody asked anyone. The consent is theoretical and the taxes aren’t.
k.m: Nobody asked, and that’s the test your government is failing.

k.f: Tacit consent: you agreed by being here. Check the terms and conditions of standing on a road.
k.m: Staying is the weak version and he knew it. Full membership, he says, takes express consent.

t.t: “There’s a right to revolution when government breaks its trust”

k.f: With no judge of when the trust is broken except the people rebelling, the right amounts to: revolutions are justified when they succeed.
k.m: He answers that the people judge, and that they’re slow to it: they bear a long train of abuses before stirring. Rulers who break the trust are the rebels.

k.f: Who decides the trust was broken? Whoever wins. So it’s a right that’s awarded afterwards, like a trophy.
k.m: Whoever wins is who decides under every theory. His says which side was in the right before the result.

k.f: Locke defended the right to revolution, published it anonymously, and denied writing it until he died.
k.m: Men were being hanged for manuscripts that said less. Anonymous was prudent.

t.t: “Toleration should extend to all peaceful beliefs”

k.f: His own letter excludes Catholics and atheists. The principle is narrower in his hands than in his admirers’.
k.m: The exclusions were about allegiance to a foreign power and oath-keeping. His own principle, that belief can’t be forced, later overturned both.

k.f: All beliefs should be tolerated, except two, which were the two he didn’t like.
k.m: He excluded two groups on grounds that turned out to be false. The argument he built removed the exclusions.

k.f: The philosopher of liberty held shares in the Royal African Company and helped write a slave constitution for Carolina.
k.m: He did. The same texts were quoted by the people who ended it.

t.t: “Power may be used over someone only to prevent harm to others”

k.f: “Harm” is the contested term. Almost any conduct affects others somehow, so the principle settles little until harm is defined, and Mill doesn’t.
k.m: He specifies it in practice: harm to interests that ought to be treated as rights. The principle rules out one class of reasons, the person’s own good.

k.f: Everything affects somebody. Under the harm principle either nothing’s allowed or the word “harm” is doing a quiet shift.
k.m: Affecting someone isn’t harming them. He draws the line at their protected interests, in chapter four.

k.f: The harm principle is “mind your own business,” with exceptions to be announced.
k.m: With the exceptions listed. Most people don’t get as far as the list.

k.f: Markets in ideas reward what’s vivid and flattering as much as what’s true. The evidence that open debate reliably sorts them is thin.
k.m: He never promises truth wins quickly. He says suppression assumes infallibility, and even true beliefs go dead when nobody may challenge them.

k.f: The internet is the freest discussion in history. Check on how the truth is doing.
k.m: And every correction of those falsehoods is on the same internet. Try the version with a censor.

k.f: Mill thought the best argument wins. He’d never seen a comment section.
k.m: He saw the Victorian pamphlet wars. He’d recognize it.

k.f: Some experiments impose costs on children and neighbors who didn’t volunteer, and a society can reasonably decline to run them all.
k.m: The harm principle already covers those cases: children and neighbors are others. The liberty is for what’s left over.

k.f: Experiments have control groups and ethics boards. He meant “let me do what I want,” with a lab coat on it.
k.m: He meant that nobody knows in advance which ways of living are good. A lab coat fits fine.

k.f: On Liberty: everyone should be free to live as they like, by a man who spent his career administering India.
k.m: He drafted the company’s defense, and its critics won. He then spent a career arguing for the losers of other fights.

t.t: “Better Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied”

k.f: The judges are people who’ve known both pleasures, but someone formed by one kind of life can’t fairly sample the other. The test is rigged toward the examiner.
k.m: It’s the best test available: ask those who know both. The alternative is a judge who knows one side only.

k.f: The fool is satisfied. That’s the whole point of being satisfied. Mill lost and wrote it down as a win.
k.m: The fool doesn’t know what he’s missing. That’s the argument.

k.f: “Better to be Socrates dissatisfied” is a sentence only ever said by people who think they’re Socrates.
k.m: He’d had a breakdown at twenty from a life of pure intellect, and poetry got him out. He’d tried both.

t.t: “The invisible hand turns self-interest into public good”

k.f: It does under conditions he listed and his admirers skip: competition, information and no power to rig the game. He was scathing about merchants.
k.m: That is the claim: under competition and with justice enforced, self-interest serves the public. The conditions are part of it, and he listed them.

k.f: If self-interest produced public good, burglars would be philanthropists.
k.m: Burglary isn’t exchange. He said self-interest within the rules of justice, and it’s in the sentence.

k.f: The invisible hand appears once in The Wealth of Nations. One time. In a book of a thousand pages.
k.m: Once was enough. Newton states the law of gravity once too.

t.t: “The division of labor is the source of wealth”

k.f: He also wrote that it makes the worker as stupid and ignorant as a human can become, and called for public schooling to offset it.
k.m: He saw the cost and prescribed the remedy in the same book: public education. Naming a trade-off and paying for the fix is what you want from an economist.

k.f: He said the pin factory makes pins faster and makes the men idiots. Same book. Nobody quotes the second half.
k.m: Same book, and then he says what to do about it. That’s the half his critics don’t quote.

k.f: Smith’s proof of capitalism is a factory that makes pins.
k.m: Eighteen operations, ten men, forty-eight thousand pins a day. It’s a good proof.

k.f: He supported regulation of banks, usury limits, public works and taxes that fall on the rich. The laissez-faire Smith is a later invention.
k.m: He’s for markets freed from the privileges merchants arrange for themselves, with a state that does justice, defense and public works. The cartoon belongs to his fans.

k.f: Smith wanted bank regulation and progressive taxes. His fans haven’t read him. He’s the Marx of the right.
k.m: Smith is against monopoly, tariffs and merchants writing the law. That’s still the right-wing position where there is one.

k.f: Everyone who cites Adam Smith has read the same one paragraph.
k.m: The book is a thousand pages and every one of them is against somebody’s subsidy.

k.f: Sympathy is partial and fades with distance. He patches it with an imagined impartial spectator, who brings in a standard sympathy doesn’t supply.
k.m: The spectator is built from sympathy: we learn to see ourselves as others see us and correct for bias. The standard grows out of the feeling.

k.f: We sympathize with people like us. So it’s a theory of being nice to your friends, which was not in short supply.
k.m: We start with friends and learn to imagine a stranger watching. That’s how anyone has ever become fair.

k.f: The father of economics lived with his mother.
k.m: And wrote two of the most important books of the century at her house.

t.t: “No planner can have the knowledge that prices carry”

k.f: Prices miss what isn’t traded, like pollution and future generations, and large firms plan internally at vast scale without collapsing.
k.m: Firms plan inside a market that tells them, through profit and loss, when the plan is wrong. Take that away and you have the plan without the correction.

k.f: Walmart is a planned economy bigger than most countries. It plans every shelf. Somebody tell the knowledge problem.
k.m: Walmart buys and sells at market prices and loses money when it guesses wrong. The prices are what it plans with.

k.f: Hayek proved central planning is impossible, and then logistics software happened.
k.m: The software runs on prices set by rivals. Remove them and it has nothing to optimize.

t.t: “Economic planning is the road to serfdom”

k.f: Postwar Western Europe built large welfare states with heavy planning and stayed free. The slide he predicted didn’t happen.
k.m: The book warns about central direction of production. He says in it that a safety net and regulation are compatible with freedom, and Europe built those.

k.f: Sweden’s been on the road to serfdom for ninety years. Lovely road. Bike lanes.
k.m: Sweden has free trade, private firms and school vouchers. That’s the road he recommended.

k.f: The Road to Serfdom predicted Britain would turn totalitarian. It got the NHS.
k.m: He supported a basic minimum and health insurance in that book. Britain nationalized steel and reversed it.

k.f: Markets rest on designed institutions: property law, courts, central banks. “Spontaneous” order had a lot of drafting behind it.
k.m: He includes law in the order: common-law rules grown case by case, which no one drafted whole. Legislation tidies what custom found.

k.f: Nothing about a stock exchange is spontaneous. It has a rulebook and a building.
k.m: The rulebook records practices traders had already worked out. It came after.

k.f: Spontaneous order: nobody planned it, except all the people who wrote the laws.
k.m: The laws were mostly writing down what people were already doing.

k.f: That no one intended a distribution doesn’t make it beyond assessment. We judge unintended outcomes of systems we could change all the time.
k.m: We can judge and change rules. His point is that calling an unplanned outcome “unjust” implies a culprit, and it licenses someone to assign shares.

k.f: Nobody intended traffic deaths either, and there’s still a department for it.
k.m: Traffic deaths get reduced by rules that apply to everyone. He’s for that. He’s against deciding who should arrive first.

k.f: He said liberty mattered most, and he preferred a liberal dictator to a democracy that wasn’t liberal. He said that about Chile, out loud.
k.m: It was a bad thing to say. His argument against central planning doesn’t depend on it.

k.f: Later research suggests Eichmann was a committed ideologue who performed the dull clerk at trial. The thesis may fit some functionaries and not its famous example.
k.m: She may have misread Eichmann. The thesis doesn’t need him: most of the people who made it run were clerks, drivers and schedulers who never asked.

k.f: The recordings came out. He was a true believer and proud of it. She watched a performance and reviewed it as real.
k.m: A true believer who talks entirely in clichés and office-speak is still her specimen.

k.f: The banality of evil is the most quoted idea ever based on misjudging one man in a glass booth.
k.m: Take him out and the camps were still staffed by thousands who were only doing a job.

t.t: “Totalitarianism is a wholly new form of government”

k.f: Putting Nazism and Stalinism under one concept flattens deep differences in ideology and structure, and historians of each have resisted it.
k.m: She compares structures: terror as a method, ideology as logic, the camps as the central institution. The two differed in content and matched on those.

k.f: Every tyranny in history felt new to the people in it. She had a better publisher.
k.m: Tyrants wanted obedience. These wanted to remake what a person is, and built institutions for it.

k.f: “Unprecedented” is what every generation calls its own disasters.
k.m: She gave reasons, at five hundred pages.

t.t: “Politics is action among equals, distinct from the social”

k.f: Separating the political from questions of poverty and work leaves politics oddly empty, and she was criticized for what that separation made her say about schools and welfare.
k.m: The distinction protects something: a space where people decide together as equals, which administration by experts can’t supply. She misapplied it in places.

k.f: Politics that isn’t about who gets what is a book club.
k.m: Who gets what can be settled by a spreadsheet. Whether we’re the kind of people who settle it that way is politics.

k.f: Arendt’s ideal politics is ancient Athens, minus the part where most people there couldn’t take part.
k.m: Athens for the form. She’s explicit that the question is how to have it without the exclusions.

k.f: Highly educated, reflective people have joined and led terrible movements. Whatever protects against that, thoughtfulness alone isn’t it.
k.m: She means the habit of stopping to ask whether you could live with yourself afterwards. It differs from intelligence, and the clever joined in numbers.

k.f: Plenty of the people in charge had doctorates. Some had read philosophy. One had taught her.
k.m: Doctorates measure cleverness. She says cleverness is no protection at all.

k.f: “Evil comes from not thinking,” wrote the best student of a man who thought a great deal and joined anyway.
k.m: That’s why she drew the distinction. She’d seen the cleverest man she knew fail it.

t.t: “Sovereign is he who decides on the exception”

k.f: Constitutional states handle emergencies under rules, with review afterwards. That someone could seize the decision doesn’t make the seizure the essence of law.
k.m: Emergency powers written into law still need someone to say when they apply and when they end. That decision can’t be fully written down in advance.

k.f: So the law is whoever breaks it most successfully. Every coup leader agrees with him, which should bother him more than it did.
k.m: Every coup leader agrees because it describes what happens. A theory isn’t refuted by who finds it accurate.

k.f: Schmitt’s theory is that the rules only count until somebody important doesn’t feel like it.
k.m: It’s a theory of what’s underneath the rules on the day they’re tested.

t.t: “Politics is the distinction between friend and enemy”

k.f: That describes politics at its worst and leaves out bargaining, coalition and persuasion, which is most of what it is.
k.m: He says it’s the limiting case that gives politics its seriousness. Bargaining goes on in the shadow of the possibility that it fails.

k.f: If politics is friends against enemies, a city council meeting about parking isn’t politics. That’s most of politics.
k.m: The council’s decision is enforced, in the end, by police. Parking is downstream of who has that power.

k.f: The friend–enemy distinction is high school with armies.
k.m: High school has no monopoly on force. That’s the missing ingredient.

t.t: “Liberalism only postpones decisions with endless talk”

k.f: Talk and procedure are how decisions get made without bloodshed. That it’s slow is the cost of that, not evidence that it’s empty.
k.m: His claim is narrower: when the divide is over what kind of state to be, procedure can’t settle it, because the procedure is what’s in dispute.

k.f: The alternative to endless discussion was tried in his country, in his lifetime, with his help.
k.m: The other option showed the diagnosis right and the cure monstrous. Both are true.

k.f: He complained that parliaments just talk, and then found out what the other option was.
k.m: He described a parliament that couldn’t govern in 1923. It then failed to.

t.t: “His diagnosis stands apart from his politics”

k.f: He joined the Nazi party in 1933, defended the purge killings in print, and never recanted. The theory of the exception was the one he applied.
k.m: What he did is on the record and it was vile. Thinkers on the left and right still use the analysis because it describes what constitutional texts leave out.

k.f: He had a theory about what politics is and then a chance to use it, and he joined the party in 1933.
k.m: Applied by a careerist with no decency. The theory says someone decides. It doesn’t say they’ll be any good.

k.f: People cite Schmitt “for the critique,” the way people read certain magazines for the articles.
k.m: Liberal lawyers assign him to learn what a constitution has to be defended against.

t.t: “Workers should control the means of production”

k.f: Worker cooperatives are legal and exist, and they stay a small share of firms. That suggests costs in raising capital, sharing risk and deciding things that the argument has to face.
k.m: Co-ops that get going survive as long as other firms and pay better. The obstacle is at the start: banks lend against ownership, and workers have none.

k.f: Nobody’s stopping them. A co-op takes a form and a bank account. The revolution is available at the county clerk.
k.m: A form and a bank account, and then a loan no bank will make to people with no collateral. The clerk isn’t the obstacle.

k.f: Workers can already own the means of production. It’s called buying stock.
k.m: With what? The bottom half owns about one percent of it.

t.t: “Planning can beat markets at meeting needs”

k.f: The calculation problem: without prices that come from exchange, planners lack the information to allocate capital sensibly, and computing power doesn’t supply the missing data.
k.m: The modern proposal isn’t one ministry. It’s public ownership with markets or with democratic planning by sector, and every large firm already plans internally.

k.f: The Soviet Union had the best mathematicians alive and a shortage of soap.
k.m: They also put the first satellite up and taught a country to read in a generation. The soap was a choice of priorities.

k.f: Socialism works until someone has to decide how many shoes.
k.m: Amazon decides how many shoes, for every size in every city. It can be done.

k.f: Those are market economies with private ownership, free trade and high taxes. Their own leaders have rejected the label.
k.m: They got there through the strongest unions on earth and decades of socialist governments. Markets were part of it, and so was the labor movement the label refers to.

k.f: Sweden has more billionaires per person than America. That’s the model.
k.m: With union density above sixty percent and a welfare state he’d have to pay into. Take the billionaires and the bargaining together.

k.f: Denmark’s prime minister asked people to stop calling it socialist.
k.m: He asked Americans to stop. The party that built it is called the Social Democrats.

k.f: What matters may be whether everyone has enough, not the gap. And some inequalities come from choices people are entitled to make.
k.m: Enough for everyone would be a start. Large gaps also buy political power and turn into unequal chances for the next generation, so the gap matters too.

k.f: If inequality were injustice, the tallest person in every room would owe something.
k.m: Nobody’s height comes out of anybody else’s. Wealth gets made in a workplace, by more than one person.

k.f: Everyone’s a socialist until they have something.
k.m: Most socialists have something. They want to keep it and want you to have it too.

k.f: Profit signals where resources meet wants, and systems that suppressed it didn’t serve needs better. The slogan opposes two things that aren’t opposites.
k.m: Profit tracks what people can pay for. Insulin and yachts send different signals, and that’s the complaint.

k.f: Bakeries feed more people for profit than any ministry of bread has for free.
k.m: Bakeries don’t feed people who can’t pay. That gap gets filled by somebody not making a profit.

k.f: Socialism is when the government does stuff. Its fans love that definition.
k.m: It’s when workers own things. The government part is your definition.

k.f: The efficiency results hold under conditions, such as full information and no spillover costs, that fail in health care, climate and finance.
k.m: Those failures are the textbook exceptions and each has a market-compatible fix: price the pollution, disclose the risk. Every other system fails without any exception clause.

k.f: If markets were efficient there’d be no marketing department. Half the economy is persuading people the prices are right.
k.m: Marketing is information about what exists. The alternative is one kind of soap and a queue.

k.f: The invisible hand needed a bailout in 2008.
k.m: And the planned economies needed a bailout from 1989 onward.

k.f: The largest falls came in state-directed economies like China’s. Crediting capitalism as such ignores industrial policy, public health and schooling.
k.m: China’s poverty fell when it let farmers sell their crops and firms keep profits. The state was there before 1978 too, and so was the poverty.

k.f: Poverty went down while capitalism was around. So did smoking.
k.m: Poverty fell fastest exactly where and when markets opened, country by country. Smoking didn’t follow that schedule.

k.f: The line goes up. Nobody asks whose line.
k.m: The line for the poorest billion went up most of all. That’s whose.

k.f: That holds in the textbook competitive market. Bargaining power, dominant employers and luck drive much of pay, and “contribution” is hard to define for joint work.
k.m: Not perfectly. Over time and across countries, pay follows productivity closely, and the gaps people point to are mostly cases where competition is being blocked.

k.f: A fund manager makes a thousand times what a nurse does, so he contributes a thousand nurses. Count them.
k.m: One manager’s decision moves a billion dollars of other people’s savings. A mistake that size is worth paying to avoid.

k.f: The market pays people what they’re worth, which is why the richest man posts all day.
k.m: He was paid for the rockets and the cars. The posting is free, and you get what you pay for.

t.t: “Free exchange is voluntary, so it’s just”

k.f: Whether it’s voluntary depends on the alternatives. A choice among bad options made out of need isn’t free in the sense justice requires.
k.m: The bad options aren’t made by the employer who adds one. Taking away the offer leaves the person with the same need and one choice fewer.

k.f: “Take the job or starve” has the same structure as “your money or your life,” and only one of them gets called freedom.
k.m: The mugger takes away an option you had. The employer adds one you didn’t. That’s the whole structure.

k.f: It’s voluntary. They could always not eat.
k.m: In every other system they also had to eat, and there was less of it.

k.f: Many core technologies came from public money, including the internet, GPS and much drug research, and incumbents often profit by suppressing competition.
k.m: The research was public and sat on shelves. Turning it into something a billion people can afford took firms that would go broke if they got it wrong.

k.f: The iPhone is a pile of government research in a nice case.
k.m: The government had all those parts for decades and didn’t make a phone.

k.f: Innovation: the same app, with a subscription now.
k.m: The phone in your hand would have been a supercomputer in 1995. Complain on it.

k.f: Property rights are defined by a legal system that taxes pay for. There’s no pre-tax ownership to steal from.
k.m: If rights were only what law defines, nothing a legal system did to property could be unjust. People do judge confiscations unjust, so some claim comes first.

k.f: Theft is illegal and taxes are legal, so it’s not theft. That’s what the word means.
k.m: Slavery was legal. Legal isn’t the test of whether something is taken by force.

k.f: Libertarians hate the government and love the roads, the courts, the patents and the police.
k.m: I use the road because it’s the only one they allowed. Using the monopoly isn’t endorsing it.

k.f: Getting from owning oneself to full ownership of land and resources needs a rule of first acquisition, and Locke’s own rule, taken seriously, limits holdings a great deal.
k.m: The acquisition problem is real, and every theory of property has one. This one at least starts from a premise most people accept: that nobody else owns you.

k.f: If you own yourself you can sell yourself. So the theory starts at freedom and reaches slavery in two steps.
k.m: You can also choose not to sell. A right you may waive is still a right. You can give away your books too.

k.f: The non-aggression principle is a great rule as long as the libertarian decides what counts as aggression.
k.m: And the state’s rule is fine so long as the state decides what counts as a crime.

k.f: Nozick’s derivation pays off the people who never signed up in a way critics found improvised, and it rules out public goods most people would agree to fund.
k.m: Whatever one makes of the derivation, the conclusion stands as a burden: each further function has to be justified to the people forced to pay for it.

k.f: A state that only does police, courts and army is a state made entirely of men with guns. That’s the freedom one.
k.m: Men with guns who aren’t permitted to do anything but stop other men with guns. The limit is the freedom part.

k.f: Minimal state: just the parts that protect what they own.
k.m: And what you own. Courts work for tenants too.

k.f: Spillover costs, unequal information and collective action problems are textbook cases where voluntary exchange falls short, and the era before regulation supplies examples.
k.m: Many of those failures have property-rights fixes, and regulators fail as well, often at the request of the firms they regulate. Compare real markets with real agencies.

k.f: Before regulation, milk had chalk in it. The market had decades and chose chalk.
k.m: The chalk ended when buyers could sue and newspapers could print brand names. Liability law did that.

k.f: Somalia had no government for twenty years and nobody moved there.
k.m: Somalia had warlords, which is several governments. Its phone network did improve, as it happens.

k.f: Private power can constrain as well as the state can, and a purely negative idea of liberty counts the destitute as fully free.
k.m: Poverty is a serious evil and it’s a different one. Folding it into “unfreedom” lets coercion be justified as liberation, which is how that argument has usually been used.

k.f: A man alone in the desert is completely free of coercion. He’s the freest man alive, for about two days.
k.m: Free and dead of thirst are different words. He’s free. He’s also in trouble. Both are true and only one is my topic.

k.f: Libertarianism is a phase between the first paycheck and the first kid.
k.m: The kid is why the tax bill matters more.

t.t: “No one has the right to rule another”

k.f: Legitimacy might rest on fair procedures or the benefits of coordination, not consent. With no authority at all, collective decisions bind nobody.
k.m: Procedures bind those who took part in them. Anarchists don’t reject organization or decisions. They reject orders backed by force from people you can’t recall.

k.f: Somebody has to decide which side of the road. That’s ruling. It starts there.
k.m: People settled which side of the road by convention before any traffic law existed. That’s coordination. Ruling is the fine.

k.f: Anarchism works great until the second person shows up.
k.m: The second person is a neighbor. You’re thinking of the third one, with the badge.

k.f: Voluntary cooperation works in small groups that deal with each other repeatedly. Large anonymous societies have free-rider and enforcement problems it hasn’t solved.
k.m: Scale is the open problem, and federation is the proposed answer: small units, recallable delegates. Large voluntary networks exist, from the Red Cross to open-source software.

k.f: Every group project.
k.m: The group project fails when a teacher assigned the groups. People who chose each other finish.

k.f: An anarchist commune is a homeowners association with worse meetings.
k.m: An HOA has a board, fines and a lien on your house. That’s the thing we’re against.

t.t: “Catalonia and the Zapatistas show it works”

k.f: These were short-lived or local, relied on wartime conditions and their own coercion, and Catalonia was crushed. They show mobilization, not lasting order.
k.m: Being crushed by two armies and betrayed by a third isn’t evidence it didn’t work. While it stood, factories and farms ran and output held.

k.f: The best example lasted under a year and lost. That’s the highlight reel.
k.m: It lost to Franco, Hitler’s air force and Stalin’s police at once. That’s a strong opponent list for a pilot program.

k.f: Anarchism’s golden age was ten months in 1936.
k.m: Ten months in which several million people ran a region. Your system needed a century to get the trains running.

t.t: “Hierarchy is the root of social problems”

k.f: Some hierarchy is useful and agreed to. “Unjustified hierarchy” pushes the question to what justifies, where anarchists differ from liberals less than advertised.
k.m: The test is the one stated: authority has to justify itself to those under it and be removable. A surgeon passes. A landlord has to make the case.

k.f: An operating room with no hierarchy is five people holding the knife.
k.m: The patient picked the surgeon and can fire him. That’s the kind of authority anarchists have always accepted.

k.f: Every anarchist group has a guy who’s in charge of saying nobody’s in charge.
k.m: He rotates out next month. That’s the difference between a facilitator and a boss.

k.f: Proudhon also wrote that property is freedom. The slogan targets absentee owners, and without secure possession the reasons to build and maintain things collapse.
k.m: He distinguished possession, what you use and live in, from property, a title to charge others for what you don’t use. Possession is the one he called freedom.

k.f: If property is theft, it was stolen from an owner, so there was property first. The sentence needs the thing it bans.
k.m: It was held in common before the first fence. You can steal from everyone.

k.f: Property is theft, and somebody’s still mad about their bike.
k.m: The bike is a possession. The building it’s chained to is the property.

k.f: Traditions also carry accumulated error and the interests of whoever shaped them. The argument needs a way to tell which is which, and offers deference.
k.m: The claim is a presumption: what has survived generations of trial has passed a test no new plan has. The burden sits with the reformer, and it can be met.

k.f: Every tradition was new once, and somebody conservative was against it.
k.m: And the tradition absorbed the changes that worked. That’s the filter running.

k.f: Conservatism is defending the last thing liberals did.
k.m: Somebody has to check which of them were mistakes. You’re welcome.

k.f: Doing nothing has unintended consequences too. A presumption for things as they are counts existing harms at zero.
k.m: Existing harms are known and bounded. The harms of a sweeping change aren’t, and they can’t be undone. Preferring the reversible step is a view about risk.

k.f: The fence was put up by a guy who also didn’t know why the last fence was there.
k.m: He put it up because the cattle kept getting out. Somebody remembers. Ask before you pull it.

k.f: Chesterton’s fence: nobody can touch anything until they’ve done a history degree.
k.m: A history degree is about four years. The fence took four centuries.

t.t: “Free markets and traditional values go together”

k.f: Markets are the great solvent of tradition, through mobility, consumerism and constant upheaval. The pairing is a coalition, not a coherent philosophy.
k.m: The tension is real, and conservatives have said so for a century. Family, church and local ties are what make a market society livable, which is why they get defended.

k.f: The market sells whatever people buy, and they are not buying tradition.
k.m: People buy tradition every December, and at every wedding and funeral.

k.f: Conservatives want small government and a list of things for it to ban.
k.m: A short list. Yours is longer, it just has different things on it.

t.t: “Burke was right about the French Revolution”

k.f: He foresaw the Terror, and he also defended an old regime whose injustices produced the revolution, about which he had little to say.
k.m: He’d defended the Americans, the Irish and India against his own government. His objection was to tearing down every institution at once in the name of a theory.

k.f: France is a republic with rights and the metric system. Burke’s side is a gift shop at Versailles.
k.m: France took five republics, two empires and a terror to get there. Britain reformed and skipped that part.

k.f: Burke predicted the Revolution would go badly. He predicted that about everything, so it’s one hit.
k.m: He predicted the Terror, the wars and a general in 1790. That’s three.

t.t: “Society is a pact among the dead, the living and the unborn”

k.f: The dead and the unborn can’t speak, so the idea hands their vote to whoever is invoking them.
k.m: It works as a restraint on the living: you aren’t the owner of what you inherited, only a tenant with duties in both directions.

k.f: The dead don’t pay taxes and the unborn don’t vote. It’s a partnership where two of the three partners are unavailable for comment.
k.m: The unborn are exactly who gets the bill for whatever’s decided today. They’re the most affected party in the room.

k.f: Conservatism has been losing slowly for three hundred years and calls it prudence.
k.m: Three hundred years of losing slowly is called surviving.

k.f: “The people” don’t have a single will. Voting theory shows that no way of adding up preferences reliably gives a coherent collective one.
k.m: No voting rule is perfect, and that’s a result about every way of deciding together, juntas and committees included. Elections remain the one where losers accept the result.

k.f: The people ruled in Athens, and they voted to execute Socrates and invade Sicily. Two for two.
k.m: Athens also lasted two centuries, beat Persia and invented most of what you’re citing. Two bad votes in two hundred years.

k.f: The best argument against democracy is five minutes with the average voter. Churchill never said that, which most voters don’t know either.
k.m: Five minutes with the average king would settle that one.

k.f: Voter ignorance is well documented, and it’s rational given how little one vote weighs. Some argue it tilts policy in predictable ways.
k.m: Voters lack detail and still do the one job that matters: noticing when things go badly and removing those in charge. No other system manages that.

k.f: Most people can’t name their representative. They’re governing themselves the way a passenger is flying the plane.
k.m: The passenger doesn’t fly the plane. He picks the airline and stops using it after a crash. That’s the job.

k.f: Half the electorate is below average, and they all show up.
k.m: Half of every profession is below average, including the one that writes about voters.

k.f: That’s a comparative factual claim. Some non-democracies have done better on growth and state capacity, and the verdict depends on which goods are weighed.
k.m: Those regimes do well under a good ruler and catastrophically under the next one. The case is the worst outcome avoided, and averages hide it.

k.f: “Least bad” is what people say about the only one they’ve tried.
k.m: Every alternative has been tried, for most of history, by most of the world. That’s why they stopped.

k.f: “The worst system except for all the others” is a joke, and people use it as the argument.
k.m: It’s a joke with a ninety-year track record.

k.f: Voters judge on the recent past and on irrelevant events. Studies find incumbents punished for droughts and rewarded for growth in election year.
k.m: Even crude punishment is feedback. Leaders who know they can be thrown out for a bad year behave differently from those who can’t be.

k.f: In the U.S. House, incumbents win about nine times in ten. That’s the accountability.
k.m: They win because they vote the way the district wants. Losing is the threat that makes them.

k.f: Elections: pick between two people chosen by people nobody elected.
k.m: And then you can fire one of them. Try that with the other kind.

k.f: Majorities can oppress lasting minorities, which is why constitutional democracies bind them with rights and courts that the majority can’t overrule.
k.m: Rights and courts are part of modern democracy, adopted by supermajorities. Binding yourself in advance is something majorities chose to do.

k.f: Two wolves and a sheep. Fair vote, clean count.
k.m: Under every other system it’s one wolf and nobody counts.

k.f: 51% of people can’t be wrong, according to 51% of people.
k.m: 51% can be wrong. They can also be outvoted next time. That’s the feature.

k.f: Peoples are intermingled and nations overlap, so the principle applied anywhere creates new minorities, and has done so at great cost.
