k.m: The principle is self-rule for peoples who want it. Where populations mix, it argues for autonomy and federation, and the worst cases came from denying both.

k.f: There are several thousand peoples and about two hundred states. Somebody’s doing the map in pen.
k.m: The map was drawn in pen by empires. Nationalism is the people on it asking to be consulted.

k.f: Nationalism: the people on this side of the river are completely different from the ones over there. Look, there’s a line.
k.m: The line is where one group of people agreed to pay for each other’s schools.

k.f: Most national identities were assembled in the last two centuries by schools, armies and newspapers, with traditions often invented for the purpose.
k.m: The modern form is recent. It was built from shared languages, stories and territory much older than the railway.

k.f: Most “ancient national traditions” date to about 1850. The kilt pattern was a marketing decision.
k.m: The kilt pattern is new. The language, the songs and the fact of being ruled from elsewhere weren’t.

k.f: Every nation’s eternal identity was invented around the time of the railway.
k.m: Invented the way a house is: by people, from materials already on the site.

t.t: “We owe more to compatriots than to strangers”

k.f: Special ties may justify some priority, but birthplace is as arbitrary as any trait, and the priority is rarely kept within decent bounds.
k.m: The priority comes from shared institutions: you pay into the same system and live under the same law. It’s the same kind of tie as family, at larger scale.

k.f: He owes more to a stranger four hundred miles north than to one four miles east, because of a river.
k.m: He and the man four hundred miles north fund each other’s hospitals. The river comes with a treasury.

k.f: Patriotism is the belief that your country is the best because you were born in it.
k.m: It’s the belief that your family is yours, extended. Nobody demands a ranking for that.

t.t: “Shared identity is what makes solidarity possible”

k.f: Solidarity also forms around class, religion, city and cause, and national feeling has divided societies as often as it has bound them.
k.m: Class and religion divide a country as readily as they unite it. A national “we” is the one that can include both sides of those.

k.f: The country with the strongest national feeling isn’t the one with the best welfare state. Check any list.
k.m: The strong welfare states were built when national feeling was high and trust followed it.

k.f: National unity is mostly agreeing on who doesn’t count.
k.m: Every “we” has an edge. Yours does too, and it just isn’t on a map.

t.t: “Capitalism can be tamed by the welfare state”

k.f: The arrangement depended on unusual postwar conditions: fast growth, strong unions and capital that couldn’t leave. All three have weakened.
k.m: The conditions changed and the model adapted: more training, portable benefits, public childcare. The countries that kept it are still the best places to be poor.

k.f: Capital can move now and the welfare state can’t. It’s a leash where the dog holds the other end.
k.m: Capital threatens to leave and mostly stays where the workers are skilled and the courts work.

k.f: Social democracy is capitalism with an apology.
k.m: An apology with paid parental leave and a pension attached.

t.t: “The Nordic model can be adopted anywhere”

k.f: It grew out of small, high-trust countries with strong unions and broad taxes on ordinary earners. Copying the spending without the rest hasn’t worked well.
k.m: The parts transfer separately: bargaining by sector, active job programs, universal services. Countries with none of the supposed prerequisites have adopted pieces and they worked.

k.f: Step one is to be five million people who all trust each other and have oil. Step two is easy.
k.m: Four of the five have no oil to speak of. Trust rose after the programs came in.

k.f: “Why can’t we be like Denmark?” Because Denmark is full of Danes who pay 25% sales tax and don’t complain.
k.m: The Danes complain constantly. They vote for it anyway.

t.t: “High taxes and strong growth can coexist”

k.f: They have, in some places, with tax systems that fall heavily on consumption and wages. That’s not the version usually on offer.
k.m: That is the honest version, and its advocates say it: everyone pays in and everyone gets it back in services. Broad taxes are why it’s stable.

k.f: The Nordics fund it by taxing the middle class a lot. That part gets left out of the brochure.
k.m: It’s in the brochure. Everyone pays and everyone gets childcare. The middle class comes out ahead.

k.f: The plan is Scandinavian services at American tax rates, and nobody will say which half is the joke.
k.m: Then the honest half is the taxes. Some of us do say so.

k.f: Reforms can be reversed as soon as the balance of power shifts, and many have been. What’s granted without changing ownership stays revocable.
k.m: Reforms that become universal are hard to reverse: nobody has abolished a public pension or a health service once people had it.

k.f: Every reform is one election from being undone. They’ve been rebuilding the same sandcastle since 1945.
k.m: The sandcastle is eighty years old and has a health service in it.

k.f: Social democrats have been one more election away from socialism for a hundred years.
k.m: A hundred years in which the working week halved and children left the mines. That’ll do.

t.t: “The truth is usually somewhere in the middle”

k.f: The midpoint depends on where the extremes happen to be, so it moves with whoever shouts loudest. It isn’t a method for finding anything.
k.m: The claim isn’t that you average. It’s that each camp tends to be right about what the other ignores, so a good policy usually has parts from both.

k.f: One guy says two plus two is four, another says six. The centrist says five and feels mature.
k.m: If one says four and the other says six, check the sum. The centrist is the one who checks.

k.f: Centrism is having no opinions, strongly.
k.m: Strong opinions about tax credits and zoning. They’re just boring ones.

k.f: Sometimes. As a standing rule it’s a way to avoid assessing which points are true, and symmetry is rarely what the evidence shows.
k.m: It’s a starting presumption, dropped when the evidence says so. The alternative is assuming one side has no point before looking.

k.f: Both sides had a point about whether the earth moves, too. One of the points was wrong.
k.m: One was wrong, and working out which took listening to both.

k.f: “Both sides” is what people say when they haven’t read either.
k.m: It’s what people say when they’ve read both and found each leaving something out.

k.f: A compromise between a good policy and a bad one is half a bad policy. Whether to split the difference depends on what’s being split.
k.m: In a divided country a compromise that sticks beats a good policy repealed in four years. Durability is part of whether a policy is good.

k.f: Half a bridge is a compromise. Ask how it’s working for traffic.
k.m: Half a bridge is a bad compromise. A bridge with a toll neither side wanted is a normal one.

k.f: The compromise position on everything is to do it, but badly.
k.m: Done badly and still in place twenty years later. Check what happened to the pure versions.

t.t: “Extremes on both ends resemble each other”

k.f: The comparison picks out style, such as certainty and anger, and ignores content. What people want to do with power matters more than how loudly they want it.
k.m: The resemblance is in methods: contempt for procedure, an enemy inside, an end that excuses means. Those matter whatever the goal.

k.f: Being very sure is not a political position. Abolitionists were very sure.
k.m: Abolitionists won through elections, courts and an amendment. Sure of the end, moderate in the means.

k.f: Horseshoe theory is how someone who knows nothing about politics explains all of it.
k.m: It explains who ends up attacking the same courts and the same journalists.

k.f: “The people” is never everyone. It’s a part claiming to be the whole, and those outside it become illegitimate by definition.
k.m: When policy tracks the preferences of the top tenth and ignores everyone else’s, “the people” names the rest. The studies say that’s roughly the situation.

k.f: Every populist leader is a millionaire explaining who the real elites are.
k.m: It takes a man with money to say it without being fired. The message doesn’t depend on the messenger’s bank account.

k.f: Populism is the elite’s favorite way of running against the elite.
k.m: When both parties’ donors agree, somebody has to run against the donors.

k.f: Common sense is local and often wrong about systems nobody experiences directly, like trade, epidemics or monetary policy.
k.m: Experts know how. Who pays and who benefits is a question about interests, and the people who pay are the experts on that.

k.f: Common sense is great until the plane needs landing.
k.m: The passengers don’t land the plane. They do get to say where it’s going.

k.f: “I trust regular people over experts,” he says, to his doctor.
k.m: He trusts the doctor on the diagnosis. He decides whether he wants the surgery.

t.t: “A strong leader can express the popular will”

k.f: There’s no single popular will to express, and a leader who claims to embody it has a standing excuse to override courts, press and elections.
k.m: Institutions that have stopped answering to voters sometimes need someone with a mandate to break the logjam. The risk is real, and so is the logjam.

k.f: If he is the will of the people, anyone against him is against the people. It’s a nice trick and it’s the whole trick.
k.m: It’s also how every reform got past people whose job was to block it.

k.f: The voice of the common man always seems to own several homes.
k.m: He owns homes and still says what they’ve been saying at the kitchen table for twenty years.

t.t: “Elites and institutions are rigged against us”

k.f: Sometimes they are, in specific ways that can be shown and fixed. As a blanket claim it can’t be tested, since every counterexample is part of the rigging.
k.m: Specific claims can be tested: who wrote the bill, who got bailed out, who went to prison. Those have answers, and the answers are the argument.

k.f: If everything is rigged, the election he won was too. He never mentions that one.
k.m: He won in spite of it. A rigged game can still be lost by the house now and then.

k.f: The system is rigged, say people the system keeps electing.
k.m: They elect them when the alternative is someone the system preferred.

k.f: Policy turns on values and trade-offs as well as facts. Expertise says what will happen, not which outcome to want.
k.m: Set the goals democratically and hand the means to people who can calculate them. Central banks work that way and nobody wants monetary policy by referendum.

k.f: Experts can say what a tax will do. They can’t say whether to want that. That’s the part with all the fighting.
k.m: The fighting part goes to the voters. The plumbing goes to plumbers.

k.f: Technocracy: rule by the people who were confident about the last crisis.
k.m: And about the one before, which is why it wasn’t worse.

k.f: Framing a choice as technical hides the value judgment inside it and removes it from the people who’ll live with it.
k.m: Many do, once the goal is agreed: how to cut emissions at least cost has an answer. Pretending it’s all values is how nothing gets built.

k.f: “It’s not political, it’s just the optimal solution” is the most political sentence there is.
k.m: Whether to cut emissions is political. How to do it cheapest isn’t, and the second question is most of the work.

k.f: Every technocrat thinks politics is a math problem and voters are the rounding error.
k.m: A rounding error is still counted. It’s better than being ignored for a slogan.

k.f: Experts have their own blind spots and interests, and without accountability to the public nothing corrects them.
k.m: Experts err, and they err less and get checked by other experts. Accountability can run through performance targets as well as elections.

k.f: The experts were informed in 2008. Very informed. They had models.
k.m: The models missed 2008, and the experts stopped it becoming 1929. Compare the two.

k.f: “People are too dumb to vote” is always said by someone who’s sure he’d be on the committee.
k.m: He would be. That’s rather the argument.

k.f: Insulation from voters is also insulation from correction. Agencies drift toward the industries they regulate or toward their own convenience.
k.m: Capture is the known risk, and the fix is design: fixed terms, published reasoning, courts. Elected politicians are captured by donors with none of those.

k.f: An agency nobody can vote out is called a what, in any other context?
k.m: A court. You’re fine with courts.

k.f: Technocrats want government run like a business, by people who’ve never run one.
k.m: They’d settle for it being run like a competent hospital.

t.t: “Positions should go to the most able”

k.f: “Ability” is measured after unequal upbringing, schooling and luck have done their work. The contest ratifies the head start.
k.m: Head starts are an argument for fixing the start. They aren’t an argument for handing the scalpel to someone who can’t operate.

k.f: The most able are, by remarkable coincidence, the children of the last most able.
k.m: And the alternative is the children of the well-connected with no exam at all. That was the previous system.

k.f: Meritocracy is aristocracy with an entrance exam the aristocrats’ kids are tutored for.
k.m: An exam anyone may sit beats a title you have to be born with.

k.f: Luck in genes, family, timing and country accounts for much of any outcome. Effort matters, and the capacity for it is partly inherited too.
k.m: Luck sets the range and effort decides where in it you land. Policy can reward only the part people control, and that’s a reason to reward it.

k.f: Every successful person worked hard. So did the guy who delivers their groceries.
k.m: He did, and the pay gap is the problem being pointed at. That’s an argument about wages.

k.f: “I earned everything I have,” says a man who chose his parents very carefully.
k.m: Nobody earns their parents. What you do with the start is still yours.

k.f: Opportunities are never equal, and one generation’s outcomes are the next one’s starting line.
k.m: It’s a direction, and it’s measurable: how far a parent’s income predicts a child’s. Some countries have cut that in half.

k.f: The race is fair, and some people start at the finish, and their kids start past it.
k.m: So move the start. Nobody’s proposal for fixing the race is to stop timing it.

k.f: Equal opportunity: everyone is free to compete with people who had tutors since age three.
k.m: Free to compete, and in the countries that fund the schools, a lot of them win.

k.f: An elite convinced it earned its place owes nothing to anyone, and tends to read everyone else’s situation as deserved.
k.m: The smugness is real and fixable. Compare the alternatives on results: selection by birth, by party loyalty or by lot.

k.f: The old aristocrats at least knew it was luck.
k.m: The old aristocrats knew it was luck and kept the land anyway.

k.f: The word “meritocracy” was coined in a satire warning against it. They took it as a business plan.
k.m: The author was warning about an elite chosen by test alone. People who read it added other checks.

k.f: Assessing land separately from buildings is hard and contestable, and a full tax would wipe out the savings of ordinary owners who paid market price.
k.m: Assessors already value land separately in several places. And a tax can be phased in over decades, which protects current owners.

k.f: The retiree who bought her house in 1980 is not a feudal lord. The tax can’t tell the difference.
k.m: Phase it in and let her defer the bill until the house is sold. This was worked out long ago.

k.f: Georgists have one idea, and they would like to tell you about it.
k.m: It’s one idea that covers housing, sprawl, speculation and taxes on work. Most movements would like one of those.

t.t: “A single tax on land could fund government”

k.f: Total land rents fall well short of modern public spending. It could be a good tax among several and still not be the only one.
k.m: Fair, the single-tax claim is too strong at today’s budgets. Shifting what we can from wages and buildings onto land is the live proposal.

k.f: The math worked in 1879, when government was a post office and a navy.
k.m: Land values rose along with government. Urban land is now the largest asset class there is.

k.f: The single tax has been the obvious solution to everything since 1879 and has been adopted by nowhere.
k.m: Pittsburgh, Denmark, Singapore, Taiwan and Hong Kong have all used versions. Where it’s been tried it’s hard to get repealed.

t.t: “A land tax has no deadweight loss”

k.f: In theory, if assessed perfectly. In practice, valuation errors and politics bring back the distortions the theory assumes away.
k.m: Imperfect assessment means some error. Every other tax has the error and also discourages work or building. A tax can’t reduce the supply of land.

k.f: “No distortions, assuming perfect assessment.” Assuming perfect anything, every tax is fine.
k.m: Assuming rough anything. A sloppy land tax still can’t make there be less land.

k.f: Economists all agree the land value tax is the best tax, which is how you know it’ll never happen.
k.m: It’ll happen when the people who’d pay it stop being the ones who vote on it.

t.t: “Land speculation is the root of poverty”

k.f: Poverty has many causes. Housing costs matter a great deal in some cities, and that doesn’t make land the master key to the rest.
k.m: He meant it as the reason progress and poverty arrive together: gains in productivity end up in rents. For cities now, the data fit.

k.f: There were poor people before there were landlords. They were called everyone.
k.m: And when the landlords arrived, the ones doing the work started paying to stand on the ground.

k.f: Monopoly was invented to teach Georgism. It’s now a game about loving being the landlord.
k.m: The inventor wrote two sets of rules. The cooperative set is the one that got dropped.

k.f: Democracies have the best record on famine, mass killing by the state and long-run prosperity. The comparison class is what matters.
k.m: The record belongs to rich countries with strong institutions, several of which were built under monarchs. The claim is about where the present trend leads.

k.f: The failed experiment contains every country he’d agree to live in.
k.m: He’d live in the ones still running on capital built up before the franchise widened. That’s the argument.

k.f: Neoreaction: a man with a blog has figured out that kings were good.
k.m: A blog was enough for Luther.

k.f: Companies can fail and be replaced, and nobody is forced to stay. A state run that way has the powers of a CEO and none of the checks.
k.m: The design includes owners who can replace the executive. The proposal is to make government answer to someone with a stake in its long-run value.

k.f: CEOs get fired by boards. He left out the board. Without it that’s just a guy.
k.m: There’s a board in the proposal. People skip the corporate governance section.

k.f: The plan is to run the country like a startup. Nine in ten startups fail, and usually nobody dies.
k.m: A country can’t fail quietly either way. A structure where somebody owns the downside is the point.

t.t: ““The Cathedral” of universities and media runs society”

k.f: The theory treats decentralized agreement among educated people as a ruling body, and can’t be wrong, since dissent within it is also the Cathedral.
k.m: It’s a claim about incentives: nobody coordinates, and the career rewards in universities and press point the same way. That predicts which errors go uncorrected.

k.f: An institution with no leader, no members list and no meetings is called “a lot of people disagreeing with him.”
k.m: A lot of people who disagree with him, who all hire and promote each other.

k.f: The Cathedral controls everything except, somehow, the people writing about the Cathedral for major publications.
k.m: They publish him as a curiosity. Watch what happens to staff who agree.

t.t: “People should exit rather than have a voice”

k.f: Exit is cheap for the mobile and rich and close to impossible for everyone else. A world of exit without voice is a world run for those who can leave.
k.m: Exit disciplines governments the way it disciplines firms. Lowering what it costs to leave is the program, and it would help the poor most.

k.f: “If you don’t like it, leave” is not a political philosophy. It’s a thing dads say.
k.m: “Leave” is how most people have improved their lot. Ask an immigrant.

k.f: Monarchists never picture themselves as the peasant. Not once. Not one of them.
k.m: Most of his ancestors were peasants, like everyone’s. They did better under some kings than others.

k.f: Refusing force against an aggressor leaves the victims to pay for one’s principles. Clean hands purchased with others’ lives isn’t obviously the moral position.
k.m: Most pacifists reject war and killing and accept restraint and defense short of that. And the tradition is full of people who went unarmed into the danger.

k.f: Somebody’s breaking into a house. The pacifist has a position, and the family has a problem.
k.m: The pacifist stands in the doorway. Several are remembered for doing just that.

k.f: Pacifism works as long as someone else isn’t one.
k.m: It also works when enough people are. That’s how most wars have been ended.

k.f: The cases where it worked involved opponents with a press and a public that could be shamed. Against regimes with neither, the record is grim.
k.m: In studies of campaigns over a century, nonviolent ones succeeded about twice as often as violent ones, including against dictatorships.

k.f: It worked on the British, who had newspapers. Ask how it goes without the newspapers.
k.m: It also worked in Poland, the Philippines, Chile and East Germany, against secret police and without the newspapers.

k.f: Gandhi’s advice to those facing the Nazis was nonviolence. He gave it. It’s in print.
k.m: He was wrong about that case. The record across a hundred others isn’t.

k.f: Some wars ended things: slavery in one country, a genocide in another. Others bred more. The record is mixed, and the slogan isn’t.
k.m: The second war grew out of the settlement of the first. The peace that held came from occupation, aid and rebuilding.

k.f: Germany and Japan have been at peace for eighty years. Something bred that.
k.m: Reconstruction bred it. The same countries after the first war got a punitive treaty and twenty years.

k.f: “War never solved anything,” except the ones in all the history books.
k.m: Read on a chapter. Most of them are the opening of the next one.

t.t: “Refusing to fight keeps one’s hands clean”

k.f: Standing aside is also a choice with consequences. The appeal to clean hands puts the pacifist’s purity above the outcome for others.
k.m: Purity isn’t the claim. It’s a refusal to be the one who kills, and someone has to hold that line or nobody does.

k.f: Hands are clean. Everything else is on fire.
k.m: Medics, stretcher-bearers and relief workers were on that fire, unarmed.

k.f: Pacifists are protected by people who aren’t, and are very brave about it.
k.m: A good number were jailed, beaten or shot for it. Brave is right.

t.t: “The answer to bad speech is more speech”

k.f: Lies spread faster than corrections, and some speech works by intimidation, which more speech from its targets doesn’t answer.
k.m: The alternative is an official who decides what’s a lie. That power has been used against the truth at least as often as for it.

k.f: A lie gets around the world while the more-speech is still looking for its keys.
k.m: Slower than the lie and faster than a ministry.

k.f: “The answer to speech is more speech” is said by people with large platforms about people with none.
k.m: Censorship rules are written by people with platforms too. The powerless are who they’ve been used on.

t.t: “Truth wins out in the marketplace of ideas”

k.f: Markets deliver what sells. There’s no reason the true idea should be the popular one, and plenty of history where it wasn’t.
k.m: He never promised quick victory. The claim is that no one can be trusted to pick the winner in advance, and open contest corrects error over time.

k.f: Markets also gave us the pet rock. Whatever’s winning, it’s what people buy.
k.m: The pet rock is gone. That’s the market working.

k.f: The marketplace of ideas has a bestseller list and it is mostly horoscopes.
k.m: And an astronomy shelf nobody had to ban the horoscopes to stock.

k.f: Every legal system restricts fraud, threats, perjury and libel without sliding into tyranny. Lines get drawn and held all the time.
k.m: Those limits are narrow and old, tied to concrete injury. The slope worry is about the new category: opinions restricted for being false or hurtful.

k.f: Fraud is banned. Perjury is banned. The slope has been right there for three hundred years and nobody’s slid.
k.m: The old limits held because they’re tied to a specific injury. The new ones are tied to how someone feels, and that has no edge.

k.f: Free speech absolutists have a list of exceptions. It’s just shorter than yours and they made it.
k.m: A short list fixed in advance is the whole idea. A list that grows by complaint is something else.

k.f: Some speech does more than offend: it targets, excludes and silences. The line between offense and harm is real and less tidy than the slogan.
k.m: Threats and harassment are conduct and already covered. What’s left is being confronted with a view you hate, and that is the cost of living among free people.

k.f: “Words can’t hurt anyone,” he posts, furious about something someone said.
k.m: He’s furious and he’s posting back. That’s the system.

k.f: The loudest defenders of free speech block the most people.
k.m: Blocking is choosing not to listen. That was always allowed.

k.f: At a level that ends poverty the cost is enormous, and at an affordable level it’s too small to live on. Pilots can’t test the financing, since they don’t tax the participants.
k.m: A modest amount paid to everyone, clawed back through the tax system, costs far less than the headline figure. Most people are paying themselves.

k.f: Multiply any real amount by the population. Then look at the budget. Then stop.
k.m: Subtract what the same people pay in tax and the net figure is a fraction of that.

k.f: UBI: every pilot is a success, and every pilot was paid for by somebody else.
k.m: Every pilot of anything is. That’s how you find out before spending the real money.

k.f: Short pilots can’t show what a permanent, universal guarantee would do, since people behave differently when they know it will end.
k.m: Alaska has paid a permanent dividend for forty years and employment there looks like anywhere else. The long experiments show small effects.

k.f: A two-year study where everyone knows it stops in two years. Of course they kept their jobs.
k.m: Alaska’s has run for forty years with no end date. They kept their jobs.

k.f: “People will use the free time to make art.” There’s a lot of evidence about what people do with free time.
k.m: They look after children, study and start businesses. That’s what the data show for the hours given up.

t.t: “It’s simpler and less paternalistic than welfare”

k.f: A flat payment gives the same to people with very different needs. Keeping extra programs for disability and housing brings the complexity back.
k.m: It replaces the cash programs and the forms that go with them. Disability and housing support stay, with one fewer layer of means-testing underneath.

k.f: One check replaces everything, except all the things it can’t replace, which stay.
k.m: It replaces the programs with a caseworker and a waiting list. Those are most of the paperwork.

k.f: It’s the only policy loved by both libertarians and socialists, and each thinks the other hasn’t read it.
k.m: Each has read it and likes a different half. That’s what a coalition is.

k.f: The prediction that machines will end work has been made for two centuries, and employment has kept shifting, not vanishing. It may be different this time, and that isn’t known.
k.m: It may not be needed for that reason. The case stands without the robots: the bargaining power to refuse a bad job is worth having now.

k.f: The robots have been about to take all the jobs since the loom.
k.m: The loom took the weavers’ jobs and their grandchildren did fine. The weavers didn’t.

k.f: Tech executives love UBI. It’s the tip jar for the economy they’re planning.
k.m: A tip jar funded by the people who replaced your job is a start.
